paragraphs: Brief answers to the big questions notes
Interesting things I underlined:
Stephen said he enjoyed the film. He also stated that he thought there should have been more physics and fewer feelings. This is impossible to argue with.
I was brought up by my parents to have an unwavering curiosity and, like my father, to research and try to answer the many questions that science ask us.
The problem is, most people believe that real science is too difficult and complicated for them to understand. But I don’t think this is the case.
When we see the Earth from space, we see ourselves as a whole. We see the unity, and not the divisions. It is such a simple image with a compelling message; one planet, one human race.
I was born exactly 300 years after the death of Galileo.
When you are faced with the possibility of an early death, it makes you realise that there are lots of things you want to do before your life is over.
After my expectations had been reduced to zero, every new day became a bonus, and I began to appreciate everything I did have. While there’s life, there is hope.
As a father, I would try to instils the importance of asking questions, always.
We are all time travellers, journeying together into the future. But let us work together to make that future a place we want to visit.
Be brave, be curious, be determined, overcome the odds. It can be done.
You can say the laws are the work of God, but that is more a definition of God than a proof of his existence.
Physical laws, as well as being unchangeable, are universal. They apply to everything in the universe.
One could define God as the embodiment of the laws of nature.
Asking if God exists is a valid question for science.

The universe was spontaneously created out of nothing, according to the laws of science. These laws may have been decorated by God, but he cannot intervene to break the laws. So the God would have no freedom at all.

To make an universe you only need three ingredients: matter, energy and space. Since we know that basically energy and mass are basically the same thing, two sides of the same coin, you need only two: energy and space.
Space and energy were spontaneously invented in an event we now call Big Bang.
When the Big Bang produced a massive amount of positive energy, it simultaneously produced the same amount of negative energy. Space is a vast store of negative energy.
If the universe adds up to nothing, the you don’t need a God to create it.
What triggered the whole process in the first place? Particles can appear at random, stick around for a while and then vanish again, to reappear somewhere else.

The universe itself could simply have popped into existence without violating the known laws of nature. They tell us that not only could the universe have popped into existence without any existence, and have required nothing in terms of energy, but also that it is possible that nothing caused the Big Bang. Nothing.

At the instant of the Big Bang time itself began. You can’t get to a time before the Big Bang because there was no time before the Big Bang. It doesn’t have a cause, because there was no time for a cause to exist in. This means that there is no possibility of a creator. There is probably no heaven and afterlife either.
If the universe had a beginning, why did it wait an infinite time before it began? If the universe had existed for ever, why did it tae an infinite time to reach the present stage?
Both questions depended on Kant’s assumption that time was absolute.
The universe is expanding, and if galaxies are moving apart, they must have been closer together in the past.
It is difficult to argue with a mathematical theorem.
Physics was needed for the bomb, and it was important that it worked.

There seems to be a certain level of randomness or uncertainty in nature that cannot be removed however good our theories. One cannot accurately predict both the position and the speed of a particle. Einstein objected and his feelings were summed up into: “God does not play dice”.
Maybe the universe has not boundary in space and time.

In M-theory space has ten dimensions, but it is thought that seven of the ten spatial directions are curled up very small, leaving only three directions. It’s like a drinking straw. The surface is two dimensional, but one is curled and from far away it looks like one-dimensional line.

Although the multiple-history idea would allow any number of nearly flat directions, only histories with three flat directions will contain intelligent beings (A two-dimensional animal would have a hard job digesting food, higher dimensions have problem with gravitational formulas).

Some regions of the universe had slightly higher density than others. The gravitational attraction of the entra density can eventually cause it to collapse to form galaxies and starts. We are product of quantum fluctuations in the very early universe.

The appearance of intelligent beings depend on the amount of matter in the universe. If there is more than a certain critical amount, galaxies will start falling towards each other. If it is below a critical amount, galaxies will fly apart forever, all stars will burn out, and the universe will get emptier and emptied, colder and colder.
The total amount disorder, or entropy, in the universe always increases with time.

The order in one body can increase provided that the amount of disorder in its surroundings increases by a greater amount. This is what happens in a living being (ordered form: food, sunlight, electric power -> unordered form: heat).
A living beings has two element: instructions and a mechanism to carry out the instructions. In a living being, those are respectively genes and metabolism.
Computer viruses should count as life. Maybe it says something about human nature that the only form of life we have created so far is purely destructive.
It seems remarkable that the universe is so finely tuned. But if the universe had not been suitable for life we wouldn’t be asking why it is so finely adjusted.

There are two techniques to discover planets around other stars. One is to look at the start and see if the amount of light coming from it is constant or it changes regularly. One is to measure the position of the star accurately, and if a planet is orbiting around the start, it will introduce a small wobble in the position of the star.
People suggested that life came to Earth on rocks, but it’s unlikely that DNA could survive for long in the radiation of space.

If the probability of life developing on a given planet is very small, why did it happen on Earth in about one-fourteenth of the time available? There might be a reasonable probability of RNA being made by chance.

At first, evolution proceeded by natural selection - from random mutations. But in the last 10000 years we have been in an external transmission phase. Information are not transmitted via DNA anymore but with books and other long-lasting forms of storage.
Now no one person can be the master of more than a small corner of human knowledge.
With self-designed evolution we will be able to change and improve your DNA. People will discover how to modify both intelligence and instinct like aggression.

Space warps, travel through extra dimensions. I don’t think these will ever be possible, no matter how intelligent life becomes. If one can travel faster than light, one can also travel back in time. And if that’s the case, one would also expect to have already seen large numbers of tourists from the future.

There ought to be many other starts whose planets have life on them. Some of these stellar systems could have formed five billion years before Earth - so why is the galaxy not crawling with sea-designing mechanical or biological life forms? Why hasn’t the Earth been visited and even colonised? Maybe Earth is the only planet in which life happened. Maybe other forms of life didn’t develop intelligence. Or maybe a collision with asteroids is more likely than we think, we had the lucky chance that no major collision happened in the last sixty-six million years. Or maybe the intelligent life is doomed to destroy itself. Or maybe there are other forms of intelligent life out there that we have overlooked.

Laplace said that if at one time we knew the positions and speeds of all the particles in the universe, then we would be able to calculate their behaviour at any other time in the past or future. However, our ability to predict the future is severely limited by the complexity of the equations, and the fact that they often have a property called chaos. Laplace’s vision cannot be realised. Also because you cannot measure simultaneously both the position and speed of a particle exactly.
Gravity can warp space-time so much that there can be regions of space that we can’t observe.
Whatever you throw in, or however it is formed, black holes look the same.

Although you wouldn’t notice anything in particular as you fell into a black hole, someone watching you from a distance would never see you cross the event horizon. Instead, you would appear to slow down and hover just outside. Your image would get dimmer and dimmer, and redder and redder, until you were effectively lost from sight.
Black hole cannot emit anything, it cannot emit heat.
The antiparticle falling into the black hole can be regarded as a particle coming out of the black hole but travelling backwards in time.

The particles that come out of a black hole seem to be completely random and to bear no relation to what fell in. The information about what fell in is lost, apart from the total amount of mass and the amount of rotation.
If information were really lost in black holes, we wouldn’t be able to predict the future, because a black hole could emit any collection of particles. We can’t be sure of our past either.

Space-time far away from any matter has an infinite collection of symmetries known as supertranslations. This supertranslation might encode some of the information about what is inside the black hole, and then perhaps there is no loss of information.

One can describe the location of an event by four numbers. Three numbers describe the position of the event. The fourth number is the time of the event. This four-dimensional entity is called space-time.
All we need for time travel is a spaceship that will go faster than light.

Gödel was more famous for proving you couldn’t prove everything that is true even in such an apparently simple subject as arithmetic. But what he proved about general relativity allowing time travel really upset Einstein, who had thought it wouldn’t be possible.
Since general relativity can permit time travel, does it allow it in our universe? And if not, why not?
If time travel will be possible in the future, why hasn’t someone come back from the future to tell us how to do it. It could be that such travel can occur only in the future (one-way time travel).
Chronology Protection Conjecture: the laws of physics conspire to prevent time travel on a macroscopic scale.
Rapid space travel and travel back in time can’t be ruled out according to our present understanding.
The Earth is under threat from so many areas that it is difficult for me to be positive. The threats are too big and too numerous.

The Earth is becoming too small for us. Climate change is solvable but so far have not been solved. The danger is that global warming may become self-sustaining. The melting of the Artic and Antarctic ice cap reduces the fraction of solar energy reflected back into space, and so increases temperature further. We have the technology. We just need the political will.
An asteroid collision would be something against which we have no defence.
Nuclear war is still probably the greatest threat to humanity at the present time. It is a danger we have rather forgotten.
We are acting with reckless indifference to our future on planet Earth. I am convinced that humans need to leave Earth. If we stay, we risk being annihilated.
The ultimate theory will place no limit on the complexity of systems that we can produce, and it is in this complexity that I think the most important developments of the next millenium will be.
An asteroid collision and a rise in ocean temperature could make our climate like that of Venus, but with a temperature of 250 Celsius.
I’m not advocating human genetic engineering as a good thing, I’m just saying that it is likely to happen in the next millenniums, whether we want it or not.
DNA will increase its complexity quite rapidly.

If very complicated chemical molecules can operate in humans to make them intelligent, then equally complicated electronic circuits can also make computers act in an intelligent way. And if they are intelligent they can design computers that have even greater complexity and intelligence.
I think the present world order has a future, but it will be very different.
Spreading out into space will completely change the future of human race, and maybe determine whether we have any future at all.
What are the possible sites of a human colony in the solar system? The most obvious is Moon. Mars is the obvious next target.
We must be very careful not to bring back any Martian life. We would have no resistance to it, and it might wipe out life on Earth.
Mercury and Venus are too hot, while Jupiter and Saturn are gas giants with no solid surface. Some of the moons of Jupiter and Saturn might be possible.
With current technology interstellar travel is utterly impractical.

Computers can, in principle, emulate human intelligence, or even better it. Computers are likely to overtake humans in intelligence at some point in the next hundred years. We need to ensure that computers have goals aligned with ours.
Success in creating AI would be the biggest event in human history.
The best time to stop the autonomous-weapons arms race is now.

Whereas the short-term impact of AI depends on who controls it, the long-term impact depends on whether it can be controlled at all. AI would be either the best or the worst thing ever happened to humanity. We should plan ahead.
Perhaps with the tools of this new technological revolution we will even be able to undo some of the damage done to natural world by industrialisation.
The rise of technology pointed to a future where we would all enjoy more leisure time. But in fact the more we can do, the busier we become.
The future of communication is brain-computer interfaces. There are two ways: electrodes on the skull and implants.
Computational power is growing and quantum computing is likely to be realised.
There is already one technique to edit DNA precisely, called CRISPR.
We all have the potential to push the boundaries of what is accepted, to expected, and think big.
This world is an exciting, if precarious, place to be, and we are the pioneers.
Our future is a race between the growing power of our technology and the wisdom with which we use it. Let’s make sure that wisdom wins.
Einstein was undaunted by common sense, the idea that things must be the way they seemed. He had the courage to pursue ideas that seemed absurd to others.
If you know how something works, you can control it.
If you look behind every exceptional person there is an exceptional teacher.

The future of those who are young now will depend more on science and technology than any previous generation’s has done. They need to know about science more than any before them because it is part of their daily lives in an unprecedented way.

Emerging problems: global warming, finding space and resources for the massive increase in the Earth’s human population, rapid extinction of other species, the need to develop renewable energy sources, the degradation of the oceans, deforestation and epidemic diseases, just to name a few.

The huge questions of existence still remain unanswered - how did life begin on Earth? What is consciousness? Is there anyone out there or are we alone in the universe? These are questions for the next generation to work on.
The future of learning and education is the internet.
All young people should be familiar with and confident around scientific subjects, whatever they choose to do.

What world-changing idea, small or big, would you like to see implemented by humanity? I would like to see the development of fusion power to give an unlimited supply of clean energy, and switch to electric cars.
We never really know where the next great scientific discovery will come from, nor who will make it.
Creating innovative and accessible ways to reach out to the widest young audience possible, greatly increases the chances of finding and inspiring the new Einstein. Whenever she might be.

So remember to look up at the stars and not down at your feet. Try to make sense of what you see and wonder about what makes the universe exist. Be curious. And however difficult life may seem, there is always something you can do and succeed at. It matters that you don’t just give up. Unleash your imagination. Shape the future.
Like so many family holidays, mysteriously coincided with an overseas physics conference.

At the age of seventy-five, completely paralysed and able to move only facial muscles, he still got up every day, put on a suit and went to work. He had stuff to do and was not going to let a few trivialities get in his way.
Chaos notes
Definitions, formulas, important concepts (I'll not write all of them, look them up if you need):
Where chaos begins, classical science stops.

"Relativity eliminated the Newtonian illusion of absolute space and time; quantum theory eliminated the Newtonian dream of a controllable measurement process; and chaos eliminates the Laplacian fantasy of deterministic predictability".
As the revolution in chaos runs its course, the best physicist find themselves returning without embarrassment to phenomena on a human scale. They study not just galaxies but clouds.

Tiny differences in input could quickly become overwhelming differences is output - a phenomenon given the name "sensitive dependence on initial conditions". In weather, for example, this translates into what is only half-jokingly known as Butterfly Effect - the notion that a butterfly stirring the air today in Peking can transform storm systems next month in New York.

(What scientific community previously believed) Measurements could never be perfect. Given an approximate knowledge of a system's initial conditions and an understanding of natural law, one can calculate the approximate behavior of the system. Very small influences can be neglected. Small influences don't blow up to have arbitrarily large effects.
Lorenz found out that using purely deterministic system of equations, small errors proved catastrophic.

Any physical system that behaved nonperiodically is unpredictable. If the weather ever did reach a state exactly like the one it had reached before, every gust and cloud the same, then presumably it would repeat itself forever after and the problem of forecasting would become trivial.
A particular kind of fluid motion inspired Lorenz's three equations: the rising of hot gas or liquid, known as convection.
Lorenz attractor: a system that always stayed in certain bounds, never running off the page but never repeating itself, either. All the richness of chaos is there.

Normal science consists largely of mopping-up operations. Experimentalists carry out modified versions of experiments that have been carried out many times before. Under normal conditions the research scientist is not an innovator but a solver of puzzles, and the puzzles upon which he concentrates are just those which he believes can be both stated and solved within the existing scientific tradition. Then there are revolutions. A new science arises out of one that has reached a dead end.
Shallow ideas can be assimilated; ideas that require people to reorganize their picture of the world provoke hostility.
To accept the future, one must renounce much of the past.
Students learned that nonlinear systems were usually unsolvable, which was true, ant that they tended to be exceptions, which was not true.
Disorderly behavior of simple systems acted as a creative process.
Linking topology and dynamical systems is the possibility of using a shape to help visualize the whole range of behaviors of a system. If you can visualize the shape, you can understand the system.
Chaos and instability are not the same at all. Chaos is locally unpredictable, globally stable.
Chaos was too artificial to be useful, still too much a creature of mathematical topology to appeal to physicists.
(Way to create chaos) Difference equations can be used for processes that jump from state to state, taking a starting figure and applying the same function again and again (quadratic map).
x_next = rx(1-x), where x, x_next in [0, 1] and r in [0, 4]
After a certain value of r, chaos starts.
If the population kept bouncing back and forth, ecologists assumed that it was oscillating around some underlying equilibrium. It didn't occur to them that there might be no equilibrium.

Faculty members are familiar with a certain kind of person who looks to the mathematicians like a good physicist and look to the physicist like a good mathematician. Very properly, they do not want that kind of person around.
(Way to create chaos) Take a number, a fraction between zero and one, an double it. Then drop the integer part, the part to the left of the decimal point. Then repeat the process.
Physicists had learned not to see chaos.
Most differential equations cannot be solved at all. If you can write down the solution to a differential equation, then necessarily is not chaotic.
Calling the study of chaos "nonlinear science" is like calling a zoology "the study of nonelephant animals". But people have to know about disorder if they are going to deal with it.

"Period Three Implies Chaos": in any one-dimensional system, if a regular cycle of period three ever appears, then the same system will also display regular cycles of every other length, as well as completely chaotic cycles.

In stock market trend, each particular price change is random and unpredictable. But the sequence of changes is independent of scale: curves for daily price changes and monthly price changes matched perfectly.
Poincaré would say, I know it must be right, so why should I prove it?
A mathematician could take pride in saying that his work explained nothing int the world of science.

Every serious mathematician understands that rigor is the defining strength of the discipline, the steel skeleton without which all would collapse. Rigor is what allows mathematicians to pick up a line of thought that extends over centuries and continue it, with a firm guarantee.

(Way to create fractal) To make a Cantor set, you start with the interval numbers from zero to one, represented by a line segment. Then you remove the middle third. That leaves two segments, and you remove the middle third of each, and so on to infinity. What remains? A dust of point, infinitely many yet infinitely sparse.

"How Long Is the Coast of Britain?" The answer depends on the length of your ruler. Common sense suggest that the estimates will approach some particular final value, the true length. But as the scale of measurement becomes smaller, the measured length of the coastline rises without limit.

Fractional dimension becomes a way of measuring qualities that otherwise have no clear definition: the degree of roughness or brokenness or irregularity in an object. With this definition Mandelbrot created the world fractal.

(Way to create fractal) Koch curve: begin with a triangle with sides of length 1. At the middle of each side, add a new triangle one-third the size, and so on. The length of the boundary is infinity. Yet the area remains less than the aria of a circle drawn around the original triangle. Thus an infinitely long line surrounds a finite area.

(Way to create fractal) Sierpinski carpet: start with a square, divide it three-by-three into nine equal squares, and remove the central one. Then repeat the operation on the eight remaining squares, putting a square hole in the center of each.
Koch curve is more than a line, yet less than a plane. It is greater than one-dimensional, yet less than two-dimensional form
Self-similarity is symmetry across scale. It implies recursion, pattern inside of patter.
Things that could be fractal: earthquake, clouds, hurricane, fluid flow, blood vessels, lungs, urinary collecting system, biliary duct, fibers in the earth.
To Mandelbrot, art that satisfies lacks scale, in the sense that it contains important elements at all sizes.
Suppose you have a perfectly smooth pipe, with a perfectly even source of water, perfectly shielded from vibrations. How can such a flow create something random?
The orbit produced by a chaotic system is an infinitely long line in a finite area. It is a fractal.

Strange attractors seemed fractal, implying that their true dimension was fractional, but no one knew how to measure the dimension or how to apply such a measurement in the context of engineering problems ((written by me) so strange attractors do are fractals?).
Order in chaos. It was the science's older cliché. The idea of hidden unity and common underlying form in nature.

A possible equilibrium for weather is White Earth climate: an earth whose continents are covered by snow and whose oceans are covered by ice. Computer models have such a strong tendency to fall into the White Earth equilibrium that climatologist find themselves wondering why it has never come about.

In the quadratic map, there was an unexpected regularity hidden in the system, the numbers were converging geometrically. The ratio of convergence is 4.669. The most stunning thing is that also different nonlinear systems converged geometrically with the same ratio.
Numbers are to mathematicians what bags of coins are to an investment banker: nominally the stuff of his profession, but actually too gritty and particular to waste time on.

Universality of convergence ratio made the difference between beautiful and useful. But what made universality useful also made it hard for physicist to believe. Universality meant that different systems would behave identically.
One has to look for scaling structures - how do big details relate to little details. The only things that can ever be universal, in a sense, are scaling things.

In the presence of nonlinearity, a perturbation can feed on itself until it dies away and the system returns automatically to a stable state. Libchaber believed that biological systems used their nonlinearity as a defense against noise.
Leaves come in just a few shapes, of all shapes imaginable; and the shape of a leaf is not dictated by its function.
To many, even more convincing than Libchaber's results was a fluid model created by Valter Franceschini of the University of Modena, Italy.

The Mandelbrot Set is the most complex object in mathematics. A numerical description of the set's outline would require an infinity of information. But to send a full description of the set over a transmission line requires just a few doze character of code. The Mandelbrot Set is a kind of public emblem for chaos.

(Way to create fractal) Mandelbrot Set: it is a collection of points. Every point in the complex plane, is either in the set or outside it. One way to define the set is in terms of a test for every point: take the complex number, square it, add the original number, square the result, add the original number; square the result - and so on, over and over again. If the total runs away to infinity, then the point is not in the set. If the total remains finite (it could be trapped in some repeating loop, or it could wander chaotically), then the point is in the set.

Standard geometry takes an equation and asks for the set of numbers that satisfy it. But when a geometer iterates an equation instead of solving it, the equation becomes a process instead of a description, dynamic instead of static.

"In a structured subject, it is known what is known, what is unknown, what people have already tried and doesn't lead anywhere. There you have to work on a problem which is known to be a problem, otherwise you get lost. But a problem which is known to be a problem must be hard, otherwise it would already have been solved."

(Way to create fractal) Chaos game: you choose a starting point somewhere on the paper. You invent two rules, a heads rule and a tails rule. Now you start flipping the coin and marking points, using the heads rule when the coin comes up head and the tails rule when it comes up tails. You will find the chaos game producing not a random field of dots but a shape.

"There's only so much of information in the spore that encodes one fern, so there's a limit to the elaborateness with which a fern could grow. It's not surprising that we can find equivalent succinct information to describe ferns. It would be surprising if it were otherwise."

You would say, 'Where is this random motion coming from? I don't see it in the equations'. It seemed like something for nothing, or something out of nothing. The system is deterministic, but you can't say what it's going to do next.
To Robert Shaw, strange attractors were engines of information. They created unpredictability. They raised entropy. They created information where none existed.
A dripping faucet is not necessarily relentlessly periodic.
Truly random data remains spread out in an undefined mess. But chaos pulls the data into visible shapes.
Universality meant finding properties that were exactly the same in quantifiable ways for everything in the class. Predictable properties.

"The sciences do not try to explain, they hardly even try to interpret, they mainly make models.By a model is meant a mathematical construct which, with the addition of certain verbal interpretations, describes observed phenomena. The justification of such a mathematical construct is solely and precisely that is expected to work." - John Von Neumann
A linear process, given a slight nudge, tends to remain slightly off track. A nonlinear process, given the same nudge, tends to return to its starting point.
Mode locking explains why satellites tend to spin in some whole-number ration of their orbital period.

Before: simple systems behave in simple ways. Complex behavior implies complex causes. Different systems behaves differently. Now all that has changed. Simple systems give rise to complex behavior. Complex systems give raise to simple behavior. The laws of complexity hold universally, caring not at all for the details of a system's constituent atoms.
Sensitive dependence on initial conditions serves not to destroy but to create.

Any pair of snowflakes will experience very different paths. The final flake records the history of all the changing weather conditions it has experienced, and the combinations may as well be infinite.

Clean Code Takeaways
Names should be intention-revealing (can be long names).
Functions should be small (20 lines), do only one thing, and have not too many parameters (3 max). Don’t use flags, if you’re attempted to do so, create two distinct functions.
If you can, rather than comments, create a new function with explanatory name.
You shouldn't have more than two arguments. If you need more informations, wrap some of the arguments into a class.
Files should be short (200 lines).
Use wrappers when dealing with third party libraries, and test those wrapper functions to make sure they behave as intended.
Write tests before the code, minimise the number of asserts per test.
Classes should be small, have one responsibility and little attributes and methods.
Clean code notes
Things I underlined:
Chapter 1: Clean Code
Writing clean code is what you must do in order to call yourself a professional. There is no reasonable excuse for doing anything less than your best.
Because small things matter.
In these days of Scrum and Agile, the focus is on quickly bringing the product to market.
The 5S philosophy:
Seiri, or organization (think "sort" in English). Knowing where things are (naming).
Seiton, or tidiness (think "systematize" in English). A piece of code should be where you expect to find it.
Seiso, or cleaning (think "shine" in English). Keep the workplace free of hanging wires, grease, ...
Seiketsu, or standardization. Consistent coding style and set of practices within the group.
Shutsuke, or discipline (think "self-discipline" in English). Discipline to follow the practices and to frequently reflect on one's work.
You should name a variable using the same care with which you name a first-born child.
Such preoccupation with detail is common to all endeavors of excellence.
Consistent indentation style was one of the most statistically significant indicators of low bug density. Such style distinguishes excellence from mere competence.
Code is anti-evil, and clean code is perhaps divine.

There are two parts to learning craftsmanship: knowledge and work. You must gain the knowledge of principles, patterns, practices, and heuristics that a craftsman knows, and you must also grind that knowledge into your fingers, eyes and gut by working hard and practicing.
Learning to write clean code is hard work. You must sweat over it.
We need better programmers.

We will never get rid of code, because code represents the details of the requirements. At some level those details cannot be ignored or abstracted; they have to be specified. And specifying requirements in such detail that a machine can execute them is programming. Such a specification is code.
The level of abstraction of our languages will continue to increase. The number of domain-specific languages will continue to grow.
We know good code matters because we've had to deal for so long with its lack.
Have you ever been significantly impeded by bad code? We call it wading. We wade through bad code.
We've all said we'd go back and clean it up later. Of course, in those days we didn't know LeBlanc's law: Later equals never.
Spending time keeping your code clean is not just cost effective; it's a matter of professional survival.
So too is unprofessional for programmers to bend to the will of managers who don't understand the risks of making messes.

Conundrum: all developers know messes slow them down, and yet all developers feel the pressure to make messes in order to meet deadlines. The only way to meet deadlines is to keep the code as clean as possible at all times.
Writing clean code is a lot like painting a picture. Being able to recognize clean code from dirty code does not mean that we know how to write clean code.
Clean code does one thing well.
Clean code is pleasing to read.
Bad code tempts the mess to grow! When others change bad code, they tend to make it worse.
Clean code never obscures the designer's intent.
Clean code makes it easy for other people to enhance it.
Code without test, is not clean.
Clean code always looks like it was written by someone who cares. There is nothing obvious that you can do to make it better.
Clean code contains no duplication. When the same thing is done over and over, it's a sign that there is an idea in our mind that is not well represented in the code.
In clean code, each routine turns out to be pretty much what you expected. In beautiful code, it look like the language was made for that problem.
The next time you write a line of code, remember you are an author, writing for readers who will judge your effort.
The code has to be kept clean over time.
"Leave the campground cleaner than you found it"
If we all checked-in our code a little cleaner then when we checked it out, the code simply could not rot.
Chapter 2: Meaningful Names
Names are everywhere in the software.
Use intention-revealing names:

The name of a variable, function, or class, should answer all the big questions. It should tell you why it exists, what it does, and how is used. If a name requires a comment, then the name does not reveal its intent.
The problem is not the simplicity of the code but the implicity of the code.
Avoid disinformation:
Avoid leaving false clues that obscure the meaning of code.
Beware of using names which vary in small ways.
Using inconsistent spellings is disinformation.
Make meaningful distinction:
If name must be different, then they should also mean something different.
Noise or redundant (e.g. variable) words are another meaningless distinction.
Use pronounceable names:
If you can't pronounce them, you can't discuss it without sounding like an idiot.
Use searchable names:
Longer names trump shorter names.
Single-letter names can only be used as local variables inside short methods.
Avoid encodings:
We have enough encodings to deal with without adding more to our burden.
Avoid mental mapping:
So readers don't have to translate your names into other names they already know.
Clarity is king.
Class names:
Should have noun or noun phrase names.
Method names:
Should have verb or verb phrase names.
Don't be cute:
Say what you mean. Mean what you say.
Pick one word per concept
Don't pun
Use solution domain names
Use problem domain names
Add meaningful, but not gratuitous context:
Short names are generally better than longer ones, so long as they're clear. Add no more context to a name than is necessary.
Chapter 3: Functions
Functions should be small:
Functions should hardly ever be 20 lines long.
The blocks within `if`, `else`, `while` and so on should be one line long. The indent level of a function should not be grater then one or two.
Functions should do one thing, they should do it well, they should do it only.
Statements within our functions are all at the same level of abstraction.
We want every function to be followed by those at the next level of abstraction so that we can read the program, descending one level of abstraction at a time.
Don't be afraid to make a name long.

The ideal number of argument for a function is zero (niliadic). Next comes one (monadic), followed closely by two (dyadic). Three arguments (triadic) should be avoided where possible. More than three (polyadic) requires very special justification - and then shouldn't be used anyway.
Arguments should be at the same level of abstractions.
Outputs arguments are harder to understand than input arguments.
Monadic functions can be:
Asking questions about that argument
Operating on that argument, transforming it, and returning it.
(Less common) Using the argument to alter the state of the system.
Flag arguments are ugly. Passing boolean into a function is a truly terrible practice. You should rather split the function into two.
When a function seems to need more than two or three arguments, it is likely that some of those arguments ought to be wrapped into a class of their own.
Side effects are lies. Your function promises to do one thing, but it also does other hidden things.
If a function must change the state of something, have it change the state of its owning object.
Functions should either do something or answering something, but not both.
Prefer exceptions to returning error codes.
Try should be at the be at the beginning, and except at the end of the function.

There should be only one return statement in a function, no break or continue statements in a loop, and never, ever, any goto statements. (If functions are really small, multiple return or break does no harm).
How to write good functions (nobody writes clean functions from the start):
Write a function long and complicated.
Create a suite of unit tests that cover every line.
Refine the code, split out function, change names, eliminate duplication. Shrink methods and reorder them. Always keep the test passing.
Wind up with functions that follow these rules.
Chapter 4: Comments
"Don't comment bad code - rewrite it"
Nothing can be quite so helpful as a well-placed comment.
Comments are, at best, a necessary evil.
Comments are always failures. Because they lie, programmers can't realistically maintain them.
Inaccurate comments are far worse than no comments at all.
If a module is confusing, don't comment it, clean it!
Some comments are necessary or beneficial:
Comments for legal reasons
Informative (even though you better use the name of the function to do that)
Explanation of the intent behind a decision
For clarification or warning of consequences
TODOs (even though they are not an excuse to leave bad code in the system)
Javadocs or docstrings
Amplification
Bad comments:
There just because you feel you should or because the process requires it
Redundant, they take more to read than the code itself
Misleading
Mandated, cause e.g. there is rule that says that every function must have a javadoc or docstring
Noise, stating the obvious and providing no information. We learn to ignore them
Don't use a comment when you can use a function or a variable
Position marker in general are clutter and should be eliminated
Commenting out code, others won't have the courage to delete it. We have source code control system for a reason.
Interesting historical discussion or irrelevant descriptions of details
Javadocs or docstrings in non-public code
Chapter 5: Formatting
When people look under the hood, we want them to be impressed with the neatness, consistency, and attention to detail that they perceive.
You should take care that your code is nicely formatted. If you are working on a team, then the team should agree to a single set of formatting rules and all member should comply.
Code formatting is important.
Small files are usually easier to understand than large files are.
The name, by itself, should be sufficient to tell us whether we are in the right module or not.
Each line represents an expression or a clause, and each group of lines represents a complete thought. Those thoughts should be separated from each other with blank lines.
Lines of code that are tightly related should appear vertically dense.
Concepts that are closely related should be kept vertically close to each other.
Variables should be declared as close to their usage as possible.
Instance variables should be declare at the top of the class, in a very well known place.
If one function calls another, they should be vertically close.
We should strive for to keep our lines short. Beyond 120 characters is probably just careless.
I surround assignment operators and operators with white space to accentuate them.
"I still am an assembly language programmer. You can take the boy away from the metal, but you can't take the metal out of the boy"
Block implementations are implemented one level to the right of their containing block, and so on. Programmers rely heavily on this indentation scheme.

it is sometimes tempting to break the indentation rule for short if or while statements, or short functions. Whenever I have succumbed to this temptation, I have almost always gone back and put the indentation back in.
A team of developers should agree upon a single formatting style, and encode those rules into the code formatter or the IDE and stick with them.
Chapter 6: Objects and Data Structures
The worst option is to blithely add getters and setters.

Procedural code (code using data structures) makes it easy to add new functions without changing the existing data structures (but it's hard to add new data structures because all the functions must change). OO code, on the other hand, makes it easy to add new classes without changing existing functions (but it's hard to add new functions because all the classes must change).
The things that are hard for OO are easy for procedures, and the things that are hard for procedures are easy for OO!
The Law of Demeter says a module should not know about the innards of the object it manipulates. A method f of the class C should only call the methods of these:
C
An object created by f
An object passed as an argument to f
An object held in an instance variable of C
Chains of calls are generally considered to be sloppy style and should be avoided.

In any give system we will sometimes want the flexibility to add new data types, and so we prefer objects for that part of the system. Other times we will want the flexibility to add new behaviors, and so in that part of the system we prefer data types and procedures. Understand these issues without prejudice and choose the approach that is best for the job at hand.
Chapter 7: Error Handling
Error handling is important, but if it obscures logic, it's wrong.
Exceptions define a scope within your program.
Your catch has to leave your program in a consistent state, no matter what happens in the try.
Try to write tests that force exceptions, and then add behavior to your handler to satisfy your tests.
Each exception that you throw should provide enough context to determine the source and location of an error. Create informative error messages.
Wrapping third-party API is a best practice so you minimize your dependencies upon it, make it easier to mock it out for tests, and aren't tied to a particular vendor's API design choices.
Don't return null, return a special case object instead.
Clean code is readable, but it must be also robust.
Chapter 8: Boundaries

There is a natural tension between the provider of an interface and the user of an interface. Providers of third-party packages and frameworks strive for broad applicability so they can work in many environments and appeal to a wide audience. Users, on the other hand, want an interface that is focused on their particular needs.
It might be in our best interest to write tests for the third-party code we use.
Instead of experimenting in our production code, we could write some test to explore our understanding of the third-party code: learning test.
The learning test end up costing nothing. We had to learn the API anyway and they verify that it work the way we expect it to.
Chapter 9: Unit Tests
The three laws of TDD (write unit tests first is taken for granted):
You may not write production code until you have written a failing unit test.
You may not write more of a unit test than is sufficient to fail, and not compiling is failing.
You may not write more production code than is sufficient to pass the current failing test.
Having dirty tests is equivalent to, if not worse than, having no tests. Tests must change as the production code evolves. The dirtier the tests, the harder they are to change.
Test code is just as important as production code.
Readability makes a test clean, and it is perhaps more important in unit test than it is in production code.

The build-operate-check pattern should be made obvious by the structure of the tests, they should be clearly split into three parts. Build up the test data, operate on that data, and check that the operation yielded the expected results. Eliminate annoying details.
The single assert for each test rule is a good guideline, but I'm not afraid to put more than one assert in a test. In general, it ought to be minimized.
We want to test a single concept in each test function. We don't want long test functions that go testing one miscellaneous thing after another.
Rule for test is F.I.R.S.T.:
Fast: they should run fast.
Independent: they should be not depend on each other. One should not set up the condition for the next.
Repeatable: they should be repeatable in any environment.
Self-Validating: they should have a boolean output. Either fail or pass.
Timely: they should be written just before the production code that makes them pass.
Chapter 10: Classes
The first rule of classes is that they should be small. They should have one responsibilities - one reason to change.

The name of the class should describe what responsibilites it fulfills. If we cannot derive a concise name for a class, then it's likely too large. The more ambiguous the class name, the more likely it has too many responsibilities.
We should be able to write a brief description of the class in about 25 words, without using the words "if", "and", "or", or "but".
We should want to have many small classes.
Classes should have a small number of instance variables. Each method should manipulate one or more of those. The more variables a method manipulates the more cohesive that method is to its class.
After refactoring, the program got a lot longer (longer name, more whitespaces).
The class is just a useful scope in which its variables can be declare and kept hidden.
Private method behavior that applies only to a small subset of a class can be a useful heuristic for spotting potential areas for improvement.
Open-Closed Principle, or OCP: Classes should be open for extension but closed for modification.
Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP): classes should depend upon abstractions, not on concrete details.
Chapter 11: Systems
Software systems should separate the startup process, when the application objects are constructed and the dependencies are "wired" together, from the runtime logic that takes over after startup.
If we are diligent about building well-formed and robust systems, we should never let little, convenient idioms lead to modularity breakdown.
Sometimes we need to make the application responsible for when an object gets created.
We can use the abstract factory.
We should implement only today's stories, then refactor and expand the system to implement new stories tomorrow.

Bid Design Up From (BDUF) inhibits adapting to change, due to the psychological resistance to discarding prior effort and because on the way architecture choices influence subsequent thinking about the design.
We can start a software project with a "naively simple" but nicely decoupled architecture, delivering working user stories quickly, then adding more infrastructure as we scale up.
Modularity and separation of concerns make decentralized management and decision making possible.

We all know it is best to give responsibilities to the most qualified person. We often forget that it is also best to postpone decisions until the last possible moment. It lets us make informed choices with the best possible information.
I have seen teams become obsessed with various strongly hyped standards and lose focus on implementing value for their customers.

Domain-Specific Languages (DSLs) are separate, small scripting languages or APIs in standard languages that permit code to be written so that it reads like a structured form of prose that a domain expert might write.
Systems must be clean too.
Whether you are designing systems or individual modules, never forget to use the simplest thing that can possibly work.
Chapter 12: Emergence
Four rules of Simple Design. A design is "simple" if it follows these rules (in order of importance):
Runs all the tests.
Contains no duplication.
Express the intent of the programmer.
Minimizes the number of classes and methods.
If there is no simple way to verify that the system actually works as intended, then all the paper effort is questionable.
Systems that aren't testable aren't verifiable. Systems that cannot be verified should never be deployed.
Writing tests leads to better design.
Duplication is the primary enemy of a well-designed system.
The template method pattern is a common technique for removing higher level duplication.

The majority of the cost of a software is in long-term maintenance. The clearer the author can make the code, the less time others will have to spend understanding it. This will reduce defects and shrink the cost of maintenance.

The most important way to be expressive is to try. All too often we get our code working and then move on to the next problem without giving sufficient thought to making that code easy for the next person to read. Remember, the most likely person to read the code will be you.
Take a little pride in your workmanship. Spend a little time with each of your functions and classes. Take care of what you've created. Care is a precious resource.

In an effort to make our classes and methods small, we might create too many tiny classes and methods. So this rule suggests that we also keep our function and class counts low. High class and method counts are sometimes the result of pointless dogmatism.
Is there a set of simple practices that can replace experience? Clearly not.
Chapter 13: Concurrency
Concurrency is a decoupling strategy. It helps us decouple what gets done from when it gets done.
Structure is not the only motive for adopting concurrency. Some systems have response time and throughput constraints that require hand-coded concurrent solutions.
Common myths and misconceptions:
Concurrency always improves performance: it can sometimes improve performance.
Design does not change when writing concurrent programs: design can be remarkably different.
Understanding concurrency issues is not important when working with a container.
Concurrency incurs some overhead.
Correct concurrency is complex, even for simple problems.
Concurrency bugs aren't usually repeatable.
Concurrency often requires a fundamental change in design strategy.
Recommendation: keep your concurrency-related code separate from other code.
Recommendation: take data encapsulation to heart; severely limit the access of any data that may be shared.
Consider writing your threaded code such that each thread exists in its own world, sharing no data with any other thread.
Recommendation: attempt to partition data into independent subset that can be operated by independent threads.
Recommendation: review the classes available to you

Recommendation: learn basic algorithms (Producer-Consumer, Readers-Writers, Dining Philosophers) and definitions (Bound Resources, Mutual Exclusion, Starvation, Deadlock, Livelock) and understand their solutions.
Recommendation: avoid using more than one method on a shared object.
Recommendation: keep your synchronized sections as small as possible.
Recommendation: think about shut-down early and get it work early. It's going to take longer than you expect and is harder than you think.
Recommendation: write tests that have the potential to expose problems and then run them frequently.
Recommendation: do not ignore system failures as one-offs. Bugs in threaded code might exhibit their symptoms once in a thousand, or a million, executions.
Recommendation: make sure your code works outside of threads.

Recommendation: make your thread-based code so that you can run it in various configurations. Find ways to time performance of your system under different configurations. Allow the number of threads to be easily tuned. Run with more threads than processors or cores.
Recommendation: run your threaded code on all target platforms early and often.
Recommendation: use jiggling strategies to ferret out errors.
Chapter 14: Successive Refinement

I did not simply write this program from beginning to end in its current form, and I am not expecting you to be able to write clean code and elegant programs in one pass. You must first write dirty code and then clean it.
Many different types, all with similar methods - that sounds like a class to me.

Test-Driven Development (TDD): One of the central doctrines of this approach is to keep the system running at all times. I'm not allowed to make a change to the system that beaks that system. Every change I make must keep the system working as it worked before.

So I proceeded to make a large number of very tiny changes. Each change moved the structure of the system, and yet each change kept the system working. To do that I started pushing the behavior down into the derivatives.
The refactoring took me ten steps, passing all the tests after each.
[My note]: Write messy code -> Write tests -> Refactor

Putting things in so that you can take them out again is pretty common in refactoring. The smallness of the steps and the need to keep tests running means that you move things around a lot. There are lots of small steps required to achieve a large goal. Each step enables the next.
Refactoring is a lot like solving a Rubik's cube.
Much of good software design is simply about partitioning - creating appropriate places to put different kinds of code.
Programmers who satisfy themselves with merely working code are behaving unprofessionally.
The solution is to continuously keep your code as clean and simple as it can be. Never let the rot get started.
Chapter 15: JUnit Internals

The code is 100 percent covered. Every line of code, every if statement and for loop, is executed by the tests. This gives me a high degree of confidence that the code works and a high degree of respect for the craftmanship of the authors.
Negatives are slightly harder to understand than positives.
No module is immune from improvement.
Chapter 16: Refactoring SerialDate
It's generally a bad idea for base classes to know about their derivatives.
It is usually a bad idea to pass a flag as an argument to a function, especially when that flag simply selects the format of the output.
Chapter 17: Smells and Heuristics
Long list of things that smell bad to me when I read code:
Comments:
Inappropriate information
Obsolete comment
Redundant comment
Poorly written comment
Commented-out code
Environment:
Build requires more than one step
Tests require more than one step (you should run all your unit tests with just on command)
Functions:
Too many arguments
Output arguments (readers expect arguments to be inputs, not outputs)
Flag arguments (means that it does more than one thing)
Dead functions (methods that are never called should be discarded)
General:
Multiple languages in one source file
Obvious behaviour is unimplemented
Incorrect behaviour at the boundaries (write a test for each boundary condition)
Overridden safeties (don't turn off failing tests)
Duplication (duplication -> missed opportunity for abstraction)
Code at wrong level of abstraction
Base classes depending on their derivatives (base classes shouldn't mention the names of the derivatives)
Too much information (a well-defined interface does not offer very many functions to depend upon, classes should have few attributes, few methods, those should use few variables)
Dead code (code that isn't executed, give it a decent burial)
Vertical separation (variables should be declared close to where they get used)
Inconsistency (principle of least surprise)
Clutter
Artificial coupling
Feature envy (methods of a class should be interested in the variables and functions of the class they belong to, and not the ones of other classes)
Selector arguments (rather split the function)
Obscure intent
Misplaced responsibility
Inappropriate static (are you sure that it'll not behave polymorphically?)
[My note: I think from now on it says what you should do, not what you shouldn't, we pass from smells to heuristics]
Use explanatory variables
Functions name should say what they do (you shouldn't look at the implementation to know what a function is doing)
Understand the algorithm (explore, refactor in a way that it is obvious how it works)
Make logical dependencies physical
Prefer polymorphism to if/else or switch/case
Follow standard conventions
Replace magic numbers with named constants (you should not have a raw number in your code, it applies to any token not self-describing)
Be precise
Structure over convention
Encapsulate conditionals
Avoid negative conditionals
Functions should do one thing
Hidden temporal couplings
Don't be arbitrary
Encapsulate boundary conditions
Functions should descend only one level of abstraction (separating levels of abstractions is one of the hardest thing to do well)
Keep configurable data at high levels
Avoid transitive navigation ("write shy code": modules should know only about their immediate collaborators)
Java:
Avoid long import lists by using wildcards
Don't inherit constants
Constants versus enums
Names:
Choose descriptive names
Choose names at the appropriate level of abstractions
Use standard nomenclature where possible
Unambiguous names
Use long names for long scopes (variables and functions with short names lose their meaning over long distances)
Avoid encodings
Names should describe side-effects (don't hide side-effects with a name, don't use a simple verb to describe a function that does more)
Tests:
Insufficient tests (you should test everything that could possibly break, otherwise they're insufficient)
Use a coverage tool!
Don't skip trivial tests
An ignored test is a question about ambiguity
Test boundary conditions
Exhaustively test near bugs
Patterns of failure are revealing
Test coverage patterns can be revealing
Tests should be fast

Clean code is not written by following a set of rules. You don't become a software craftsman by learning a list of heuristics. Professionalism and craftsmanship come from values that drive disciplines.
Appendix A: Concurrency II
This is a classic example of validating the throughput of a system. This system should complete a seres of client requests in ten seconds.

If the process is I/O bound, then concurrency can increase efficiency. When one part of the system is waiting for I/O, another part can use that wait time to process something else, making more effective use of the available CPU.
Any code that manages threads should do nothing other than thread management.

"return ++lastIdUsed;" becomes eight byte-code instructions. It is possible for the two threads to interleave the execution of these eight instructions the way a card dealer interleaves cards as he shuffles a deck.
We can define an atomic operation as any operation that is uninterruptable.
An intimate understanding of byte-code is not necessary to understand how threads can step on each other.
Some collection classes have individual methods that are thread-safe. However, any operation that involves calling more than one method is not.
Dependencies between methods can break concurrent code.
You have three options:
Tolerate the failure - A bit sloppy
Solve the problem by changing the client: client-base locking - Risky because all programmers who use the server must remember to lick it before using it and unlock when done.

Solve the problem by changing the server, which additionally changes the client: server-based locking - Better performances, reduces possibility of error, enforces a single policy because is in only one place and reduces the scope of the shared variables.
There are four conditions required for a deadlock to occur:
Mutual exclusion
Lock & wait
No preemption
Circular wait
You need to beak one of those to prevent deadlock ([My Note] And then he explains how)
Ideas to test:
Monte Carlo testing: make tests flexible, so they can be tuned. Then run the test over and over, randomly changing the tuning variables.
Run the test on every one of the target deployment platforms. Repeatedly. Continuously.
Run the tests on machine with varying loads.
There are tools that instruments classes to make it more likely that non-thread-safe code fails.
Random notes:
Four step model of habits - cue, craving, response, and reward.
Your outcomes are a lagging measure of your habits.
Plateau of Latent Potential is when you put effort but don't see progress. When you finally break through the Plateau of Latent Potential, people will call it an overnight success.
If you want better results, forget about setting goals. Focus on systems instead.
Goals are good for setting a direction, but systems are best for making progress.
We think we need to change our results, but results are not the problem. What we really need to change are the systems that cause those results.
You do not rise to the level of your goals. You fall to the level of your systems.
Outcomes are about what you get. Processes are about what you do. Identity is about what you believe.
Many people want to change their habits by focusing on what they want to achieve. The alternative is by focusing on who you wish to become.
It's hard to change your habits if you never change the underlying beliefs that led to your past behavior. True behavior change is identity change.
Once your pride gets involved, you’ll fight tooth and nail to maintain your habits.
Your identity emerges out of your habits. Every belief is learned and conditioned through experience.
First, decide who you want to be. Then ask yourself “Who is the type of person that could get the outcome I want?”. Then begin taking small steps to reinforce your desired identity.
Habits are reliable solutions to recurring problems in our environment.
Habit formation is incredibly useful because the conscious mind is the bottleneck of the brain. It can only pay attention to one problem at a time.
The people who don't have their habits handled are often the ones with the least amount of freedom.
The process of building a habit can be divided into four simple steps: cue, craving, response and reward.
The cue triggers a craving, which motivates a response, which provides a reward, which satisfies the craving and becomes associated with the cue.
How to create a good habit: make it obvious (cue), make it attractive (craving), make it easy (response), make it satisfying (reward).
How to break a bad habit: make it invisible (cue), make it unattractive (craving), make it difficult (response), make it unsatisfying (reward).
Point-and-Calling is a safety system designed to reduce mistakes. It raises the level of awareness from a nonconscious habit to a more conscious level.

Habit Scorecard: make a list of your daily habits, and sign whether is a good habit (+), a neutral habit (=) or a bad habit (-). Ask yourself "Does this behavior help me become the type of person I wish to be?”
Habit stacking: identify a current habit you already do each day and then stack your new behavior on top.
Behavior is a function of the Person in their Environment.
Actions we take each day are shaped not by purposeful drive and choice but by the most obvious option.
Creating obvious visual clues can draw your attention toward a desired habit.
Avoid mixing the context of one habit with another. When you start mixing contexts, you’ll start mixing habits (e.g. issue with phone, laptop etc…)
Disciplined people live in a way that does not require heroic willpower and self control, they spend less time in tempting situations.
Bad habits are autocatalytic: the process feeds itself.
You can break a habit, but you're unlikely to forget it.
Self-control is a short-term strategy, not a long-term one. This is the secret of self-control. make the cues of your good habits obvious and the cues of your bad habits invisible.
Dopamine is released not only when you experience pleasure, but also when you anticipate it.
Habit stacking + temptation bundling:
After i [current habit], I will [habit I need]
After [habit I need], I will [habit I want]
Eventually you'll look forward to the habit you need.
Whatever habits are normal in your culture are among the most attractive behaviors you'll find.
We imitate the habits of: the close, the many and the powerful.
Join a culture where your desired behavior is the normal behavior (and possibly where you already have something in common with the group).
We imitate people we envy.
Most days, we'd rather be wrong with the crowd than be right by ourselves.
Motivation ritual - associate your habits with something you enjoy (e.g. concentration goes ul just by putting the headphones, without even having to play music).
Find something that makes you truly happy and then create a short routine that you perform every time before you do the thing you love.
If you want to master a habit, the key is repetition, not perfection.
Create an environment where doing the right thing is as easy as possible.
The greater the friction, the less likely the habit.
When you start a new habit, it should take less than two minutes to do. Scale it down (e.g. “Run three miles” becomes “Tie my running shoes”)
The point is not to do one easy thing, the point is mastering the habit of showing up.
How to make a habit difficult: use a commitment device. A choice you make in the present that controls your actions in the future.
What is immediately rewarded is repeated. What is immediately punished is avoided.
The human brain did not evolve for life in a delayed-return environment. The consequences of bad habits are delayed while the rewards are immediate.
First three laws are to make the habit happen, the fourth is for it to be repeated.
Habit tracking keeps you honest. Most of us have a distorted view of our own behavior. We think we act better than we do.
A simple rule: never miss twice. Missing once is an accident. Missing twice is the start of a new habit.
When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.
A habit contract is a verbal or written agreement in which you state your committments to a particular habit anf the punishment that will occur if you don't follow through.
How to nail the explore/exploit tradeoff: if you are currently winning, exploit. If you are currently losing, explore.
Where you get in the flow zone, that's where you should spend your time on.
Until you work as hard as those you admire, don't explain away their success as luck.

His pet theory: flow state resides on razor's edge between System 1 and System 2, you are using your automatic knowledge, while also working hard to rise to a challenge beyond your ability. Both brain modes are fully engaged. The conscious and nonconscious are working perfectly in sync.
The greatest threat to success is boredom. As soon as we experience the slightest dip in motivation, we begin seeking a new strategy. You have to fall in love with boredom.
Professionals stick to the schedule, amateurs let life get in the way.
When you mastered a habit, you have to use that to try to get to a more difficult or advanced habit.
Avoid making a single aspect of you identify an overwhelming portion of who you are.
You need yo check in to see if your old habits and beliefs are still serving you.
At the end of the book, for each below, find strategy to make them obvious (invisible), attractive (unattractive), easy (difficult) and satisfying (unsatisfying)
For each of these new habits, start with two minutes.
Make visually appealing: e.g. get a year calendar and sign all the weeks you didn't (or did) party.
Create habit contracts (mainly for bad habits) but also rewards for good habits.
Who do you wanna become?
A non-clubber
A non-drugs or alcohol taker
A instagram reels avoider
A writer
A board game designer
A good data scientist
A monogamous boyfriend
A creative person
An athlete
A traveller
A good sleeper
