paragraphs: Write down under what circumstances are you willing to quit. And when. And then stick with it. If you decide in the now you'll probably talk yourself into quitting or make bad decision (e.g. when to quit a marathon, and you're tired while doing it)
Goleman D. - Focus
Notes:
A failure to focus inward leaves you rudderless, a failure to focus on others renders you clueless, and a failure to focus outward may leave you blindsided.

Open awareness, in which we broadly notice what's going on around us without getting caught up in or swept away by any particular thing. In this mode we don't judge, censor, or tune out; we simply perceive.
When your mind wanders, notice that it has wandered, bring it back to your desired point of focus, and keep it there as long as you can.
[Tenacity cool game]
A simple way to shift into posi- tive mode is to ask yourself, "If everything worked out perfectly in my life, what would I be doing in 10 years?”
Statistical analysis showed that a child's level of self-control was a more powerful predictor of financial success than IQ, social class, or family circumstance.
The empathy triad
Cognitive empathy: the ability to understand another person's perspective
Emotional empathy: the ability to feel what someone else feels
Empathic concern: the ability to sense what another person needs from you
Social sensitivity appears to be related to cognitive empathy.
Any business school course on strategy will give you the two main elements: exploitation of your current advantage and exploration for new ones.
When we switch to exploration we have to make a deliberate cognitive effort to disengage from that routine in order to roam widely and pursue fresh paths.
First we prepare our minds by gathering a wide variety of pertinent information and then we alternate between concentrating intently on the problem and letting our minds wander freely.
In a small but significant number of people, a strong systems awareness is coupled with an empathy deficit.

Focused leaders can command the full range of their own attention: They are in touch with their inner feelings, they can control their im- pulses, they are aware of how others see them, they understand what others need from them, and they can weed out distractions and also allow their minds to roam widely, free of preconceptions. This is challenging.

Short-term stress raises cortisol levels (the so-called stress hormone) for short periods and can jump-start our adrenaline and motivate us to perform more efficiently in response to impending deadlines. Long-term stress, however, can lead to prolonged increases in cortisol and can be toxic to the brain. Sci- entists also suspect that high levels of cortisol over a long period of time are a key contributor to Alzheimer's and other forms of dementia.
Strategies to make better choices that keep you focused.
Do a digital detox.
Rest your brain: Commit to the recommended seven to eight hours of sleep.
Practice mindfulness.

Shift your focus to others: If you pay more attention to other people's feelings and needs and show concern for them, you can not only take your mind off of your stress but also reap the benefits of knowing that you're doing something meaningful for someone you care about.
The prime way to deal with distraction is first to be okay with it, which means noticing it.? You notice the distraction, and bring your mind back.
What happens
First, you choose a focus.
Sooner or later, your attention wanders.
Sooner or later, you wake up to the fact that your mind has wandered.
Having woken up, you may choose to return to the original theme.
1 and 4 are conscious choices. Steps 2 and 3 are unconscious.
The very act of notic- ing the distraction, and the structure of distraction will gradually strengthen your ability to stay focused and head off distraction in the first place.
Eight steps to regain focus:
Understand the dangers of multitasking.
Allow for your emotional response. but stay in charge.
Game your attention.
Rely on your values.
Put up boundaries. Once you have more awareness about what distracts you, set rules for yourself.
Choose whom you interact with wisely.
Support and be supported by your colleagues.
Take care of your body.
How to Make Yourself Work When You Just Don't Want To
Reason #1: You are putting something off because you are afraid you'll screw it up
Solution: Adopt a "prevention focus”

When you have a prevention focus, instead of thinking about how you can end up better off, you see the task as a way to hang on to what you already have-- to avoid loss. For the preven- tion focused, successfully completing a project is a way to keep your boss from being angry or thinking less of you.
Reason #2: You are putting something off because you don't feel like doing it
Solution: Make like Spock and ignore your feelings. They're getting in your way.
"Who says you need to wait until you feel like' doing something in order to start doing it?”
Reason #3: You are putting something off because it's hard, boring, or otherwise unpleasant
Solution: Use if-then planning.
If-then plans dramatically reduce the demands placed on your willpower by ensuring that you've made the right decision way ahead of the critical moment.
5 Ways to Focus Your Energy During a Work Crunch:
Accept the situation:
We wish for things to be like they were last month, or we long for the pace we had during vacation. By not being present to the here and drain our energy by ruminating on the situation.
Observe and label your underlying emotions
Preserve your sense of choice and agency
Communicate with your colleagues and loved ones
Renegotiate deadlines.
Set tighter boundaries.
Ask for help and support.
Practice self-compassion
Your Team's Time Management Problem Might Be a Focus Problem.
What leaders do wrong about that:
They create an environment that undermines focus.
All communication, regardless of the subject or source, carries the same level of presumed urgency and is ex- pected to produce an immediate response.
They don't offer clear instruction on which communication channel is appropriate in which situation.
They assign the same workers to receive and solve customer issues.
They don't realize that monitoring internal systems is still work, even if there is rarely an emergency.
Two skills define a mindful mind: focus and awareness
Suggestions:
2 minutes of meditation after you wake up
10 minutes of meditation before starting your day
2 minutes of meditation before you enter a meeting
1 minute of meditation every hour after lunch
10 minute of meditation on your way home
How to activate Default Mode Network (DMN)
Using positive constructive daydreaming (PCD)
Taking a nap
Pretending to be someone else
Haidt J. - The Anxious Generation
Notes:
Play-based childhood:
Embodied
Synchronous
One-to-one or one-to-several
In groups or communities where there is some cost to join or leave so people invest in relationships.
Phone-based childhood:
Disembodied
Asynchronous
One-to-many
Done either alone or in virtual groups that are easy to join and easy to leave.
We made two big mistakes:
Overprotecting children in the real world
Underprotecting children online
Antifragile describe things that actually need to get knocked over now and then in order to become strong (e.g. trees, immune system, and kids)
Risks that children seek out:
Heights
High speed
Dangerous tools
Dangerous elements
Rough-and-tumble play
Disappearing
Risk of minor injuries should be a feature, not a bug, in playground design.
“Concept creep” is the expansion of psychological concepts in two directions: downward (to apply to smaller or more trivial cases) and outward (to encompass new and conceptually unrelated phenomena).
Safetysm is a culture or belief system in which safety has become a sacred value. It trumps everything else, no matter how unlikely or trivial the potential danger.
The human brain contains two subsystem that put it into two common modes:
Discover mode (for approaching opportunities)
Defend mode (for defending against threats)
Differently from animals, children's brains grow to 90% of full size by age 5, and then take a long time to learn culture.
Two experience blockers:
Safetysm
Smarphone
How much stress a kid needs?
“Chronic stress”, meaning it lasts long, is much worse than “acute stress”, meaning it does not last long.
There is an inverted U-shaped pattern in the relationship between stress and well-being.
Rites of passage around the world take the child through the same three phases:
Separation
Transition
Reincorporation
Increased responsibility suggestion:
Age 6: The age of family responsibility (e.g. list of chores and weekly allowance)
Age 8: The age of local freedom (e.g. freedom to play and hang out without adult supervision)
Age 10: The age of roaming (e.g. freedom to roam more widely, and get a flip phone as gift)
Age 12: The age of apprenticeship (e.g. start earning their own money by doing chores for neighbors or relatives)
Age 14: The beginning of high school (e.g. getting first smartphone)
Age 16: The beginning of internet adulthood (e.g. getting a car, open social media accounts)
Age 18: The beginning of legal adulthood (e.g. voting, car in Europe, drink in Europe, signing contracts, separation from childhood)
Age 22: The full legal adulthood (e.g. buy alcohol and cigarettes)
The four foundational harms:
Social deprivation
Sleep deprivation
Attention fragmentation
Addiction
The proliferation of advertising-driven apps caused a change in the nature of time spent using a smartphone.
Features of social media:
User profiles
User-generated content
Networking
Interactivity
“The cost of a thing is the amount of … life which is required to be exchanged for it, immediately or in the long run” - H. D. Thoreau
The Hooked model:
(External or internal) Trigger
Action
Variable Reward
Investment
The universal symptoms of withdrawal from addictive substance are:
Anxiety
Irritability
Insomnia
Dysphoria
Boys are more focused on agency and girls are more focused on communion:
Agency arises from striving to individuate and expand the self and involves quality such as efficiency, competence and assertiveness.
Communion arises from striving to integrate the self in a larger social unit through caring for others and involves qualities such as benevolence, cooperativeness, and empathy.
Reasons why girls are more vulnerable
Girls are more affected by visual social comparison
Girls’ aggression is more relational
Girls more easily share emotions and disorders
Girls are more subject to predation and harassment

“Failure to launch” describe anyone who gets off track, doesn't find employment, and ends up living back with their parents for an indefinite period of time (boys are almost twice as likely to "fail to launch”).
NEET (Not in Euducation, Employment, or Training).
Hikikomori, in Japanese “pulling inward” are modern home hermit.
A world with too much supervision and not enough risk seems to be having a larger impact on boys.
What if teenagers are not doing as much of the bad stuff teenagers used to do not because Gen Z is getting wiser, but because they are withdrawing from the physical world?
It is often said these days that “data is the new oil.” But so is attention.
Two areas that most affect boys:
Pornography
Videogames
Human children and human bodies need to be rooted in human communities.
How phone-based life affect people spiritually by counteracting or blocking:
Shared sacredness
Embodiment
Stillness, silence and focus
Self-transcendence
Being slow to anger, quick to forgive
Finding awe in nature
Collective action problems require collective responses. There are four main types of collective responses:
Voluntary coordination
Social norms and moralization
Technological solutions
Laws and rules
There are three basic imperatives (for business that earn revenue based on ads alongside user-generated content):
Get more users
Get users to spend more time using the app
Get users to post and engage with more content, which attracts other users to the platform
Four ways governments and tech companies could improve the virtual world for adolescents:
Assert a duty of care
Raise the age of internet adulthood to 16
Facilitate age verification
Encourage phone-free schools
What governments can do to incentivize more (and better) real-world experience:
Stop punishing parents for giving children real-world freedom
Encourage more play in school
Design and zone public space with children in mind
More vocational education, apprenticeship, and youth development programs
For parents of young children (0 to 5)
More and better experience in the real world (give them playtime with some age diversity, watch your own phone habits)
Less and better experiences on screens (e.g. interacting with family members via video call could be helpful)
For parents of children (6 to 13)
More and better experience in the real world (e.g. letting them out of our sight without them having a way to reach us (e.g. me buying cigarettes for my grandma))
Less and better experiences online
For parents of teens (13 to 18)
More and better, … (Same as before, but tailored for teens)
[Note] For each of these ages, there is a list of good points about how to behave if you have kids that age
The cure for parental anxiety is exposure
Main suggestions:
No smartphones before high school
No social media before 16
Phone-free schools
Far more unsupervised play and childhood independence

paragraphs: Hands-on machine learning with scikit-learn, keras & tensorflow notes
Everything I underlined:
Chapter 1 - The Machine Learning Landscape
The first ML application that really became mainstream is the spam filter.
Machine learning is the science (and art) of programming computers so they can learn from data.
The examples that the system uses to learn are called the training set. Each training example is called a training instance (or sample). The ratio of correctly classified emails is called accuracy.
Another area where Machine Learning shines is for problems that either are too complex for traditional approaches or have no known algorithm.
Applying ML techniques to dig into large amounts of data can help discover patterns that were not immediately apparent. This is called data mining.
Machine learning is also great for:
Problems for which existing solutions require a lot of fine-tuning or long list of rules.
Fluctuating environments
In supervised learning, the training set you feed to the algorithm includes the desired solutions, called labels.
A typical supervised learning task is classification. Another typical task is to predict a target numeric value, regression.
In unsupervised learning, the training data is unlabeled. Use cases:
Clustering
Anomaly detection and novelty detection

Visualization and dimensionality reduction (it is often a good idea to try to reduce the dimension of your training data using a dimensionality reduction algorithm before you feed it to another Machine Learning algorithm)
Association rule learning
Some algorithms can deal with data that's partially labeled. This is called semisupervised learning.

In Reinforcement Learning an agent can observe the environment, select and perform actions, and get rewards in return (or penalties). It must then learn by itself what is the best strategy, called policy, to get the most reward over time.

In batch learning, the system is incapable of learning incrementally: it must be trained using all the available data. First the system is trained, and then it is launched into production and runs without learning anymore; it just applies what it has learned. It is called offline learning.

In online learning, you train the system incrementally by feeding it data instances sequentially, either individually or in small groups called mini-batches. (online learning can be confusing name, think of it as incremental learning)
Generalizing means having good performances on new instances.
In instance-based learning the system learns the examples by heart, then generalizes to new cases by using similarity measure to compare them to the learned examples (or a subset of them)
Another way to generalize from a set of examples is to build a model of these examples and then use that model to make predictions. This is called model-based learning.
You feed the model your training examples, and it finds the parameters that make it fit the best to your data. This is called training the model.
There are two things that can go wrong: "bad algorithm" and "bad data". In detail you can have:
Insufficient quantity of training data
Nonrepresentative training data (e.g. sample is too small -> sampling noise, sampling method is flawed -> sampling bias)
Poor-quality data (with errors, outliers and noise)
Irrelevant features
Process of feature engineering involves: feature selection and feature extraction.
Overfitting the training data: the model performs well on the training data but it does not generalize well.
Possible solutions: simplify the model, gather more training data, reduce the noise in the training data
Underfitting the training data: the model is too simple to learn the underlying structure of the data.
Possible solutions: select a more powerful model, feed better features, reduce the constraints on the model.

A hyperparameter is a parameter of a learning algorithm, not of the model. AS such, it is not affected by the learning algorithm itself; it must be set prior to training and remains constant during training.
You train your model on the training set, and you test it using the test set. The error rate on new cases is called generalization error.
If the training error is low but the generalization error is high, it means that your model is overfitting.

The validation set is used to train multiple models and select the model that performs best on the validation set. After this you train the best model on the full training set and this gives you the final model. Lastly, you evaluate this final model on the test set to get an estimate of the generalization error.

Cross-validation consists of using many small validation sets. Each model is evaluated once per validation set after it is trained on the rest of the data. By averaging out the evaluations of a model, you get a much more accurate measure of its performance.
Chapter 2 - End-to-End Machine Learning Project
TAKE A LOOK AT MACHINE LEARNING PROJECT CHECKLIST ([Appendix B in the book and my version on Evernote])
A sequence of data processing components is called a data pipeline.
A typical performance measure for regression problems is the Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) (N.B. it gives higher weight for large errors).
Another measure is the Mean Absolute Error (MAE).
RMSE corresponds to the Euclidean norm, while MAE to the Manhattan norm.
When outliers are exponentially rare, the RMSE performs very well and is generally preferred.
You should list and verify the assumptions that have been made so far, by you or others.
If you created a virtualenv, you need to register it to Jupyter and give it a name.
Plot a histogram for each numerical attribute.

Many histograms are tail-heavy: they extend much farther to the right of the median than to the left. This may make it a bit harder for some Machine Learning algorithms to detect patterns. ([My note: should we log those?])
Before you look at the data any further, you need to create a test set, put it aside, and never look at it.

If you look at the test set, you may stumble upon some seemingly interesting pattern in the test data that leads you to select a particular kind of Machine Learning model. When you estimate the generalization error using the test set, you estimate will be too optimistic, and you will launch a system that will not perform as well as expected. This is called data snooping bias.
You will often see people set the random seed to 42. This number has no special property, other than to be the Answer to the Ultimate Question of Life, the Universe and Everything.

We call stratified sample when the population is divided into homogeneous subgroups called strata, and the right number of instances are sampled from each stratum to guarantee that the test set is representative of the overall population (Scikit-Learn's StratifiedShuffleSplit).
Test set generation is often neglected but critical part of a Machine Learning project.
The correlation coefficient only measures linear correlations, it may completely miss out on nonlinear relationships.
To deal with missing features you can:
Get rid of the corresponding rows
Get rid of the corresponding column
Set the values to some value (zero, the mean, the median, etc...) ([My note: inpute])
Scikit-Learn's API is remarkably well designed. These are the main design principles:
Consistency, all objects share a consistent and simple interface:
Estimator
Transformers
Predictors
Inspection
Nonproliferation of classes
Composition
Sensible default (it has reasonable default values for most parameters)
One-hot encoding consists of setting only one attribute to 1 (hot). The new attributes are sometimes called dummy attributes.

If you have a large number of possible categories, you may want to replace the categorical input with useful numerical features related to the categories, like low dimensional vector called embedding.
If you add TransformerMixin as a base class you get the fit_transform method.
If you add BaseEsetimator as a base class you get the get_params and set_params methods.
Min-max scaling (many people call this normalization): values are shifted and rescaled so that they end up ranging from 0 to 1 (you can use MinMaxScaler).
Standardization first subtract the mean value and then it divides by the standard deviation so that the resulting distribution has unit variance (you can use StandardScaler)
Pipeline class help with sequence of transformations.

If you call the pipeline's fit() method, it calls fit_transform sequentially on all transformers, passing the input of each call as the parameter to the next call until it reaches the final estimator, for which it calls the fit() method.
The pipeline's transform() method applies all the transforms to the data in sequence.

If you need a single transformer able to apply the appropriate transformation to each column, use ColumnTransformer (in there, if you specify "drop", the column will be dropped, if you specify "passthrough" the column will be passed untouched).
A great solution is to use Scikit-Learn's K-fold cross-validation feature.

At the beginning you should try out many other models from various categories of Machine Learning algorithms without spending too much time tweaking the hyperparameters. The goals is to shortlist a few promising models.

You should save every model you experiment with so that you can come back easily to any model you want. Make sure you save both the hyperparameters and the trained parameters, as well as the cross-validation scores and perhaps the actual predictions as well.
When you do a grid search, if best values are the maximum values in the grid, you should probably try searching again with higher values; the score may continue to improve (same with minimum values).
RandomizedSearchCV instead of trying out all possible combinations, it evaluates a given number of random combinations by selecting a random value for each hyperparameter at each iteration.

You should look at the specific errors that your system makes, then try to understand why it makes them and what could fix the problem (adding extra features or getting rid of uninformative ones, cleaning up outliers, etc.)

To present your solution document everything, and create nice presentations with clear visualization and easy-to-remember statements like "the median income is the number one predictor of housing prices".
You will need to update your datasets and retrain your model regularly.
You should also make sure you evaluate the model's input data quality.

Make sure you keep backups of every model you create and have the process and tools in place to roll back to a previous model quickly, in case the new model starts failing badly for some reason (backup the datasets too).

You may want to create several subsets of the test set in order to evaluate how well your model performs on specific parts of the data. For example, you may want to have a subset containing only the most recent data, or a test set for specific kinds of inputs.
Try adding a transformer in the preparation pipeline to select only the most important attributes.
Chapter 3 - Classification
If you want more control over the cross-validation, implement it yourself.
from sklearn.base import clone creates a new unfitted estimator with the same hyperparameters.
Accuracy is generally not the preferred performance measure for classifiers, especially when you are dealing with skewed datasets.

cross_val_predict() performs K-fold cross-validation, but instead of returning the evaluation scores, it returns the predictions made on each test fold. This means that you get a "clean" prediction for each instance in the training set.
Each row in a confusion matrix represent an actual class, while each column represents a predicted class.
Precision is true positives divided by true positives plus false positives.
Recall is true positives divided by true positives plus false negatives.
F1 score is a combination of precision and recall.

Increasing precision reduces recall, and vice versa. This is called the precision/recall trade-off. Use precision_recall_curve() to visualize it. (if someone says "Let's reach 99% precision," you should ask, "At what recall?")
The receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve plots the true positive rate (also call recall, tp/(tp+fn)) against the false positive rate (fp/(fp + tn)).
As a metric, area under the curve (AUC) can be used.
You should prefer the PR curve whenever the positive class is rare or when you care more about the false positives than the false negatives. Otherwise, use to ROC curve.
Multiclass classifiers can distinguish between more than two classes.

One way to create a system the can classify the digit images into 10 classes is to train 10 binary classifiers, one for each digit (one-versus-the-rest OvR strategy) or train a binary classifier for every pair of digits (ti distinguish them) (in this case it would be 45 classifiers) (one-versus-one OvO strategy).
Under the hood, Scikit-Learn actually used the OvO strategy, but you can force it to use one or the other with OneVsOneClassifier and OneVsRestClassifier.
When a classifier is trained, it stores the list of target classes in it classes_ attribute.
Analyzing individual errors can also be a good way to gain insights on what your classifier is doing and why it is failing.
A classification system that outputs multiple binary tags is called a multilabel classification system.
Multioutput-multiclass classification it's simply a generalization of multilabel classification where each label can be multiclass.
Chapter 4 - Training Models
A closed form solution is a mathematical equation that gives the result directly.
The pseudoinverse (Moon-Penrose inverse) itself is computed using a standard matrix factorization technique called Singular Value Decomposition.

Gradient Descent is a generic optimization algorithm capable of finding optimal solutions to a wide range of problems. The general idea of Gradient Descent is to tweak parameters iteratively in order to minimize a cost function. It measures the local gradient of the error function with regard to the parameter vector, and it goes in the direction of descending gradient. The size of the steps is determined by the learning rate hyperparameter.

The MSE cost function for a Linear Regression model happens to be a convex function (if you pick any two points on the curve, the line joining them never crosses the curve). This implies that there is just one global minimum and no local minima.
When using Gradient Descent, you should ensure that all features have a similar scale (e.g. using StandardScaler), or else it will take much longer to converge.
Batch gradient descent uses the whole batch of training at every step (terribly slow on very large training sets)
How to set the number of iterations? Set a very large number of iterations but interrupt the algorithm when the norm of the gradient vector becomes smaller than a tiny number.

Stochastic gradient descent picks a random instance in the training set at every step and computes the gradients based only on that single instance (it's faster, huge training set are possible to train, but less regular than Batch gradient descent).
To jump out of local minima one can start with big learning rate and gradually reduce it (learning schedule).
Mini-batch gradient descent: at each step computes the gradients on small random sets of instances called mini-batches. It's a middle ground.
You can use a linear model to fit nonlinear data with Polynomial Regression.
After you add the polynomial features, you can fit a LinearRegression model to this extended training data ([My note: nice approach, I wouldn't have thought about that])
PolynomialFeatures(degree=d) transforms an array containing n features into and array containing (n + d)!/d!n! features.
It's useful to take a look at the learning curves: plots of the model's performance on the training set and the validation set as a function of the training set size (or the training iteration).
If your model is underfitting the training data, adding more training examples will not help.
The Bias/Variance Trade-off:
Bias: part of generalization error due to wrong assumptions. A high-bias model is most likely to underfit the training data.
Variance: part of generalization error due to the model's excessive sensitivity to small variations in the training data. A high-bias model is most likely to overfit the training data.
Irreducible error: part of generalization error due to the noisiness of the data itself.

Increasing a model's complexity will typically increase its variance and reduce its bias. Reducing a model's complexity increases its bias and reduces its variance. This is why it's called a trade-off.

Ridge Regression is Linear Regression with a regularization term equal to alpha times the sum of parameters squared. This forces the learning algorithm to not only fit the data but also keep the model weight as small as possible. Once the model is trained, you want to use the unregularized performance measure to evaluate the model's performance.

It is quite common for the cost function used during training to be different from the performance measure used for testing. A good training cost function should have optimizer-friendly derivatives, while the performance measure used for testing should be as close as possible to the final objective.
Scale the data (e.g. with StandardScaler) before performing RidgeRegression.

Lasso Regression (or Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator Regression) adds a regularization term to the cost function, but it uses the l1 norm of the weight vector instead of half the square of the l2 norm.
It automatically performs feature selection and outputs a sparse model.
To avoid Gradient Descent from bouncing around the optimum at the end when using Lasso, you need to gradually reduce the learning rate during training.
Elastic Net is a middle ground between Ridge Regression and Lasso Regression, mixing the regularization terms.

It's almost always preferable to have at least a little bit of regularization, so generally you should avoid plain Linear Regression. Ridge is a good default, but if you suspect that only a few features are useful, you should prefer Lasso or Elastic Net. In general, Elastic Net is preferred over Lasso.

Early Stopping is a way to regularize iterative learning algorithms such as Gradient Descent, and it consists to stop training as soon as the validation error reaches a minimum. You want to stop when the validation error stops decreasing and starts to go back up (meaning that the model is starting to overfitting).

Logistic Regression is commonly used to estimate the probability that an instance belongs to a particular class. If the estimated probability is greater than 50%, then the model predicts that the instance belongs to that class and otherwise that it does not. It uses the sigmoid function.

The score (before passing through the logistic function) is often called the logit or log-odds, since it is the log of the ratio between the estimated probability for the positive class and the estimated probability for the negative class.
The loss used is the log loss.

There is no known closed-form equation to compute the value of the parameters that minimizes the log loss cost function. But since the function is convex, Gradient Descent is guaranteed to find the global minimum.
Logistic Regression can be regularized using l1 and l2 penalties. Scikit-Learn adds an l2 penalty by default.

The Logistic Regression model can support multiple classes directly, the Softmax Regression, or Multinomial Logostic Regression. It first computes a score for each class, then estimates the probability of each class by applying the softmax function.
It predicts only one class at a time, so it should be used only with mutually exclusive classes.
The cost function is cross entropy.
The cross entropy between two distributions is defined as H(p, q)=-sum(p(x)*log(q(x)))
Kullback-Leiber (KL) divergence is the increase in cross entropy between your assumptions and intrinsic unpredictability.
LogisticRegression uses one-versus-the-rest by default when you train it on more than two classes, but you can set multi_class hyperparameter to "multinomial" to switch it to Softmax Regression.
Chapter 5 - Support Vector Machines

A Support Vector Machine (SVM) is a model capable of performing linear or nonlinear classification, regression and outlier detection well suited for classification of complex small- or medium-sized datasets.
You can think of an SVM classifier as fitting the widest possible street. Instances located on the edge of the street are called support vectors.
SVMs are sensitive to feature scales, so scale the dataset before fitting.

Strictly imposing that all instances must be off the street (hard margin classification) works only if data is separable and it's sensitive to outliers. Better allowing some margin violations, while limiting them (soft margin classification).
Reduce C if the model is overfitting.
For nonlinear datasets you need kernel trick.
To improve grid search you can do first a very coarse grid search, then a finer grid search around the best values found.

For regression you can reverse the objective: instead of trying to fit the largest possible street between two classes while limiting margin violations, SVM Regression tries to fit as many instances as possible on the street while limiting margin violations.
Given a constrained optimization problem, known as the primal problem, it is possible to express a different but closely related problem, called its dual problem.
Under some conditions the dual problem can have the same solution as the primal problem.
In case of the Gaussian RBF kernel, it can be shown that the kernel trick maps each training instance to an infinite-dimensional space.
The function max(0, 1-t) it's called the hinge loss function.
it's possible to implement online kernelized SVMs.
Chapter 6 - Decision Trees

How decision trees make predictions: you start at the root node, and the you evaluate a condition about one of the features. If it's true, you move down to the root's left child, if not on the right. Repeat until you find a node without condition (leaf node), and look at the predicted class for that node.
Decision Trees require very little data preparation. In fact, they don't require feature scaling or centering at all.
A node's samples attribute counts how many training instances it applies to.
A node's gini attribute measure its impurity: a node is "pure" (gini=0) if all training instances it applies to belong to the same class.

Scikit-Learn uses the CART (Classification And Regression Tree) algorithm, which produces only binary trees: nonleaf nodes always have two children. Other algorithms such as ID3 can produce Decision Trees with nodes that have more than two children.

CART works by first splitting the training set into two subsets using a single feature and a threshold, and to choose feature and threshold it searches for the pair that produces the purest subset (weighted by their size). It keep splitting recursively and it stops once it reaches the maximum depth, or it cannot find a split that reduces impurity. There are also other hyperparameters that control stopping conditions (min_sample_split, ...).

Decision trees are intuitive, and their decisions are easy to interpret. Such models are often called white box models. In contrast, Random Forests or neural networks are generally considered black box models.
A Decision Tree can also estimate the probability.
CART is a greedy algorithm, because finding the optimal tree is known to be a NP-Complete problems, and this is why we must settle for a "reasonably good" solution.
Predictions are very fast cause they require traversing the tree from root to leaf.
By default, Gini impurity measure is used, but you can select the entropy impurity measure. They both lead to similar trees, but entropy tends to produce slightly more balanced trees.
Decision Trees make very few assumptions about the training data, and they tend to overfit (such models are called nonparametric models).
To regularize the main lever is the max_depth.
Pruning consists of deleting the unnecessary nodes. A node whose children are all leaf nodes is considered unnecessary if the purity improvements it provides is not statistically significant.
Decision Trees are also capable of performing regression tasks. Instead of predicting a class in each node, it predicts a value.
CART now tries to split the training set in a way that minimizes the MSE.
Decision Trees are very sensitive to small variations in the training data.
Chapter 7 - Ensemble Learning and Random Forests
A group of predictors is called an ensemble; thus, the technique is called Ensemble Learning, and an Ensemble Learning algorithm is called an Ensemble method.

A very simple way to create a good classifier is to train a few classifiers and aggregate the predictions of each of them and predict the class that gets the most votes. Even if each classifier is a weak learner, the ensemble can still be a strong learner.

Ensemble methods work best when the predictors are as independent from one another as possible. One way to get diverse classifiers is to train them using very different algorithms. This increases the chance that they will make very different types of errors, improving the ensemble's accuracy.
You can use VotingClassifier from Scikit-Learn.
Voting can be hard voting (each voter gives a class), or soft voting (each voter gives some probabilities).

Another approach is to use the same training algorithm for every predictor and train them on different random subset of the training set. When sampling is performed with replacement, this method is called bagging. When sampling is performed without replacement, it is called pasting.

Both bagging and pasting allow training instances to be sampled several times across multiple predictors, but only bagging allows training instances to be sampled several times for the same predictor.
Bagging often results in better models.
The aggregation function is typically the statistical mode.
Predictors can all be trained in parallel, so they scale very well.
Bagging -> BaggingClassifier (BaggingRegressor)
Pasting -> BaggingClassifier (BaggingRegressor), bootstrap=False
You can also sample the features, using max_features and bootstrap_features. It's useful when dealing with high-dimensional inputs.

Random Forest is an ensemble of Decision Trees, generally trained via the bagging method, typically with max_samples set tot the size of the training set. Instead of searching for the best feature when splitting a node, it searches for the best feature among a random subset of features.
Extremely Randomized Trees use also random thresholds for each features rather than searching for the best possible threshold (ExtraTreesClassifier).
The BaggingClassifier class remains useful if you want a bag of something other than a Decision Tree.

Scikit-Learn measures a feature's importance by looking at how much the tree nodes that use that feature reduce impurity on average (across all trees in the forest): it is a weighted average, where each node's weight is equal to the number of training samples that are associated with it. (feature_importances_ variable). It's useful to perform feature selection.
Boosting (originally called hypothesis boosting) refers to any Ensemble method for which the general idea is to train predictors sequentially, each trying to correct its predecessor.

In AdaBoost, the algorithm first trains a base classifier (e.g. Decision Tree) and uses it to make predictions on the training set. The algorithm then increases the relative weight of misclassified training instances. Then it trains a second classifier, using the updated weights, and so on. At the end, predictors have different weights depending on their overall accuracy on the weighted training set.
The algorithm stops when the desired number of predictors is reached, or when the perfect solution is found.
Boosting cannot be parallelized.
SVMs are generally not good base predictors for AdaBoost: they are slow and the boosting tend to be unstable with them.
Multiclass AdaBoost in Scikit-Learn is called SAMME.

Gradient Boosting is similar to AdaBoost, but instead of tweaking the instance weights at every iteration like AdaBoost does, this method tries to fit the new predictor to the residual errors made by the previous predictor.
The learning_rate hyperparameter scales the contribution of each tree.
In order to find the optimal number of trees, you can use early stopping.
If you add warm_start=True, Scikit-Learn will keep the existing trees when the fit() method is called.
You can also choose your loss function and subsample parameter.
An optimized version of Gradient Boosting is available in the library XGBoost. It also offers nice features, such as automatic early stopping.
Stacking, or stacked generalization, uses a model (blender or meta learner) to perform the aggregation between other models.
DESlib is a library for stacking.
Chapter 8 - Dimensionality Reduction
The problem of finding a good solution in higher dimensionality space is called curse of dimensionality.
One unintuitive thing that happens in a high-dimensional hypercube is that most points are very close to the border.

It is often possible to reduce the number of features considerably, turning an intractable problem into a tractable one. (Sometimes reducing dimensionality of the training set may filter out some noise and unnecessary details and thus result in higher performance, but in general it won't; it will just speed up training).
Dimensionality reduction is also extremely useful for data visualization.
High-dimensional datasets are at risk of being very sparse. New instance will be far away from any other, making predictions much less reliable.
One solution would be to increase the training size, but the number of training instances required to reach a given density grows exponentially with the number of dimensions.
All training instances lie within a much lower-dimensional subspace of the high-dimensional space
A d-dimension manifold is a part of an n-dimensional space (d < n) that locally resembes a d-dimensional hyperplane.
Modeling the manifold is called Manifold Learning, and relies on the manifold hypothesis: most real-world high-dimensional datasets lie close to a much lower-dimensional manifold.
It is also accompanied by another implicit assumption: the task at hand will be simpler if expressed in the lower-dimensional space of the manifold.
The degrees of freedom available if you try to create a digit image are dramatically lower than the degrees of freedom you would have if you were allowed to generate any image you wanted.

Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is the most popular dimensionality reduction algorithm. It project the dataset into a lower dimension hyperplane, selecting the axes that preserves the maximum amount of variance - the axis that minimizes the mean squared distance between the original dataset and its projection onto that axis (simple idea behind PCA).
PCA assumes that the dataset is centered around the origin (Scikit-Learn's PCA classes take care of centering the data for you).
Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) decompose the training set matrix into the matrix multiplication of three matrices, one on which that contains all the components we are looking for PCA.
Explained variance ratio indicates the proportion of the dataset's variance that lies along each principal component.
To choose the number of dimensions for PCA, choose the number that add up to a sufficiently large portion of the variance (e.g. 95%).
The mean squared distance between the original data and the reconstructed data (compressed and then decompressed) is called the reconstruction error.
Randomized PCA quickly finds an approximation of the first d principal components (if some conditions are met, Scikit-Learn uses this automatically).
Incremental PCA (IPCA) allow you to split the training set into mini-batches and feed the algorithm one mini-batch at a time.
NumPy's memmap allows you to manipulate a large array stored in a binary file on disk as if it were entirely in memory.
Kernel PCA (kPCA) applies kernel trick to PCA, making it possible to perform complex nonlinear projections for dimensionality reduction.

You can use grid search to select the kernels and hyperparameters that lead to the best performance. If you feed a pipeline to GridSearchCV, you can still select parameters for different steps of the pipeline.
With kPCA is harder to reconstruct.

Locally Linear Embedding (LLE) is another powerful nonlinear dimensionality reduction (NLDR) technique. It is a Manifold Learning technique and works by first measuring how each training instance linearly relates to its closest neighbors and the looking for a low-dimensional representation of the training set where these local relationships are best preserved.
Other dimensionality reduction techniques:
Random Projections: projects the data to a lower-dimensional space using random linear projections.
Multidimensional Scaling: reduces dimensionality while trying to preserve the distances between the instances.
Isomap: creates a graph by connecting each instance to its nearest neighbors, the reduces dimensionality while trying to preserve the geodesic distances between the instances.
t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbot Embedding (t-SNE): reduces dimensionality while trying to keep similar instances close and dissimilar instances apart.

Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA): is a classificaiton algorithm, but during training it learns the most discriminative axes between the classes, and these axes can be used to define a hyperplane onto which to project the data.
Chapter 9 - Unsupervised Learning Techniques
The vast majority of data is unlabeled.
Unsupervised learning tasks:
Clustering: group similar instances together into clusters.
Anomaly detection: learn what "normal" data looks like, and then use that to detect abnormal instances.
Density estimation: estimate the probability density function of the random process that generated the dataset.
Clustering can be used:
For customer segmentation
For data analysis
As a dimensionality reduction technique (new features are the affinity of each row with each cluster)
For anomaly detection
For semi-supervised learning
For search engines
To segment an image

The K-Means algorithm starts by placing the centroids randomly, assign each point to the cluster whose centroid is closest, replace each centroid with the mean of the point of its cluster, and continue this way until the centroids stop moving.
It does not behave well when the blobs have very different diameters, sizes, densities or nonspherical shapes. Also, you have to specify at the beginning how many clusters you want.
By hard clustering you assign each point to a cluster, by soft clustering you give each instance a score per cluster (can also be dimensionality reduction technique).
In Scikit-Learn, you can init the centroids with the points you know if you happen to know approximately where they are.

To get better results, you can run K-Means multiple times with different random initialization and keep the one with lowest inertia, mean squared distance between each instance and its closest centroid.
Scikit-Learn's score respect Scikit-Learn's "greater is better" rule.
K-Means++ has smarter initialization, and it's default in Scikit-Learn.
You can also train K-Means in mini-batches with MiniBatchKMeans.
Inertia keep decreasing as we increase number of clusters. As number of cluster, you can take the point where the #clusters-inertia graph make an "elbow".
Silhouette coefficient can also be used, it doesn't always decrease with number of clusters.

Image segmentation is the task of partitioning an image into multiple segments. In semantic segmentation, all pixels that are part of the same object type get assigned to the same segment. In instance segmentation, all pixels that are part of the same individual object are assigned to the same segment (to achieve state of the art to these, you need convolutional neural networks). Color segmentation will assign pixel the same segment if they have similar color.

For semi-supervised learning, you can cluster the training set into some clusters and find the instances closest to the centroids (representative instances). If you manually label those, you can propagate the labels to all the other instances in the same cluster (or at least the x% closest to the centroid) (label propagation).
To continue improving you model you can do few round of active learning, using a technique like uncertainty sampling:
Train on the instances gathered so far
Ask the human expert to label the instances for which the model is most uncertain
Iterate this process
DBSCAN defines clusters as continuous regions of high density:
For each instance, the algorithm counts how many instances are located within a small distance (neighborhood)
If an instance has at least min_sample instances in its neighborhood it is considered a core instance.
All instances in the neighborhood of a core instance belong to the same cluster. This may include other core instances, therefore a long sequence of neighboring core instances forms a single cluster.
Any instance that is not a core instance and does not have one in its neighborhood is considered an anomaly.
Other clustering algorithms:
Agglomerative clustering: hierarchy of clusters built from the bottom up.
BIRCH (Balanced Iterative Reducing and Clustering using Hierarchies): designed specifically for very large datasets.
Mean-shift
Affinity propagation
Spectral clustering: takes a similarity matrix between instances and creates a low-dimensional embedding from it, and then uses another clustering algorithm in this low-dimensional space.

A Gaussian mixture model (GMM) is a probabilistic model that assumes that the instances were generated from a mixture of several Gaussian distributions whose parameters are unknown (GaussianMixture class).
To solve this, Expectation Maximization (EM) algorithm is used. It's like K-Means, but with soft assignments. ([if you want more details, go to the book]).

For this reason, you might need to run it several times with different initialization. You can also reduce the difficulty of the task by limiting the range of shapes and orientations the clusters can have (imposing constraints on the covariance matrix).
A Gaussian mixture model is a generative model, meaning you can sample new instance from it. You can also estimate the density of the model at any given location.

Anomaly detection (or outlier detection) is the task of detecting instances that deviate strongly from the norm. These instances are called anomalies, or outliers, while the normal instances are called inliers.
Using a gaussian mixture model, any instance located in a low-density region can be considered an anomaly.
Novelty detection differs from anomaly detection in that the algorithm is assumed to be trained on a "clean" dataset, uncontaminated by outliers.
If you have too many outliers some of them might be considered normal. To avoid that you can fit, filter and refit.
You can find the model that minimizes a theoretical information criterion, such as Bayesian information criterion (BIC) or the Akaike information criterion (AIC).

Probability is used to describe how plausible a future outcome is, while likelihood is used to describe how plausible a particular set of parameter values are, after the outcome is known. (likelihood function is not probability distribution).
Given a dataset, a common task is to try to estimate the most likely values for the model parameters.
BayesianGaussianMixture class is capable of giving weights equal or close to zero to unnecessary clusters (you can set a high number of cluesters).
Other algorithms for anomaly and novelty detection:
PCA (and other dimensionality reduction techniques with an inverse_transform() method)
Fast-MCD (minimum covariance determinant): assume inliers generated from a single Gaussian distribution.
Isolation Forest: works well in high-dimensional datasets. Builds a Random Forest picking features and threshold randomly. Anomalies tend to get isolated in fewer steps than normal instances.
Local Outlier Factor (LOF): compares the density of instances around a given instance to the density around its neighbors. An anomaly is often more isolated.

One-class SVM: better suited for anomaly detection, but doesn't scale to large datasets. It maps all the instances to a high-dimensional space and find a small region that encompasses all the instances.
Chapter 10 - Introduction to Artificial Neural Networks with Keras
Artificial neural networks (ANNs) are Machine Learning models inspired by the networks of biological neurons found in our brains.
Reason for renew interest in ANNs:
Huge quantity of data
Increase in computing power
Training algorithms have improved
Some theoretical limitations (stuck in local optima) have turn out to be begnign
Seem to have entered a virtuous circle of funding and progress

The Perceptron is one of the simplest ANN architectures. It is based on a threshold logic unit (TLU), for which the inputs and outputs are numbers and each input connection is associated with a weight. The TLU computes a weighted sum of its inputs and then applies a step function that sum and outputs the result.
Training it means find the right value for its weights.
A Perceptron is composed of a single layer of TLUs. When all the neurons in a layer are connected to every neuron in the previous layer, the layer is called fully connected layer, or a dense layer.
"Cells that fire together, wire together"
By stacking multiple layers of Perceptrons we get a Multilayer Perceptron (MLP).
It is composed by one input layer, one or more layers called hidden layers, and one final layer called the output layer.
Since the signal flows only in one direction, it's called a feedforward neural network (FNN).
When an ANN contains a deep stack of hidden layers, it is called a deep neural network (DNN).

To train a MLP we use the backpropagation algorithm. In just two passes the algorithm compute the gradient of the network's error with regard to every single model parameter. To do that, first makes a prediction (forward pass) and measures the error, then goes through each layer in reverse to measure the error contribution from each connection (reverse pass).
Once it has these gradients, it just performs a regular Gradient Descent step to tweak the connection weights to reduce the error, and the whole process is repeated until converges to the solution.
The algorithm handles one mini-batch at a time, and it goes through the full training set multiple times. Each pass is called epoch.
The idea is to propagate the error gradient backward through the network.
It is important to initialize all the hidden layers' connection weights randomly.
Step functions contain to gradient so instead could be used:
Logistic (sigmoid) function
Hyperbolic tangent function
The Rectified Linear Unit function: ReLU(z) = max(0, z) (nice thing: it has no maximum value)
We need activation functions because otherwise if you chain several linear transformation you get a linear transformation.
A large enough DNN with nonlinear activations can theoretically approximate any continuous function.
To use MLPs for regression, just do not use any activation function for the output neurons. As loss, typically you'll use mean squared error.
Huber loss is quadratic when the error is smaller than a threshold (typically 1) but linear when the error is larger than the threshold.
To use MLPs for binary (or multilabel binary) classification, you just need a single (or number of labels for multilabel) output neuron using the logistic activation function.

To use MLPs for multiclass calssification (multiple classes, but only one can be active at a time), you need to have one output neuron per class, and use the softmax activation function for the whole output layer.
Keras is a high-level Deep Learning API that allows you to easily build, train, evaluate, and execute all sorts of neural networks.
Once you know Keras, it is not difficult to switch to PyTorch.
Healthy competition is beneficial to everyone.
The Sequential API is used for neural networks that are just composed of a single stack of layers connected sequentially.
Code examples documented on keras.io will work fin with tf.keras, but you need to change imports.
Dense layers often have a lot of parameters. That gives them a lot of flexibility at the risk of overfitting.
Biases were initialized to zero, which is fine.
kernel_initializer or bias_initializer to change initialization method.
If you know ht input shape when creating the model, it is best to specify it.

If the training set was very skewed, it would be useful to set the class_weight argument. Per instance weights could be useful if some instances were labeled by experts while others were labeled using crowdsurcing platform.
The validation error is computed at the end of each epoch, while the training error is computed using a running mean during each epoch.

To tune hyperparameters: first check the learning rate. Then try another optimizer. If that doesn't work too, try chaning the number of layers, the number of neurons per layer, and the types of activation functions. Also batch size can be changed.
The Functional API is provided by Keras for more complex topologies.
When we build the model we are just telling Keras how it should connect the layers together; no actual data is being processed yet.
You should name at least the most important layers, especially when the model gets a bit complex.
You can have multiple outputs for:
Multitask classification
As regularization technique (adding some auxiliary outputs to ensure the underlying part of the network learns something useful on its own.
If we pass a single loss, Keras will assume that the same loss must be used for all outputs.

Both the Sequential API and the Functional API are declarative: you start by declaring which layers you want to use and how they should be connected, and only then can you start feeding the model some data for training or inference.
Keras will use the HDF5 format to save both the model's archtecture and the values of all the model parameters for every layer (it also saves the optimizer).

The fit() method accepts a callbacks argument thta lets you specify a list of objects that Keras will call at the start and end of training, at the start and end of each epoch, and even before and after processing each batch.
ModelCheckpoint saves checkpoints of your model.
You can implement all sorts of callbacks (pag. 316).
TensorBoard is a great interactive visualization tool.
You must modify your program so that it ouputs the data you want to visualize to special binary log files called event files. Each binary data record is called a summary.
The flexibility of Neural Networks is also one of their drawback: there are many hyperparameters to tune.
To use GridSearchCV you need to wrap our Keras model in objects that mimic regular Scikit-Learn estimators (example pag. 320).
It is good practice to provide reasonable defaults to as many hyperparameters as you can.

Assist the search process manually: first run a quick random search using wide ranges of hyperparameter values, then run another search using smaller ranges of values centered on the best ones found during the first one, and so on.
There are techniques that explore the search space much more efficiently than randomly:
Hyperopt
Hyperas, kopt or Talos
Keras Tuner
Scikit-Optimize
Spearmint
Hyperband
Sklearn-Deap
Many companies offer services for hyperparameter optimization.
Evolutionary algorithms might make a comeback.
Deep networks can model complex functions using exponentially fewer neurons than shallow nets.
Neural Networks Suggestions:
The number of neurons in the input and output layers is determined by your task.

As for hidden layers, it used to be common to size them to form a pyramid. It has been proved that using the same number of neurons in all hidden layers performs just as well (and has only one hyperparameter to tune).
It's often simpler and more efficient to pick a model with more layers and neurons than you actually need, then use early stopping and other regularization techniques to prevent it from overfitting.
In general you will get more bang for your buck by increasing the number of layers instead the number of neurons per layer.
LeCun tweeted "Friends don't let friends use mini-batches larger than 32". Large sizes often lead to training instablilities.

Chapter 11 - Training Deep Neural Networks
It's called vanishing gradients problem when the gradients gets very little in the first layers, it's called exploding gradients when they get very big.
How to alleviate these problems:
Using Xavier initialization or Glorot initialization, that try to keep the variance of the output of each layer equal to the variance of its input.

Using LeakyReLU (LeakyReLU_a(z) = max(az, z), where a is typically 0.01) to avoid dying ReLUs (which outputs only 0s). Other similar activation functions are Randomized Leaky ReLU or Parametric Leaky ReLU.
Other activations which address the same problem are Exponential Linear Unit (ELU) and Scaled ELU (SELU).

Using Batch Normalization (to keep variance output and input equal even while training). It adds an operation in the model just before or after the activation function which zero-centers and normalizes each input (over the current mini-batch), then scales and shifts the result using two new parameter vectors per layer (one for scaling and one for shifting).
At test time (we have no mini-batches) to zero-center and scale, it uses a moving average computed while training.
It acts also as regularizer, but it adds some complexity to the model and slow it down in inference.
Gradient Clipping is to clip the gradients during backpropagation so that they never exceed some threshold. (You can do it by value or by norm)
Wall time is the time measured by the clock on your wall (e.g. with Batch Norm the wall time will be less, beacuse each epoch takes more but the model converges much faster).

If you ever need to write a custom layer, and it must behave differently during training and testing, add a training argument tot the call() method and use this argument int he method to decide what to compute.

Transfer Learning: instead of randomly initializing the weights and biases of the first few layers of the new neural network, you can initialize them to the values of the weights and biases of the lower layers of the first (pretrained) network.
You might need to resize the input.
The more similar the tasks are, the more layers you want to reuse. The more data you have , the more layers you can unfreeze.
It doesn't work very well with small dense networks and works best with deep convolutional neural networks.
Unsupervised pretraining consists in train an unsupervised model (autoencoder or GAN) and reuse the lower layers and add the output layer for your task on top.
I "tortured the data until it confesses": tried many configurations until I found one that demonstrated a strong improvement. You shouldn't do that.
For natural landuage processing (NLP) applications, you can download a corpus of millions of text documents and automatically generate labeled data from it.
Self-supervised learning is when you automatically generate the labels from the data itself, then you train a model on the resulting "labeled" dataset using supervised learning techniques.
Momentum optimization is helpful in plateaus. It will start out slowly, but it will quickly pick up momentum until it eventually reaches terminal velocity.
The Nesterov Accelerated Gradient measures the gradient of the cost function not at the local position but slightly ahead in the direction of the momentum.

The AdaGrad algorithm scales down the gradient vector along the steepest dimensions. It decays the learning rate, but it does so faster for steep dimensions than for dimensions with gentler slopes. This is called adaptive learning rate. You should not use it to train deep neural networks.

The RMSProp algorithm fixes the risk of slowing down of AdaGrad by accumulating only the gradients from the most recent algorithms. (Fun Fact: Geoffrey Hinton and Tijmen Tieleman did not write a paper to describe the algorithm, so researches oftern cites "slide 29 in lecture 6" in their papers).
Adam, which stands for adaptive moment estimation, combines the ideas of momentum optimization and RMSProp. (Default parameters are usually momentum decay beta1=0.9 and scaling decay beta2=0.999).
Two vairants worth naming:
AdaMax
Nadam (Adam + Nesterov trick)
When you are disappointed by your model's performance, try using plain Nesterov Acceleration Gradient instead: your dataset may just be allergic to adaptive gradients.

You can start with a large learning rate and then reduce it once training stops making fast progress, or you can start low, increase and drop it again. These strategies are called learning schedules. They can considerably speed up convergence, so give them a try!
They cant be:
Power scheduling
Exponential scheduling
Piecewise contstant scheduling
Performance scheduling
Icycle scheduling (increasing and decreasing cyclically)
Some info about implementation of learnign schedules (p.363).
You can use l2 reglarization to constrain a neural network's connection weights and/or l1 if you want a sparse model.
If you find yourself repeating a lot the same arguments you can refactor your code to use look or use functools.partial().
Dropout: at every training step, every neuron (including input, but ont outputs) has a probability p of being temporarily "dropped out", meaning entirely ignored during this training step.
Even state-of-the-art neural networks get a 1-2% accuracy boost simply by using dropout.
It's surprising that this destructive technique works at all. Turns out that the model becomes much more resiliten, you get a much more robust network that generalizes better.
A unique neural network is generated at each training step, and the resulting neural network can be seen as an averaging ensemble of all these smaller neural networks.
N.B.: We need to muliply each input connection wight by the keep probability (1-p) after training or divide each neuron's output by the keep probability during training.
Many state-of-the-art architectures only use dropout after the last hidden layer.

Monte Carlo (MC) Dropout averages over multiple predictions with dropout on to get an estimate that is generally more reliable than the result of a single prediction with dropout off. It is a fantastic techinque.
Max-Norm Regularization: for each neuron, it constrains the weights of the incoming conntection.

tf.Tensor

Ingesting a large dataset and preprocessing it efficiently can be tricky, but TensorFlow makes it easy thanks to the Data API (will take care of multithreading, queuing, batching, and prefetching).
It revolves around the concept of Dataset, a sequence of data items.
Transformations get and return datasets, so can be chained.

By calling prefetch(1) we are creating a dataset that will do its best to always be one batch ahead. While your training algorithm is working on one batch, the dataset will already be working in parallel on getting the next batch ready.
You can also cache the dataset.
Now we can build and train Keras model using these datasets.
If you're happy with CSV files, you do not have to use TFRecords, which is the preferred format for storing large amounts of data and reading it efficiently.
Protocol buffers (protobufs) are used as binary format.
Preparing your data for a neural network require converting all features into numerical features, generally normalizing them, and more.
You can implement standardization using a Lambda layer (there is also a Normalization layer from contribution).
We need also to encode features.
The more unknown categories you expect to find during training, the more oov (out-of-vocabulary) buckets you should use (not enough oov buckets -> collisions).
If the number of categories is lower than 10, then one-hot-encoding is the way to go. If the number is grater than 50, embeddings are usually preferable. In between, you may want to experiment.
An embedding is a trainable dense vector that represents a category.
Training tends to make embeddings useful representations of the categories (representation learning).
Word embeddings are embeddings of individual words (you better use pretrained ones).
They trained on a huge corpus and they found that synonyms and semantically relate words had very close embeddings. They were also organized along meaningful axes in the embedding space.
Sometimes they capture the worst biases.
There is an Embeddings layer in Keras.
The TensorFlow team is working on providing a set of standard Keras preprocessing layers (e.g. Discretization).
Term-Frequency Inverse-Document-Frequency (TF-IDF) computes the ration of training instance in which the word appears, and multiply the word count by the log of the inverse of that ratio.
During training you might want to preprocess data beforehand, otherwise you would redo it every epoch.
Tensorflow Datasets project makes it very easy to download common datasets.
Chapter 14 - Deep Computer Vision Using Convolutional Neural Networks
Many neurons in the visual cortex have a small local receptive field, meaning they react only to visual stimuli located in a limited region of the visual field.

The most important building block of a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) is the convolutional layer: neurons in the first convolutional layer are not connected to every single pixel in the input image but only pixels in their receptive field. (keras.layer.Conv2D).

In order for a layer to have the same height and width as the previous layer, it is common to add zeros around the inputs (zero padding). The shift form one receptive field to the next is called stride.

A neuron's weights can be represented as a small image the size of the receptive field called filter. A convolutional layer has multiple filters and outputs one feature map per filter, so it is more accurately represented in 3D.

Convolutional layers require a huge amount of RAM. If you get OOM, try reducing the mini-batch size. Alternatively, you can reduce the dimensionality using stride or removing a few layers. Or you can use 16-bit float instead of 32-bit float. Or distribute the CNN across multiple devices.

Pooling layers are used to subsample. They have no weights, all it does is aggregate the inputs using an aggregation function (usually working on every channel independently, so the depth don't change (but you could also pool depth, but is not common)). An example is max pooling layer, which also introduces some level of invariance to small translations (also small amount of rotational invariance). It is obviously very destructive.
There is also average pooling layer, but max usually performs better.

Typical CNN architecture stack a few convolutional layers, then a pooling layer, than another few convolutional layers, then pooling and so on. The image gets smaller and smaller and deeper and deeper (more feature maps). At the top of the stack, a regular feedforward neural network is added, and the final layer outputs the prediction.

One common mistake is to use convolution kernels that are too large (usually they should be 3x3). One exception is for the first convolutional layer: it can typically have large kernel (e.g. 5x5) usually with stride 2 or more to reduce spatial dimension of the image without losing too much information.

Data augmentation artificially increases the size of the training set by generating many realistic variants of each training instance. You can slightly shift, rotate, flip, and resize every picture in the training set by various amount and add the resulting pictures to the training set. This teaches the model to be more tolerant to those transformation.

Residual Networks: use skip connections (also called shortcut connections): the signal feeding into a layer is also added to the output of a layer located a bit higher in the stack (residual learning).

Separable convolutional layers use fewer parameters, less memory, and fewer computations than regular convolutional layers, and in general they even perform better, so you should consider using them by default (except in layers with few channels).

Squeeze-and-Excitation Network (SENet): an SE block analyzes the output of the unit it is attached to, focusing only on the depth dimension and it learns which features are usually most active together. It then uses this information to recalibrate the feature maps.
Pretrained networks are readily available with a single line of code in the kers.applications package.
After training the top layer, accuracy will stop making progress -> Unfreeze lower ones, but lower learning rate.
One of the hardest and most costly parts of Machine Learning projects is annotate images with bounding boxes (VGG Image Annotator is an open source tool).
Bounding boxes should be normalized and it is common to predict the square root of the height and width
The most common metric for localization is Intersection over Union.

The task of classifying and localizing multiple object in an image is called object detection. A common way to do it was to create a CNN to classify and locate a single object, and make it slide across the image (but it will locate the same object multiple times in different positions). Another way is to have a convolutional layer instead of dense (cause it accepts image of any size).
YOLO (You Only Look Once) is a fast and accurate object detection architecture.

A very common metric used in object detection tasks is mean Average Precision (maximum precision you can get with at least 0% recall, 10% recall, ... and then average it. Then take the mean for each class).
In semantic segmentation each pixel is classified accordingly to the class of the object it belongs to.

It uses upsampling layer: transposed convolution layer: first stretching the image by inserting empty rows and column, then performing a regular convolution (or regular convolutional layer with fractional stride).
Researchers are now focusing on harder and harder problems, such as adversarial learning, explainability, realistic image generation, and single-shot learning.
Chapter 15 - Processing Sequences Using RNNs and CNNs
A recurrent neural network looks like a feedforward neural network, except it also has connections pointing backwards.

Since the output of a recurrent neuron at time step t is a function of all the inputs from previous time steps, you could say it has a form of memory. The part of the neural network that preserves some state across time steps is called a memory cell. A cell's state is a function of some input and the state at previous step.
A RNN can take a sequence of input and produce a sequence of output (sequence-to-sequence network).
Feed the network a sequence of inputs and ignore all outputs except for the last one (sequence-to-vector network) (or encoder).
Feed the network an input vector over and over again at each step and let it output a sequence (vector-to-sequence network) (or decoder).
To train an RNN, the trick is to unroll it through time and then simply use regular backpropagation (backpropagation through time) (BPTT).

A time series is a sequence of one (univariate) or more (multivariate) values per time step. A typical task is to predict future values (forecasting). Another common task is to predict missing values from the past (imputation).

When dealing with time series, the input features are generally represented as 3D arrays of shape (batch size, time steps, dimensionality), where dimensionality is 1 for univariate, more for multivariate.
The simplest approach is to predict the last value in each series, naive forecasting.
By default , recurrent layers in Keras return the final output. To make them return one output per time step, you must set return_sequences=True.
There are many other models to forecast time series, such as weighted moving average models or autoregressive integrated moving average (ARIMA) models.
Stacking multiple layers of cell and you'll get a deep RNN. Make sure to return_sequences=True for all recurrent layers in a deep RNN.

This technique is called attention (or Bahdanau attention or additive attention).
