Chapter 17 - Representation Learning and Generative Learning Using Autoencoders and GANs

Autoencoders are artificial neural networks capable of learning dense representations of the input data, called latent representations or codings, without any supervision. They are useful for dimensionality reduction, as feature detector and as generative models.
They simply learn to copy their inputs to their outputs. It looks at the input, converts them to an efficient latent representation, and then spits out something that looks very close to the inputs.
It is composed by an encoder (recognition network) that converts the input to the latent representation, and a decoder (or generative network). The architecture is typically symmetrical.
If it has multiple hidden layers is called stacked autoencoder (or deep autoencoder).

GANs are composed by two neural networks: a generator that tries to generate data that looks familiar to the training data, and a discriminator that tries to tell real data from fake data. Generator and discriminator compete against each other during training (adversarial training).
Autoencoders can also be used as dimensionality reduction for visualization.

If you have a large dataset but most of it is unlabeled, you can first train a stacked autoncoder using all the data, then reuse the lower layers to create a neural network for your actual task and train it using the labeled data.
When the autoencoder is neatly symmetrical, a common technique is to tie the weights os the decoder layers to the weights of the encoder layers, halving them.
Rather than training the whole stacked autoencoder in one go, it is possible to train one shallow autoencoder at a time, then stack all of them into a single stacked autoencoder.
If you want to build an autoencoder for images you'll need a convolutional autoencoder.
To build a recurrent autoencoder you need a sequence-to-vector RNN which compresses the input sequence down to a single vector. The decoder is a vector-to-sequence that does the reverse.

Another way to force the autoencoder to learn useful features is to add noise to its input, training it to recover the original. noise-free inputs (stacked denoising autoencoder). The noise can be pure Gaussian noise added to the inputs, or it can be randomly switched-off inputs, like dropout. (Only active during training).

Sparsity also lead to good feature extraction, each neuron in the coding layer typically ends up representing a useful feature (sparse autoencoders). Sparsity loss measure the actual sparsity of the coding layer at each training iteration, and penalize the model when the measured sparsity differs from a target sparsity.

Variational autoencoders are probabilistic autoencoders (outputs partly determined by chance) and generative autoencoders (can generate new instances that look like they were sampled from the training set).
The encoder produces a mean coding and a standard deviation. The actual coding is then sampled randomly from a Gaussian distribution with that mean and variance. (plus other info about the loss).

We can do semantic interpolation by interpolate at the codings level. we run both images through the encoder, then we interpolate the two codings we get, and finally we decode the interpolated coding to get the final image.

Generative Adversarial Networks were proposed in a 2014 paper by Ian Goodfellow. The Generator takes a random distribution as input and outputs some data, trying to produce points that look real enough (random input is the latent representation). The Discriminator takes either a fake point from the generator or a real one from the training set, and must guess whether the input image is fake or real.
Each training iteration is divided into two phases:

We train the discriminator: a batch of real images is sampled from the training set and is completed with an equal number of fake images produced by the generator. Backpropagation only optimizes the weights of the discriminator during this phase.

We train the generator: we use it to produce a batch of fake images, and the discriminator is used to tell whether the images are real or fake. We set all the labels to 1 and run backpropagation affecting only generator's weigths.
The generator never actually sees any image, yet it gradually learns to produce convincing fake images! All it gets is the gradients flowing back through the discriminator.

The game may end up in a state that game theorists call a Nash equilibrium, no player would be better off changing their own strategy, assuming the other players do not change theirs. The author of the paper demonstrates that a GAN can only reach a Nash equilibrium when the generator produces perfectly realistic images and the discriminator is forced to guess. Nothing guarantees that the equilibrium will ever be reached, tho.

The bigger difficulty is called mode collapse: when the generator's outputs gradually become less diverse. The GAN may gradually cycle across a few classes, never really becoming very good at any of them.
Experience replay consists in storing the images produced by the generator at each iteration in a replay buffer.
Mini-batch discrimination measures how similar images are across the batch and provides this statistic to the discriminator, so it can easily reject a whole batch of fake images that lack diversity.
This is still a very active field of research.
Just changing the random seed and training the same model again will sometimes work.
GANs are very sensitive to the hyperparameters.
Being able to do arithmetic on faces feels like science fiction!

If you add each image's class as an extra input to both the generator and the discriminator, they will both learn what each class looks like, and thus you will be blae to control the class of each image produced by the generator (conditional GAN).

With GANs you often end up with locally convincing features but overall inconsistencies. To solve that they suggested generating small images at the beginning, then gradually adding convolutional layers to both the generator and discriminator to produce larger and larger images.

Minibatch standard deviation layer
Equalizer learning rate

StyleGAN uses style transfer techniques in the generator to ensure that the generated images have the same local structure as the training images, at every scale. It is composed of two networks: mapping networks and synthesis network.
The idea of adding noise independently from the codings is very important. Some parts of an image are quite random, so the generator doesn't have to store representation for that.
Chapter 18 - Reinforcement Learning
They applied the power of Deep Learning to the field of Reinforcement Learning, and it worked beyond their wildest dreams.

In Reinforcement Learning, a software agent makes observations and takes actions within an environment, and in return it receives rewards. Its objective is to learn to act in a way that will maximize its expected reward over time. You can think of positive reward as pleasure, and negative reward as pain.
There may not be any positive rewards after all.

The algorithm a software agent uses to determine its actions is called its policy. The policy could be a neural network taking observations as inputs and outputting the action to take. If the policy involves randomness, it is called stochastic policy.
Training is hard and slow in the real world, so you generally need a simulated environment.
close() method free resources.

This neural network will take an observation as input, and it will output the action to be executed. It will estimate a probability for each action, and then we will select an action randomly, according to the estimated probabilities.
The approach lets the agent find the right balance between exploring new actions and exploiting the actions that are known to work well.

If we knew what the best action was at each step it would just be regular supervised learning. In Reinforcement Learning the only guidance the agent gets is through rewards, and rewards are typically sparse and delayed. This is called the credit assignment problem: when the agent gets a reward, it is hard for it to know which actions should get credited (or blamed) for it.

A common strategy is to evaluate an action based on the sum of all rewrds that come after it, usually applying a discount factor at each step. This sum of discounted rewards is called the action's return. Discount factors vary from 0.9 to 0.99.

If you play the game enough times, on average good actions will get a higher return than bad ones. How much better or worse an action is, compared to the other possible actions, is called the action advantage.
Policy gradient algorithms optimize the parameters of a policy by following the gradients toward higher rewards.
REINFORCE algorithms are an example. They let the policy play several games before updating it.

Unless you're writing a paper, you should not hesitate to inject prior knowledge into the agent, as it will speed up training dramatically. (E.g. you could add negative rewards proportional to the pole's angle). If you have a reasonably good policy, you may want to train the neural network to imitate before using policy gradients to improve it.

A Markov chain is a process that has a fixed number of states, and it randomly evolves from one state to the another at each step. The probability for it to eveolve is fixed and depends only on the pair of states .

Markov decision processes resemble Markov chains but at each step, an agent can choose one of several possible actions, and the transition probabilities depend on the chosen action. Also, some state transitions return some reward (positive or negative), and the agent's goal is to find a policy that will maximize reward over time.
Optimal state value is the sum of all discounted future rewards an agent can expect on average after it reaches a state s, assuming it acts optimally.
Dynamic Programming breaks down a complex problem into tractable subproblems that can be tackled iteratively.
State-action values are generally called Q-Values.
Temporal Difference Learning (TD Learning) take into account the fact that the agent has only partial knowledge of the MDP.
Epsilon-greedy policy at each step it acts randomly with probability epsilon, or greedily with probability 1-epsilon (action with highest value)
Approximating these tabular methods you can get Approximate Q-Learning, Deep Q-Network, Deep Q-Learning.

You need a neural network that takes a state-action pair and outputs an approximate Q-Value, but in practice it's much more efficient to use a neural net that takes a state and outputs one approximate Q-Value for each possible action.

Instead of training the DQN based only on the latest experiences, we will store all experiences in a replay buffer (or replay memory), and we will sample a random training batch from it at each training iteration.

Catastrophic forgetting: what the agent learns in one part of the environment may break what it learned earlier in other parts of the environment. You cold increase the size of the replay buffer or reduce the learning rate. But the truth is that Reinforcement Learning is hard, training is unstable and often many hyperparameters must be tried to find a configuration that works well.

To stabilize the model you can use two model: the online model which learns at each step and is used to move the agent around, and the other is the target model used only to define target (and is a clone of the online model). At regular intervals, we copy the weights of the online model to the target model (Double DQN).

Importance sampling (IS) or prioritized experience replay (PER) use the concept of sampling experiences more important more frequently (important: higher TD error). We should also downweighting the experiences according to their importance, or else the model will just overfit the important experiences.
There is also the Dueling DQN.
The TF-Agents library provides many off-the-shelf environments.

Training architecture: a driver explores the environment using a collect policy to chose actions, and it collects trajectories (concise representation of a transition form one time step to the next), sending them to an observer, which saves them to a replay buffer. An agent pulls batches of trajectories from the replay buffer and trains some network.
You generally want the driver to explore multiple copies of the environment in parallel.
Once an episode is over, we can evaluate how good it was overalls by summing the undiscounted rewards (AverageReturnMetric).
Other RL Algorithms:

Advantage Actor-Critic (A2C).

Curiosity-based exploration: ignore the rewards, and just make the agent extremely curious to explore the environment. The agent continuously tries to predict the outcome of its actions, and it seeks situations where the outcome does not match its predictions. If the outcome is predictable (boring), it goes elsewhere. If the outcome is unpredictable but the agents notices it has no control over it, it also gets bored after a while.

There are two main approaches to training a single model across multiple devices: model parallelism, where the model is split across the devices, and data parallelism, where the model is replicated across every device, and each replica is trained on a subset of data (data parallelism is simpler and generally more efficient).
Data parallelism strategies:
Mirrored strategy: mirror all the model parameters across all the GPUs and always apply the exact same parameter updates on every GPUs.
With centralized parameters: store the model parameters outside of the GPU devices (workers) performing the computation (in parameter servers). It allows either synchronous or asynchronous updates.

Appendix D: Autodiff
Dual numbers are weird but fascinating numbers

Reverse-Mode Autodiff is the solution implemented by TensorFlow. It first goes through the graph in the forward direction to compute the value of each node. Then it does a second pass, this time in reverse direction to compute all the partial derivatives.
It can also handle functions that are not entirely differentiable, as long as you ask it to compute the partial derivatives at points that are differentiable.

TensorFlow creates a new computation graph. It implements symbolic reverse-mode autodiff. It need to be generated once, and then it can be executed over and over again, and makes possible to compute higher-order derivatives if needed.
Appendix E: Other Popular ANN Architectures

Hopfield Networks: fully connected graphs. In training, for each image, the weight between two neurons is increased if the corresponding pixels are both on or both off, but decreased if one off and one on. To show a new image to the network, you just activate the neurons that correspond to active pixels. The network then computes the output of every neuron, and this gives you a new image. You can take this image and repeat until you reach a stable state, that generally is the training image that most resembles the input image.

Boltzmann Machines: fully connected ANNs based on stochastic neurons, that output 1 with some probability, and0 otherwise. They will never stabilize. You can aslo use a generative model for classification, just add a few visible neurons to encode the training image's class.
Resticted Boltzmann Machines: a Boltzmann Machine in which there are no connections between visible units or between hidden units, only between visible and hidden units.

Deep Belief Nets: a stack of several layers of RMBs, the hidden units of the first-level RBM serve as the visible units for the second-layer RBM, and so on. You can also train them in a supervised manner by adding some visible units to represent the labels.

Self-Organizing Maps (SOMs): used to produce a low-dimensional representation of a high-dimensional dataset, generally for visualization, clustering, or classification. First the weight are initialized randomly. Then a training instance is picked randomly and fed to the network. The neuron that measure the smallest distance wins and tweaks its weight vector (and his neighbors') to be slightly closer to the input vector. Then another training instance is picked and it repeats.
Appendix G: TensorFlow Graphs

Every time you call a TF Function with a new combination of input types or shapes (input signature), it generates a new concrete function, with its own graph specialized for this particular combination.
You can get this function for a particular combination of inputs by calling the TF Function's get_concrete_function() method.
The tensors in these graphs are symbolic tensors, meaning they don't have an actual value, just a data type, a shape and a name. Thy represent the future tensors that will flow through the graph.
The print() function is not a TensorFlow operation, so it will only run when the Python function is traced, which happens in graph mode.
If your function has Python side effectos, be aware that this code will only run when the function is traced. It best to assume that the function might be traced any time the TF Function is called.
Do not use =, +=, -= or any other Python assignment operator with TF variables. Instead, you must use the assign(), assign_add() or assign_sub() methods.

Now most of us automatically see animals as essentially different and inferior.
The expulsion from Eden bears a striking resemblance to the Agricultural Revolution.
Domesticated species paid for their unparalleled collective success with unprecedented individual suffering.

Farmers routinely lock animals in tiny cages, mutilate their horn and tails, separate mothers from offspring and selectively breed monstrosities. The animals suffer greatly, yet they live on and multiply.
When our Stone Age ancestors came across sweet fruit or honey, the most sensible thing to do was to eat as much of it as quickly as possible.
A need shaped thousands of generations ago continues to be felt subjectively even if it no longer necessary for survival and reproduction in the present. (Works both for humans and animals).
Emotions are not uniquely human quality, they are common to all mammals (as well as to all birds and probably to some reptiles and even fish).
‘Algorithm’ is arguably the single most important concept in our world.
It is likely that frightened humans, frightened baboons and frightened pigs have similar experiences.
One core emption is apparently shared by all mammals: the mother-infant bond.
Mammals can’t live on food alone. They need emotional bonds too.

Both the meat and dairy industries are based on breaking the most fundamental emotional bond in the mammal kingdom. Farmers get their breeding sows and dairy cows impregnated again and again. Yet piglets and calves are separated from their mothers shortly after birth.
In Agricoltura times humans justified their actions in the name of god. They found a way to justify human superiority and the exploitation of animals.
Whereas the biblical “Thou shalt not kill” covered only humans, the ancient Indian principle of ahimsa (non-violence) extends to every sentient beings.
If you really understand the theory of evolution, you understand that there is no soul.
A traditional monotheist would say that Sapiens have a soul and other animals not. But if the Sapiens soul evolved step by step from the Erectus soul, what exactly were these steps?
Science knows surprisingly little about mind and consciousness. They don’t know how a collection of electric brain signals creates subjective experiences.
The better we understand the brain, the more redundant the mind seems. If the entire system works by electric signals passing from here to there, why the hell do we also need to feel fear?

What happens in the mind that doesn’t happen in the brain? If nothing happens in the mind except what happens in the brain, then why do we need the mind? If something does indeed happen in the mind over and above what happens in the neural network - where the hell does it happen?
Consciousness may be a kind of mental pollution produced by the firing of complex neural networks. It doesn’t do anything. It I just there.
In the nineteen century, scientist described brains and minds as if they were steam engines, because that was the leading technology of the day (cow is computer).
Are we really sure that computers have no sensations or desires?
There is no way to prove conclusively that anyone other than oneself has a mind. We just assume other humans have, we cannot know for certain.

Everything I experience is the result of electrical activity in my brain, and it should therefore be theoretically feasible to simulate an entire virtual world that I could not possibly distinguish from the ‘real’ world.
Since there is only one real world, whereas the number of potential virtual worlds is infinite, the probability that you happen to inhabit the sole real world is almost zero.

Animals are not aware that the depression or hunger they feel belongs to a unique entity called ‘I’. Only humans understand themselves as an enduring self that has a past and a future, other animals exists in an eternal present.
(In an experiment a rat freed another one) Do I really care about the beggar? Or do I simply want to feel better myself?
Like animals, we have no soul.
Humanising animals we usually underestimate animal cognition.
Homo sapiens is the only species capable of cooperating flexibly in large numbers. Victory almost invariably went to those who cooperates better.
Revolutions are usually made by small networks of agitators rather than by the masses.
Three vital conditions for dictatorship
Loyal entities in control of all networks of cooperation
Prevent the creation of any rival organisation
Really on support of sister parties
Sapiens can’t have intimate relations with more than 150 individuals.
Sapiens don’t behave according to a cold mathematical logic, but rather according to a warm social logic.
Large number of people behave fundamentally different way than do small numbers.

All large-scale human cooperation is ultimately based on our belief in imagined orders. If people believe in the same stories, they follow the same rules and it’s easier to predict the behaviour of strangers and to organise mass-cooperation networks. Chimpanzee cannot invent and spread stories, which is why they cannot cooperate in large numbers.

There is objective reality (independent or our beliefs and feelings), subjective reality (dependent or our beliefs and feelings) and intersubjective reality (depend on communication among many humans).
We don’t want to accept that our God, our nation or our values are mere fictions, because these are the things that give meaning to our lives.
Meaning is created when many people weave together a common network of stories.
A hundred years hence, our belief in democracy and human rights might look equally incomprehensible to our descendants.
No other animal can stand up to us, because they lack the necessary imagination.
For the Sumerians, Enki and Inanna were as real as Google and Microsoft are real for us.
Gods didn’t run their business because they didn’t exist anywhere except in the human imagination.
Writing has enabled humans to organise entire societies in an algorithmic fashion.

Egyptians believed that only prayers to the living-god pharaoh could save Nile Valley from devastating floods and droughts. They were right. Pharaoh did nothing to raise or lower the Nile water level, but built dams and dug canals.
Sousa Mendes issued thousands of visas. He was responsible for the largest rescue operation by a single individual during the Holocaust.
Mao ordered tripling agricoltura production. Reports exaggerated. The government sold millions of bonds of rice. The result was the worst famine in history.
Written language was conceived as way of describing reality, but it gradually became a powerful way to reshape reality. The truth hardly matters. What’s written is far more important.
Marks are a relatively new invention. The skills required to get high marks in an exam are not the same as a true understanding o literature, biology or mathematics.
No matter how mistaken the biblical world view was, it provided a better basis for large-scale human cooperation.
How do you know if an entity is real? Very simple - just ask yourself, ‘Can it suffer?'
Corporations, money and nations exist only in our imagination. We invented them to serve us; why do we find ourselves sacrificing our lives in their service?
Antibiotics, unlike God, help even those who don’t help themselves. They cure infections whether you believe in them or not.
Religion is any all-encompassing story that confers superhuman legitimacy on human laws, norms and values. It legitimate social strictures by arguing that they reflect superhuman laws.
Religion asserts that we humans are subject to a system of moral laws that we did not invent and that we cannot change.
Religion is a deal, whereas spirituality is a journey.
Religion: “If you obey God, you’ll be admitted to heaven. If you disobey Him, you’ll burn in hell."

Spiritual journeys are quests that usually begins with some big questions such as “Who am I?” Or “What is the meaning of life?”. Whereas most people accept the ready-made answers provided by the powers that be, spiritual seekers are not so easily satisfied.

Religious seek to cement the worldly order whereas spirituality seeks to escape it. “If you meet the Buddha on the road, kill him.” If while walking on the spiritual path you encounter the rigid ideas and fixed laws of institutionalised Buddhism, you must free yourself from them too.
Those who fume against stultified religious structures often end up forging new structures in their place.

The Bible is a collection of numerous different texts composed by different human authors centuries after the events they purport to describe, and these texts were not assembled into a single holy book until long after biblical times.
Religions have the nagging tendency to turn factual statements into ethical judgements.
Religion provides the ethical justification for scientific research, and in exchange gets to influence the scientific agenda and the uses of scientific discoveries.
Science is interested above all in power. Through research it aims to acquire the power to cure diseases, fight wars and produce food.
Modernity is a deal. Humans agree to give up meaning in exchange for power.
The cosmic plan gave meaning to human life, but also restricted human power. Modern culture rejects this belief in a great cosmic plan.

Funds were scarce because there was little credit in those days; there was little credit because people had no belief in growth; and people didn’t believe in growth because the economy was stagnant. Stagnation thereby perpetuated itself.
Modernity is based on the firm belief that economic growth is not only possible, but absolutely essential.
This lesson is hammered home even to children: premodern games such as chess assumed stagnant economy. Many modern board games and computer games focus on investment and growth.
Can the economy actually keep growing forever? Won’t it eventually run out of resources - and grind to a halt?

For thousands of years the scientific road to growth was blocked because people believed that holy scriptures and ancient traditions already contained all the important knowledge the world had to offer. The greatest scientific discovery was the discovery of ignorance.
We have a good chance of overcoming the problem of resource scarcity. The real nemesis of modern economy is ecological collapse.
On one hand, we feel compelled to speed up the pace of scientific progress and economic growth, on the other hand, we must stay at least one step ahead of ecological Armageddon.
Too many politicians and voters believe that as long as the economy grows, scientists and engineers could always save us from doomsday.

It wasn’t very hard to convince individuals to want more. Greed comes easily to humans. For millennia, then the pie was of fixed size, social harmony depended on restraints. Avarice was bad. In modernity, because of avarice fuels growth, it is a force for good.

Throughout history prophets and philosophers have argued that if humans stopped believing in a great cosmic plan, all law and order would vanish. Yet today, those who pose greatest threat to global law and order are precisely those people who continue to believe in God and His all-encompassing plans.
Humanism reverses the roles and expects the experiences of humans to give meaning to the cosmos. Humanism primary commandment: create meaning for a meaningless world.
Humanism has taught us that something can be bad only if it causes somebody to feel bad. And if an action does not cause anyone to feel bad, there can be nothing wrong with it.
‘Art is anything people think is art, and beauty is in the eye of the beholder’.
In the free market the customer is always right. If the consumers don’t want it, it means that is no good.
If customers ask us only for the cheapest meat possible - that’s what the customers will get. Customer need to decide what is most important to them.
Humanist:
Ethics: if it feels good - do it!
Education: think for yourself!
Formula for knowledge:
Medieval: Knowledge = Scripture * Logic
Scientific Revolution: Knowledge = Empirical Data * Mathematics
Humanism: Knowledge = Experiences * Sensitivity
You cannot experience something if you don’t have the necessary sensitivity, and you cannot develop your sensitivity except by undergoing a long string of experiences.
Premodern narratives focused on external events and actions, modern novels, films and poems often emphasise feelings.
Humanism splits into three main branches: liberalism, socialism (socialist and communist movements) and evolutionary humanism (nazist movement).

Democratic elections usually work only within populations that have some prior common bond, such as shared religious beliefs or national myths. They are method to settle disagreements among people who already agree on the basics.

(From Black Hawk Down) Close to death, he had never felt so completely alive. In those hours on the street he had not been Shawn Nelson, he had no connection to the larger world, no bills to pay, no emotional ties, nothing. He had just been a human being staying alive from one nanosecond to the next, drawing one breath after another, fully aware that each one might be his last. He felt he would never be the same.
Socialist said that under liberalism, everyone is free to starve.
Racist and fascist blamed both liberalism and socialism for subverting natural selection and causing the degeneration of humankind.
Liberalism became identified with the racist European empires. As these empires collapsed they were usually replaced by either military dictatorship or socialist regimes, not liberal democracies.
By 1970 the world contained 130 independent countries, but only thirty of these were liberal democracies.
Liberal democracy was saved only by nuclear weapons. ‘If you attack us, we will make sure nobody comes out alive.'
And then everything changed. As of 2016 there is no serious alternative to the liberal package of individualism, human rights, democracy and a free market.
While it is a favourite pastime of Western academics and activists to find fault with the liberal package, they have so far failed to come up with anything better.

Marx and Lenin succeed because they devoted more attention to understanding the technological and economic realities of their time than to scrutinising ancient texts and prophetic dreams. The experiences, needs and hopes of the new class of urban proletariats were simply too different from those of biblical peasants.
The Vatican was the closest thing twelfth-century Europe had to Silicon Valley.

Theist religions have long since turned from creative into reactive forces. What was the most influential discovery, invention or creation of traditional religions such as Islam or Christianity in the twentieth century?
Determinism and randomness have divided the entire cake between them, leaving not even a crumb for ‘freedom’. Free will exists only in the imaginary stories we humans have invented.

Can humans choose their desire in the first place? I feel a particular wish welling up within me because this is the feeling created by the biochemical processes in my brain. These processes might be deterministic or rand, but not free.
I don’t choose my desires. I just feel them, and act accordingly.
Why did I think this particular thought? Did I decide a minute ago to think this thought, and only then think it? Or did it just arise without any direction or permission from me?
If organisms lack free will, it implies that we can manipulate and even control their desires using drugs, genetic engineering or direct brain stimulation.
It is possible to create or annihilate even complex feelings such as love, anger, fear and depression by stimulating the right spots in the human brain.
If I look really deep within myself, the seeming unity that I take for granted dissolves into a cacophony of conflicting voices, none of which is ‘my true self’.
The experiencing self is our moment-to-moment consciousness, and it remembers nothing.
The narrating self retrieves memories, tells stories and makes big decisions.
The narrating self remembers only the peak moment and the end moment, and assesses the whole experience according to their average.
Nice experiment (pag. 346).
Most of us identify with our narrating self.

If you want to make people believe in imaginary entities such as gods and nations, you should make them sacrifice something valuable. The more painful the sacrifice, the more convinced they will be of the existence of the imaginary recipient.
Cyber-wars may last just a few minutes.
Humans are in danger of losing their economic value, because intelligence is decoupling from consciousness.
Which of the two is really important? Intelligence is mandatory but consciousness is optional.

Cars replaced horses because they were superior in the handful of tasks that the system really needed. Taxi drivers are highly likely to go the way horses. Bank clerks, travel agents, stock-exchange agents too. And lawyers, judges, cops and detectives? Teachers and even doctors? Pharmacists
With such a Watson around (IBM), there is not so much need for Sherlocks.
What to do with all the superfluous people?
The fact that there is always something humans can do better than machines is not a law of nature. Nothing guarantees that it will continue to be like that in the future.

Organisms are algorithms, algorithmic calculations are not affected by the materials from which the calculator is built, hence there is no reason to think that organisms algorithms can do things that non-organic algorithms will never be able to replicate or surpass.
It’s not easier to replace humans with machine only because machine are getting smarter, but also because humans are professionalising.
At VITAL, the algorithm gets to vote, like the other five board members, wether or not the firm makes an investment in a specific company.
If gods can possess lands and employ people, why not algorithms?
Liberalism eventually defeated socialism only by adopting the best parts of the socialist programme.
Since we do not know what the job market will look like in 2030 or 2040, already today we have no idea what to teach our kids.

The coming technological bonanza will probably make it feasible to feed and support these useless masses even without any effort from their side. But what will keep them occupied and content? People must do something, or they go crazy. What will they do all day? One answer might be drugs and computer games.
What’s so sacred about useless bums?
Liberalism will collapse on the day the system knows me better than I know myself.

‘People might abandon their own psychological judgements and rely on computers when making important life decisions, such as choosing activities, career paths, or even romantic partners. It is possible that such data-driven decisions will improve people’s lives'

The experiencing self can silence the alarm clock by pressing a button. In contrast, Cortana will know me so well that it will know exactly what inner buttons to push in order to make me follow its ‘advice’.
Eventually we may reach a point when it will be impossible to disconnect from this all-knowing network even from a moment.
The shifting of authority from humans to algorithms is happening all around us, not as a result of some momentous governmental decision, but due to a flood of mundane personal choices.
Will the democracy work once rich and poor are separated not merely by wealth, but also by real biological gaps?
Twentieth-century medicine aimed to heal the sick. Twentieth-fist-century medicine is increasingly aiming to upgrade the healthy.
New techno-religions:
Techno humanism: we should use technology to create Homo deus. Human model with upgraded physical and mental abilities.
Data religion: humans have completed their cosmic task and should now pass the torch on to kew kind of entities.

Most researches on the mind are biased cause they have been conducted on people suffering from various psychiatric disorders and mental diseases or on WEIRD people. Western, Educated, Industrialised, Rich and Democratic societies.
Modern humanity is sick with FOMO - Fear Of Missing Out - and though we have more choice than ever before, we have lost the ability to really pay attention to whatever we choose.

Techno-humanism may end up downgrading humans. It’s usually the brightest goat in the flock that stirs the most trouble, which is why the Agricultural Revolution involved downgrading animals’ mental abilities.
For millions of years we were enhanced chimpanzees. In future, we may become oversized ants.
Many people take great care not to probe themselves too deeply.
Dataism (data religion) declares that the universe consists of data flows, an the value of any phenomenon or entity is determined by it contribution to data processing.
Humans were supposed to distil data into information, information into knowledge, and knowledge into wisdom. However, Dataists believe that humans can no longer cope with the immense flows of data.
In a free market, if one processor makes a wrong decision, others will be quick to capitalise on its mistake.
In communism, all data is processed and all decisions are made by a single central processor.
Capitalism won the Cold War because distributed data processing works better than centralised data processing, at least in periods of accelerating technological change.

Dictatorships use centralised processing maths, whereas democracies prefer distributed processing. Under the unique conditions of the late twentieth century, distributed processing worked better. Under alternative conditions, centralised processing had an edge.
Internet is a free and lawless zone that erodes state sovereignty, ignores borders, abolishes privacy and poses perhaps the most formidable global security risk.
Power is shifting away from voters, but they are unsure where it has gone.

Because technology is now moving so fast, present-day politicians are thinking on a far smaller scale than their predecessors a century ago. Government has become mere administration, it no longer leads the country.
Some people believe that a small coterie of billionaires secretly run the world. But such conspiracy theories never work, because they underestimate the complexity of the system.

If in twenty-fist century traditional political structures can no longer process the data fast enough to produce meaningful visions, then new and more efficient structures will evolve to take their place.
The whole history can be seen as a process of improving the efficiency of the system of the entire human species, through 4 methods:
Increasing the number of processors
Increasing the variety of processors
Increasing the number of connection between processors
Increasing the freedom of movement along existing connections
Cognitive revolution: connect vast numbers of Sapiens into a single data-processing network
Agricultural revolutions: increase the number of processors and create new incentives for different networks to trade and communicate with one another.
Invention of writing: humans bonded and merged into kingdoms.
Discovery of America: network that encompass the whole world

If humankind is a single data-processing system, what is its output? Dataist would say that it’s the creation of the Internet-of-All-Things. Once this mission is accomplished, Homo sapiens will vanish.
Humans are merely tools for creating the Internet-of-All-Things.
Homo sapiens is an obsolete algorithm.
Dataist commandments:
They ought to maximise dataflow by connecting more and more media, and producing and consuming more and more information.
Link everything to the system.
Dataist greatest sin would be to block the data flow.
Freedom of information. But freedom is not given to humans, it is given to information.
What’s the point of doing or experiencing anything if nobody know about it, and if it doesn’t contribute something to the global exchange of information?
The new motto says “if you experience something - record it. If you record something - upload it. If you upload something - share it."
Dataism isn’t anti-humanist. It has nothing against human experiences. It just doesn’t think they are intrinsically valuable.
When cars replaced horse-drawn carriages, we didn’t upgrade the horses - we retired them. Perhaps it is time to do the same with Homo sapiens.

Humanists argued that ‘God is a product of the human imagination’. Dataism now tells them ‘Yes, God is a product of the human imagination, but human imagination is just the product of biochemical algorithms’.
It went from deo-centric, to homo-centric to data-centric.
Ideas change the world only when they change our behaviour.
Feelings are complex algorithms honed by evolution to help animals to make correct decisions.
Humanism: “Listen to you feelings!”. Dataism: “Listen to the algorithms! They know how you feel."
Is there perhaps something in the universe that cannot be reduced to data?

Even if Dataism isn wrong and organisms aren’t just algorithms, it won’t necessarily prevent Dataism from taking over the world. Many previous religions gained enormous popularity and power despite their factual inaccuracies.
Dataism threatens to do to Homo sapiens what Homo sapiens has done to al other animals.
All the scenarios outlined in this book should be understood as possibilities rather than prophecies.

In the past, censorship worked by blocking the flow of information. In the twenty-first century censorship works by flooding people with irrelevant information. We just don’t know what to pay attention to, and often spend our time investigating and debating side issues. In ancient times having power meant having access to data. Today having power means knowing what to ignore.
Three questions:
Are organisms just algorithms, and is life really just data processing?
What’s more valuable - intelligence or consciousness?
What will happen to the society, politics and daily life when non-conscious but highly intelligent algorithms know us better than we know ourselves?
