paragraphs: Kohavi R. - Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments
Part 1: Introductory Topics for Everyone
01 - Introduction and Motivation
Key themes in online controlled experiments:
It's hard to assess the value of an idea.
Small changes can have a big impact.
Experiments with big impact are rare.
The overhead of running an experiment must be small.
The overall evaluation criterion (OEC) must be clear.
Terminology:

Overall Evaluation Criterion (OEC): A quantitative measure of the experiment's objective. The OEC must be measurable in the short term (the duration of an experiment) yet believed to causally drive long-term strategic objectives. In statistics, this is called Response or Dependent variable.

Parameter: A controllable experimental variable that is thought to influence the OEC or other metrics of interest. Parameters are sometimes called factors or variables. Parameters are assigned values, also called levels. Multivariable tests, also called Multivariate Tests (MVTs). evaluate multiple parameters together.
Variant: A user experience being tested, typically by assigning values to parameters. In a simple A/B test, A and B are the two variants, usually called Control and Treatment.

Randomization Unit: A pseudo-randomization (e.g., hashing) process is applied to units e.g., users or pages) to map them to variants. Proper random- ization is important to ensure that the populations assigned to the different variants are similar statistically, allowing causal effects to be determined with high probability. You must map units to variants in a persistent and independent manner (suggested randomization unit is user level). Do not take randomization lightly, no factor should be allowed to influence variant assignment.
Randomized controlled experiments are the gold standard for establishing causality.
Necessary ingredients for running useful controlled experiments:
There are experimental units (e.g., users) that can be assigned to different variants with no interference.
There are enough experimental units (e.g., users)
Key metrics, ideally an OEC, are agreed upon and can be practically evaluated.
Changes are easy to make.
There are three key tenets for organizations that wish to run online controlled experiments:
The organization wants to make data-driven decisions and has formalized an OEC 2
The organization is willing to invest in the infrastructure and tests to run controlled experiments and ensure that the results are trustworthy
The organization recognizes that it is poor at assessing the value of ideas
For example, "Profit" is not a good OEC, as short-term theatrics can increase short-term profit, but may hurt it in the long run. Customer lifetime value is a strategically powerful OEC.
“If you are on an experiment-driven team, get used to, at best, 70% of your work being thrown away. Build your processes accordingly”.

In general, we recommend always having a portfolio of ideas: most should be investments in attempting to optimize “near” the current location, but a few radical ideas should be tried to see whether those jumps lead to a bigger hill.
A true experiment follows the scientific method. It begins with a clear hypothesis that makes predictions about what is supposed to happen. It then tests those predictions empirically.
One useful concept to keep in mind is EVI: Expected Value of Information, which captures how additional information can help you in decision making.

A multi-armed bandit is a type of experiment where the experiment traffic allocation can be dynamically updated as the experiment progresses. For example, we can take a fresh look at the experiment every hour to see how each of the variants has performed, and we can adjust the fraction of traffic that each variant receives.
02 - Running and Analyzing Experiments: An End-to-End Example
We want to evaluate the impact of simply adding a coupon code field. We do not implement a true coupon code system, as there are no codes available.
Our goal is simply to assess the impact on revenue by having this coupon code field and evaluate the concern that it will distract people from checking out.
Our hypothesis is: “Adding a coupon code field to the checkout page will degrade revenue.”
Revenue-per-user is a good OEC.

The next critical question is to determine which users to consider in the denominator of the revenue-per-user metric: Only users who start the purchase process. This is the best choice, given where the change is in the funnel. We include all potentially affected users. but no unaffected users (users who never start checking out) who dilute our results.

In controlled experiments, we have one sample for the Control and one sample for each Treat- ment. We quantitatively test whether the difference between a pair of Treatment and Control samples is unlikely, given the Null hypothesis that the means are the same. If it is unlikely, we reject the Null hypothesis and claim that the difference is statistically significant. Specifically, given revenue-per-user estimates from the Control and Treatment samples, we compute the p-value for the difference, which is the probability of observing such difference or more extreme assuming the Null hypothesis is true. We reject the Null hypothesis and conclude that our experiment has an effect (or the result is statistically significant) if the p-value is small enough.
Another way to examine whether the difference is statistically significant is by checking whether the confidence interval overlaps with zero.
Statistical power is the probability of detecting a meaningful difference between the variants when there really is one (statistically, reject the null wher there is a difference).
We will use this set of decisions to finalize the design:
What is the randomization unit? Usually is users
What population of randomization units do we want to target? Do you want to run the experiment only on users with a particular characteristic (e.g. geographical, platform, type)
How large (size) does our experiment need to be? Depends on variance of the OEC, min detected effect, p-value, how safe is the experiment, other experiments you're running at the same time
How long do we run the experiment?
In general, overpowering an experiment is fine and even recommended, as sometimes we need to examine segments.
To run an experiment, we need both:
Instrumentation to get logs data on how users are interacting with your site and which experiments those interactions belong to
Infrastructure to be able to run an experiment, ranging from experiment configuration to variant assignment

There are many ways for bugs to creep in that would invalidate the experiment results. To catch them, we'll look at the guardrail metrics or invariants. These metrics should not change between the Control and Treatment.
There are two types of invariant metrics:
Trust-related guardrail metrics, such as expecting the Control and Treat- ment samples to be sized according to the configuration or that they have the same cache-hit rates.
Organizational guardrail metrics, such as latency, which are important to the organization and expected to be an invariant for many experiments.
Turns out that having Cupon in our checkout reduces revenue. So we can decide not to have coupons. We didn't even have to implement cupon structure to figure this out.
The goal of running A/B tests is to gather data to drive decision makin.
A decision needs to take into consideration:
Do you need to make tradeoffs between different metrics?

What is the cost of launching this change? Cost to fully build out the feature before launch and cost for ongoing engineering maintenance after launch, since it may be more costly to maintain new code (new code usually have more bugs and less well tested on edge cases). If the cost is high, the expected gains should cover it.
What is the downside of making wrong decisions?
Appropriate decision depending on the analysis is:

The result is not statistically significant. It is also clear that there is no practical significance. This leads to an easy conclusion that the change does not do much. You may either decide to iterate or abandon this idea.
The result is statistically and practically significant. Launch!

The result is statistically significant but not practically significant. In this case, you are confident about the magnitude of change, but that magnitude may not be sufficient to outweigh other factors such as cost. This change may not be worth launching.

The result is not statistically significant but the confidence intervals are outside of what is practically significant. Say you do not have enough power to draw a strong conclusion, and it is also such that we do not have enough data to make any launch decision. For this result, we recommend running a follow-up test with more units, providing greater statistical power.
The result is likely practically significant but not statistically significant. The best recommendation would be to repeat this test but with greater power to gain more precision in the result.
The result is statistically significant, and likely practically significant. Repeat the test with more power. From a launch/no-launch decision, however, choosing to launch is a reasonable decision.
03 - Twyman's Law and Experimentation Trustworthiness

Twyman's law, perhaps the most important single law in the whole of data analysis: “The more unusual or interesting the data, the more likely they are to have been the result of an error of one kind or another”
Examples:
Misinterpretation of the Statistical Results:

Lack of Statistical Power: A common mistake is to assume that just because a metric is not statistically significant, there is no Treatment effect. It could very well be that the experiment is underpowered to detect the effect size we are seeing, that is, there are not enough users in the test.

Misinterpreting p-value: easy to say incorrect statements involving p-values. [My note] Remember: p-value is not the probability of false positive, but it's alpha that is the tolerated false positive rate.
Peeking at p-values: multiple hypothesis testing results in bias in declaring resulrs to be statistically significant.
Multiple Hypothesis Tests: run multiple tests and picking the one with lowest p-value results in bias as well.
Confidence Intervals:
A common mistake is to look at the confidence intervals separately for the Control and Treatment, and assume that if they overlap, the Treatment effect is not statistically different.

Another common misunderstanding about confidence intervals is the belief that the presented 95% confidence interval has a 95% chance of containing the true Treatment effect. The 95% refers to how often the 95% confidence intervals computed from many studies would contain the true Treatment effect.
Threats to Internal Validity
Violations of SUTVA (Stable Unit Treatment Value Assumption) which states that experiment units (e.g. users) do not interfere with one another.
Survivorship bias (e.g. analyzing users who have been active for some time)

Intention-to-Treat: In some experiments, there is non-random attrition from the variants. The Treatment effect we are measuring is therefore based on the offer, or intention to treat, not whether it was actually applied.

Sample Ratio Mismatch (SRM): If the ratio of users (or any randomization unit) between the variants is not close to the designed ratio, the experiment suffers from a Sample Ratio Mismatch (SRM). It likely indicate a problem that requires debugging.
If it's different, run a statistical test to check that (Null hypothesis: probability of getting selected for treatment is the desired one)
Threats to External Validity
Primacy Effects: When a change is introduced, users may need time to adopt, as they are primed in the old feature, that is, used to the way it works.

Novelty effect: When you introduce a new feature, especially one that's easily noticed, initially it attracts users to try it. If users don't find the feature useful, repeat usage will be small. A Treatment may appear to perform well at first, but the Treatment effect will quickly decline over time.
An important check for primacy and novelty effects is to plot usage over time and see whether it's increasing or decreasing.
Segment Differences: What are good segments? Here are several: market or country, device or platform, time of day and day of week, user type, user account characteristics.

Ideally, segmenting should be done only by values that are determined prior to the experiment, so that the Treatment could not cause users to change segments, though in practice restricting segments this way may be hard for some use cases.
Segmented views, if too different, help you find bug with the metric. They are commonly used two ways:
Segmented view of a metric, independent of any experiment.
Segmented view of the Treatment effect for a metric

Simpson's Paradox: Treatment may be better than Control in the first phase and in the second phase, but worse overall when the two periods are combined. Mostly due to dealing with weighted averages. While occurrences of Simpson's paradox are unintuitive, they are not uncommon. One must be careful when aggregating data collected at different percentage.
Encourage Healthy Skepticism: Good data scientists are skeptics: they look at anomal- ies, they question results, and they invoke Twyman's law when the results look too good.
04 - Experimentation Platform and Culture
Build vs. Buy dilemma
In an experimentation platform, there are four high-level components ([there is also a possible architecture]):

Experiment definition, setup, and management via a user interface (UI) or application programming interface (API) and stored in the experiment system configuration. Experimenters need a way to easily define, setup, and manage the experiment lifecycle. [Here specifies in depth what that UI or API should have]
Experiment deployment, both server- and client-side, that covers variant assignment and parameterization. [Here goes into more details of the software implementation nuances]

Experiment instrumentation. Get your basic instrumentation (aka logging) to reflect these new features, as these updates to your instrumentation allow you to perform proper analysis (instrument every user request and interaction with which variant and iteration is run, and maybe also with the conterfactual, meaning what would've happened if you'd be in the other variant, but since it's very expensive, only if needed). [There is a deep dive into Variant assignment methods also]
Experiment analysis, which includes definition and computation of metrics and statistical tests like p-values.
The assignment of users to buckets must be random but deterministic.
Part 2: Selected Topics for Everyone
05 - Speed Matters: An End-to-End Case Study
[Not taking many notes here since it's an end-to-end case study]
We recommend latency as guardrail metric.
The case studty is about slowdown experiments: by slowing down the product, we can assess the impact of increased latency on key metrics.
Measuring some metrics (e.g. latency) could have some real-life complexity even if it appears simple.
06 - Organizational Metrics
Three types of metrics:
Goal metrics: Also called success metrics or true north metrics, reflect what the organization ultimately cares about.
When trying to come up with a goal metric we recommend first articulating what you want in words.
Goal metrics are usually a single or a very small set of metrics that best captures the ultimate success you are striving towards. These metrics may not be easy to move in the short term.

Driver metrics: Also called sign post metrics, surrogate metrics, indirect or predictive metrics, tend to be shorter-term, faster-moving, and more-sensitive metrics than goal metrics. Driver metrics reflect a mental causal model of what it takes for the organization to succeed, that is, hypotheses on the drivers of success rather than just what success looks like.
A good driver metric indicates that we are moving in the right direction to move the goal metric(s).
Guardrail metrics: Guard against violated assumptions and come in two types: metrics that protect the business and metrics that assess the trustworthiness and internal validity of experiment results
Other possible taxonomies:
Asset vs. engagement metrics
Business vs. operational metrics
Other possible metrics:
Data quality metrics
Diagnosis or debug metrics
Ensure that your goal metrics are:
Simple
Stable: it should not be necessary to update goal metrics every time you launch a new feature
Ensure that driver metrics are:
Aligned with the goal
Actionable and relevant
Sensitive
Resistant to gaming: when given a numerical target, humans can be quite ingenious, especially when the measures are tied to rewards.
Use hypotheses from less-scalable methods t o generate ideas, and then validate them in scalable data analyses to determine a precise definition.
Sometimes it may be easier to precisely measure what you do not want, such as user dissatisfaction or unhappiness, than it is to measure what you want.
[Adds a list of organizational guardrail metrics you might wanna consider]
Just like driver metrics, it is important to establish the causal relationship between guardrail metrics and goal metrics.
[Adds a list of gamed metrics, interesting but not too relevant]
07 - Metrics for Experimentation and the Overall Evaluation Criterion
If you use multiple metrics to measure success for an experiment, ideally you may want to combine them into an Overall Evaluation Criterion.
Business metrics may not be directly useful for online experimentation, as metrics for experimentation must be:
Measurable
Attributable
Sensitive and timely
There is usually no single metric that captures what a business is optimizing for.
A single metric makes the exact definition of success clear and has a similar value to agreeing on metrics in the first place: it aligns people in an organization about the tradeoffs.
If you have multiple metrics, one possibility is to normalize each metric to a predefined range, say 0-1, and assign each a weight. Your OEC is the weighted sum of the normalized metrics.
Still try to minimize the number of key metrics (rule of thumb: limit the number to five).
One final benefit of an OEC that is agreed upon: you can automatically ship changes.
[Gives some examples of OEC]
Charles Goodhart originally wrote the law: "Any observed statistical regularity will tend to collapse once pressure is placed upon it for control purposes”.
Today it's more common to reference Goodhart's law as: "When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure”.

Campbell's law, states that "The more any quantitative social indicator is used for social decision-making, the more subject it will be to corruption pressures and the more apt it will be to distort and corrupt the social processes it is intended to monitor"

Lucas critique observes that relationships observed in historical data cannot be considered structural, or causal. Policy decisions can alter the structure of economic models and the correlations that held historically will no longer hold.
08 - Institutional Memory and Meta-Analysis

It is highly recommended that you capture meta information on each experiment, such as who the owners are; when the experiment started; how long it ran; descriptions and screen shots if the change was visual.
You should also have results summarizing how much impact the experiment had on various metrics, and capture the hypothesis the experiment is based on; what decision was made and why.
What can you get from mining data from all these experiments? This is what we refer to here as meta-analysis.
Why?
Experiment culture.
How has experimentation been contributing to the growth of the broader organizational goals?
Experiment best practices: analyze whether experiments follow them.
Future innovations.
For someone new to your company or new to a team, having a catalog of what worked and what didn't in the past is highly valuable.
Metrics: meta-analyze metric sensitivity, related metrics and probabilistic priors.
Empirical research: offers researchers empirical evidence to evaluate and study their theories through meta-analysis.
[Good to know] GoodUI.org summarizes many UI patterns that win repeatedly.
09 - Ethics in Controlled Experiments
Three key principles:
Respect for persons: focus on transparency, truthfulness, and voluntariness.
Beneficence: Protect people from harm.
Justice: Ensure that participants are not exploited and that there is a fair distribution of risks and benefits.
Key areas to consider:
In your study, what risk does a participant face?
Understand the benefits of the study.
What choices do participants have?
Experimenters or engineers should be able to answer these key questions about data collection:
What data is being collected and what do users understand about that collection
What could go wrong with the data collection?
What are user's expectations of privacy and confidentiality, and how are those expectations being guaranteed?
[Deep dive into user ids and identifiable data]
Part 3: Complementary and Alternative Techniques to Controlled Experiments
10 - Complementary Techniques
“If all you have is a hammer, everything looks like a nail” Abraham Maslow

When running experiments, you also need to generate ideas to test, create, and validate metrics, and establish evidence to support broader conclusions. For these needs, there are techniques such as user experience research, focus groups, surveys, human evaluation, and observational studies that are useful to complement and augment a healthy A/B testing culture.
You can run a survey and gather self-reported user satisfaction data and then analyze instrumented logs data to see what large-scale observational metrics correlate with the survey results.
The methods We discuss in this chapter vary along two axes: scale (i.e., number of users) vs, depth of information per user, and are:
Logs-based Analysis, help with:
Building intuition
Characterizing potential metrics
Generating ideas for A/B experiments based on exploring the underlying data
Explore whether ideas are worth investing
Natural experiments
Observational causal studies
Human Evaluation: where a company pays a human judge, also called a rater to complete some task.
One limitation of human evaluation is that raters are generally not your end users.

User Experience Research: a subset of field and lab studies that typically go deep with a few users, often by observing them doing tasks of interest and answering questions in either a lab setting or in situ.

Focus groups: guided group discussions with recruited users or potential users. More scalable than a UER study but less ground can be covered than in a UER study, and can fall prey to group-think and convergence on fewer opinions.
Surveys: you recruit a population to answer a series of questions. They are actually quite challenging to design and analyze:
Questions must be carefully worded, as they may be misinterpreted or unintentionally prime the respondents to give certain answers
Answers are self-reported
The population can easily be biased and may not be representative of the true user population
External Data: data that a party external to your company has collected data and analyzed. Could be from a company or academic papers.
In “Putting It All Together” gives a general guide how to use external data.
Using multiple methods to triangulate towards a more accurate measurement. Establishing a hierarchy of evidence can lead to more robust results.
11 - Observational Causal Studies
Sometimes running randomized controlled experiments is not possible. There are observational causal studies that can be used to assess causality, although with lower levels of trust.
Outcome for treated - Outcome for untreated =
[Outcome for treated - Outcome for treated if not treated] +[Outcome for treated if not treated - Outcome for untreated] =
Impact of Treatment on treated + Selection bias

Controlled experiments are the gold standard for assessing causality because, with random assignment of units to variants, the first term is the observed difference between Treatment and Control and the second term has an expected value of zero
Possible designs:

Interrupted Time Series (ITS): it uses multiple measurements over time, before an interven- tion, to create a model that can provide an estimate for the metric of interest after he intervention - a counterfactual. After the intervention, multiple measurements are taken, and the Treatment effect is estimated as the average difference between the actual values for the metric of interest and those predicted by the model.
Changing back and forth multiple times will help reduce the likelihood of having confounders.
Interleaved Experiments: intersperse results mixed together and evaluate the algorithms would be to compare the click-through rate on results from the two algorithms.

Regression Discontinuity Design (RDD): can be used whenever there is a clear threshold that identifies the Treatment population. We can reduce selection bias by identifying the Based on that threshold, population that is just below the threshold as Control and compared to the population that is just above the threshold as Treatment.
Instrumental Variables (IV): technique that tries to approximate random assignment (e.g. using monozygotic twins or people with similar characteristics)
Propensity Score Matching: construct comparable Control and Treatment populations, often by segmenting the users by common confounds, in something akin to stratified sampling.
Difference in Differences: assuming common trends, assigns the difference in difference to the Treatment. Geographically based experiments commonly use this technique.
The Treatment effect is estimated as the difference in a metric of interest minus the difference in Control for that metric over the same Period.
Main pitfall is confounders, and one common type of confound is an unrecognized common cause.
Another pitfall to be aware of are spurious or deceptive correlations.
Claiming causality from observational data (uncontrolled) requires multiple assumptions that are impossible to test and are easily violated.
Any claim coming from an observational study is most likely to be wrong.
Should you need to do an observational causal study, please take care.
Interesting link: https://bit.ly/experimentGuideRefutedObservationalStudies
Part 4: Advanced Topics for Building an Experimentation Platform
12 - Client-Side Experiments

With an explosive growth of mobile usage, the number of experiments running on mobile apps has also grown. Understanding the differ- ences between thin and thick clients due to release process, infrastructure, and user behavior is useful to ensure trustworthy experiments.
Differences between Server and Client Side:
Release Process
There is a significant amount of code shipped with the client itself, Any changes to this code must be released differently.
Data Communication between Client and Server
Implications for Experiments:
Anticipate Changes Early and Parameterize: As client code cannot be shipped to end users easily, controlled experiments on any client-side changes need to be planned.
Expect a Delayed Logging and Effective Starting Time
Create a Failsafe to Handle Offline or Startup Cases
Triggered Analysis May Need Client-Side Experiment Assignment Tracking
Track Important Guardrails on Device and APP Level Health
Monitor Overall App Release through Quasi-experimental Methods
Watch Out for Multiple Devices/Platforms and Interactions between Them
13 - Instrumentation
Before you can run any experiments, you must have instrumentation in place to log what is happening to the users and the system
Examples:
User actions
Performance
Errors and crashes
System response rate
System information
It is likely you will have multiple logs from different instrumentation streams, such as:
Logs from different client types (e.g., browser, mobile)
Logs from servers
Per-user state e.g., opt-ins and opt-outs)
It is important that you ensure that the relevant logs can be easily utilized and combined by downstream processing.
How to improve:
Establish a cultural norm: nothing ships without instrumentation.
Invest in testing instrumentation during development.
Monitor the raw logs for quality.
14 - Choosing a Randomization Unit
The choice of randomization unit is critical in experiment design, as it affects both the user experience as well as what metrics can be used in measuring the impact of an experiment.
One axis to consider in choosing a randomization unit is granularity:
Page-level
Session-level
User-level
We can also consider a combination of user and day to be a unit
When trying to decide on the granularity, there are two main questions to consider:
How important is the consistency of the user experience?
Which metrics matter?
Several considerations to keep in mind:
If features act across that level of granularity, you cannot use that level of granularity for randomization.
If metrics are computed across that level of granularity, then they cannot be used to measure the results.
Exposing users to different variants may violate the stable unit treatment value assumption.
We recommend that the randomization unit be the same as (or coarser than) the analysis unit in the metrics you care about.
User-level randomization is the most common as it avoids inconsistent experi- ence for the user and allows for long-term measurement such as user retention. Could be:
A signed-in user ID
A pseudonymous user ID, such as a cookie
A device ID is an immutable ID tied to a specific device.
One final option that we do not recommend unless it is the only option is I address.
15 - Ramping Experiment Exposure: Trading Off Speed, Quality, and Risk
We recommend that experiments go through a ramp process, where we gradually increase traffic to new Treatments.
Ramping effectively requires balancing three key considerations: speed, quality, and risk.
Four Ramp Phases:
Pre-MPR (short ramps): Mitigate Risk
MPR (Maximum Power Ramp) (e.g. a week): Measure
Must be long enough to capture time-dependent factors.

While we usually get smaller variance with a longer experiment, there is a diminishing return as we wait longer. In our experience, the precision gained after a week tends to be small if there are no novelty or primacy trends in the Treatment effect.
(Optional) Post-MPR (short ramps, operational only): Mitigate Risk
(Optional) Long-term holdout (as needed): Learn
Mainly used to check the long-term Treatment effect.
There are companies that have uber holdouts, where some portion of traffic is withheld from any feature launch over a long term (often a quarter) to measure the cumulative impact across experiments.
When experiment results are surprising, a good rule of thumb is to replicate them. Rerun the experiment with a different set of users or with an orthogonal re-randomization.
16 - Scaling Experiment Analyses
If you want to increase your success rate double your failure rate - Thomas J. Watson
To get the raw instrumented data into a state suitable for computation, we need to cook the data. Cooking data typically involves the following steps:
Sort and group the data.
Clean the data (e.g. use heuristics to remove sessions that are unlikely to be real users)
Enrich the data.
Given the processed data, you can now compute the segments and metrics, and aggregate the results to get summary statistics for each experiment, including both the estimated Treatment effect itself.
Highlight key tests, such as SRM, to clearly indicate whether the results are trustworthy.
Highlight the OEC and critical metrics, but also show the many other metrics, including guardrails, quality, and so on
Present metrics as a relative change, with clear indications as to whether the results are statistically significant.
Stakeholders should have visibility into the top experiments impacting the metrics they care about.
The visualization tools can also be a gateway to accessing institutional memory.
Part 5: Advanced Topics for Analyzing Experiments
17 - The Statistics behind Online Controlled Experiments
Statistics are fundamental to designing and analyzing experiments
Two-sample t-test:
The most common statistical significance tests for determining whether the difference we see between Treatment and Control is real or just noise.

Two-sample t-tests look at the size of the difference between the two means relative to the variance. The significance of the difference is represented by the p-value. The lower the p-value, the stronger the evidence that the Treatment is different from the Control.

The p-value is the probability that T would be at least this extreme if there really is no difference between Treatment and Control. By convention, any difference with a p-value smaller than 0.05 is considered “statistically significant”.
Another way to examine whether the delta is statistically significant is to check whether the confidence interval overlaps with zero.

A 95% confidence interval is the range that covers the true difference 95% of the time and has an equivalence to a p-value of 0.05; the delta is statistically significant at 0.05 significance level if the 95% confidence interval does not contain zero or if the p-value is less than 0.05.
In most cases we compute p-values with the assumption that the t-statistic T follows a normal distribution, and under the Null hypothesis the distribution has a mean 0 and variance 1.
It is a good assumption because while the sample distribution of Y does not follow normal distribution, the average Y_hat usually does because of the Central Limit Theorem.

One rule-of-thumb for the minimum number of samples needed for the average to have normal distribution is 355s? for each variant, where s is the skewness coefficient of the sample distribution [add the formula for that coefficient]
A Type I error is concluding that there is a significant difference between Treatment and Control when there is no real difference
A Type II error is when we conclude that there is no significant difference when there really is one.
You control Type I error rates at 0.05 by concluding statistical significance only if the p-value < 0.05.

The concept of Type II errors is better known as power. Power is the probability of detecting a difference between the variants, that is, rejecting the null, when there really is a difference: Power = 1- Type II error

The industry standard is to achieve at least 80% power in our tests. Therefore, it is common to conduct power analysis before starting the experiment to decide how many samples are needed to achieve sufficient power.
Assuming Treatment and Control are of equal size, the total number of samples you need to achieve 80% power is: n ~ (16*sigma^2 / delta^2)
Where sigma is the sample variance and delta the difference between Treatment and Control

A common question people ask is that how would they know delta before they run the experiment? We know the size of delta that would matter in practice, in other words, that of practical significance. To estimate the required minimum sample size, use the smallest delta that is practically significant (also called the minimum detectable effect).
When testing multiple things in parallel, the number of false discoveries increases. This is called the "multiple testing' problem.

Most approaches are either simple but too conservative, or complex and hence less accessible. For example, the popular Bonferroni correction which uses a consistent but much smaller p-value threshold (0.05 divided by the number of tests), falls into the former category. The Benjamini-Hochberg procedure uses varying p-value thresholds for different tests and it falls into the latter category.
Two-step rule-of-thumb:
Separate all metrics into three groups:
First-order metrics: those you expect to be impacted by the experiment
Second-order metrics: those potentially to be impacted (e.g., through cannibalization
Third-order metrics: those unlikely to be impacted
Apply tiered significance levels to each group (e.g., 0.05, 0.01 and 0.001 respectively).

These rules-of-thumb are based on an interesting Bayesian interpretation: How much do you believe the Null hypothesis (Ho) is true before you even run the experiment? The stronger the belief, the lower the significance level you should use.
Fisher formalizes this intuition in his meta-analysis method (Fisher 1925), saying that we can combine p-values from multiple independent statistical tests into one test statistic.
18 - Variance Estimation and Improved Sensitivity: Pitfalls and Solutions
With great power comes small effect size - Unknown

Almost all the key statistical concepts we have introduced are related to variance, such as statistical significance, p-value, power, and confidence interval. It is imperative to not only correctly estimate variance, but also to understand how to achieve variance reduction to gain sensitivity of the statis- tical hypothesis tests.
Common Pitfalls:
Delta vs. Delta %

Ratio Metrics. When Analysis Unit Is Different from Experiment Unit: the variance formula has a critical assumption behind it: the samples need to be i.i.d. (independently identically distributed) or at least uncorrelated. This assumption is satisfied if the analysis unit is the same as the experimental (randomization) unit. It is usually violated otherwise.
In some cases we may need to resort to bootstrap method where you simulate randomization by sampling with replacement and simate the variance from many repeated simulations.
Outliers: It is critical to remove outliers when estimating variance.
One way to improve sensitivity is reducing variance, Here are some of the many ways to achieve a smaller variance:
Create an evaluation metric with a smaller variance while capturing similar information.
Transform a metric through capping, binarization or log transformation.
Use triggered analysis.
Use stratification, Control-variates or CUPED
Randomize at a more granular unit.
Design a paired experiment.

Pool Control groups: If you have several experiments splitting traffic and each has their own Control, consider pooling the separate controls to form a larger, shared Control group. Comparing each Treatment with this shared Control group increases the power for all experiments involved.
[Some considerations in case you don't use mean, but quantiles, e.g. 95th quantile for site performance]
19 - The AA Test

Running A/A tests is a critical part of establishing trust in an experimentation platform. The idea is so useful because the tests fail many times in practice, which leads to re-evaluating assumptions and identifying bugs.
The idea of an A/A test is simple: Split the users into two groups as in a regular A/B test but make B identical to A (hence the name A/A test).
If the system is operating correctly, then in repeated trials about 5% of the time a given metric should be statistically significant with p-value less than 0.05.
When conducting t-tests to compute p-values, the distribution of p-values from repeated trials should be close to a uniform distribution.
You can use A/A tests for several purposes, such as to:
Ensure that Type I errors are controlled (e.g., at 5%) as expected.
Assessing metrics' variability.
Ensure that no bias exists between Treatment and Control users, especially if reusing populations from prior experiments.
Compare data to the system of record.
Are you leaking users?
Estimate variances for statistical power calculations.
We highly recommend running continuous A/A tests in parallel with other experiments to uncover problems, including distribution mismatches and platform anomalies.
[Proceeds with some examples]

Always run a series of A/A tests before utilizing an A/B testing system. Ideally, simulate a thousand A/A tests and plot the distribution of p-values. If the distribution is far from uniform, you have a problem. Do not trust your A/B testing system before resolving this issue.
Because you are not really making a change to your product and the two variants being tested are identical, you can just simulate the A/A test:
For each iteration,pick a new randomization hash seed for user assignment and replay the last week of data, splitting users into the two groups.
Then generate the p-value for each metric of interest and accumulate them into histograms, one for each metric
Now run a goodness-of-fit test, such as Anderson-Darling or Kolmogorov- Smirnoff to assess whether the distributions are close to uniform.
[Explain how to diagnose issues and fix them]

Even after an AVA test passes, we recommend regularly running A/A tests concurrently with your A/B tests to identify regressions in the system or a new metric that is failing because its istribution has changed or because outliers started showing up.
20 - Triggering for Improved Sensitivity
Triggering provides experimenters with a way to improve sensitivity (statistical power) by filtering out noise created by users who could not have been impacted by the experiment.
[Provide some examples on use cases of Triggering]
In practice, it is sometimes easier to do a non-optimal but conservative triggering, such as including more users than is optimal.
When computing the Treatment effect on the triggered population, you must dilute the effect to the overall user base, sometimes called diluted impact or side-wide impact.

If you improved the revenue by 3% for 10% of users, did you improve your overall revenue by 10%*3% = 0.3%? NO! (common pitfall). The overall impact could be anywhere from 0% to 3%! (Depending on The logic of your triggering, see after for examples)
There are two checks you should do to ensure a trustworthy use of triggering:
Sample Ratio Mismatch
Complement analysis. Generate a scorecard for never triggered users
Common Pitfalls:
Experimenting on Tiny Segments That Are Hard to Generalize
Triggered User Is Not Properly Triggered for the Remaining Experiment Duration
Performance Impact of Counterfactual Logging
Plotting a metric over time with increasing numbers of users usually leads to false trends.
21 - Sample Ratio Mismatch and Other Trust-Related Guardrail Metrics

There are two types of guardrail metrics: organizational and trust-related. Sample Ratio Mismatch (SRM) is a trust-related guardrail. The SRM guardrail should be included for every experiment, as it is used to ensure the internal validity and trustworthiness of the experiment results.

When the p-value for the Sample Ratio metric is low, that is, the probability of observing such a ratio or more extreme conditioned on the design ratio, there is a sample ratio mismatch (SRM), and all other metrics are probably invalid. You can use a standard t-test or chi-squared test to compute the p-value.
Here are some causes of SRMs:
Buggy randomization of users.
Data pipeline issues
Residual effects
Bad trigger condition
Triggering based on attributes impacted by the experiment
Debugging SRMs:
Validate that there is no difference upstream of the randomization point or trigger point.
Validate that variant assignment is correct.
Follow the stages of the data processing pipeline to see whether any cause an SRM.
Exclude the initial period. Is it possible that both variants did not start together?
Look at the Sample Ratio for segments
Look at the intersection with other experiments
At Bing over 50% of traffic in the United States is filtered out as bots, and 90% of traffic in China and Russia is bot generated!

In some cases, if the SRM is understood, it is possible to fix the cause during the analysis phase. However, in other cases the removal of traffic implies that some segments have not been properly exposed to the Treatment, and it is better to rerun the experiment.
Other Trust-Related Guardrail Metrics
Telemetry fidelity.
Cache hit rates.
Cookie write rate - the rate that the variant writes permanent (non-session) cookies.
Quick queries.
22 - Leakage and Interference between Variants

In most experiment analyses, We assume that the behavior of each unit in the experiment is unaffected by variant assignment to other units. This is a plausible assumption in most practical applications. However, there are also many cases where this assumption fails.

If the SUTVA (Stable Unit Treatment Value Assumption) assumption does not hold, the analysis results in potentially incorrect conclusions. We define interference as a violation of SUTVA, sometimes called spillover or leakage between the variants.

There are two ways interference may arise: through direct or indirect connections. As an example, two units can be directly connected if they are friends on a social network or if they visited the same physical space at the same time Indirect connections are connections that exist because of certain latent variables or shared resources, such as units in Treatment and Control that share the same ad campaign budget.
[Proceeds with a list of examples of direct and indirect connections]

[Notable indirect connection] Uber/Lyft. Imagine that Uber wants to test a different "'surge price" algorithm that is so awesome that riders in Treatment are more likely to opt-in for a ride. Now there are fewer drivers available on the road, the price for the Control group goes up leading to fewer riders. As a result, the delta comparing the Treatment and Control groups is overestimated.
Practical solutions:
Rule-of-Thumb: Ecosystem Value of an Action
You can identify actions that can potentially spill over, and only have concern about interference if these actions are materially impacted in an experiment
Once you identify metrics indicative of a downstream impact, you can establish general guidance for how each action translates to values or engagement for the whole ecosystem.
By nature, rule-of-thumb is only an approximation and may not work for all scenarios.
Isolation: Interference happens through a medium connecting the Treatment and Control groups. You can remove potential interference by identifying the medium and isolating each variant.
Possible ways:
Splitting shared resources: If a shared resource is causing interference, splitting it between Treatment and Control is the obvious first choice.

Geo-based randomization: It's reasonable to assume that units (hotels, taxis, riders, etc.) from different regions are isolated from each other. This lets you randomize at the region level to isolate the interference between Treatment and Control.
One caveat: randomizing at the geo level limits the sample size by the number of available geo locations. This leads to a bigger variance and less power for A/B tests.
Time-based randomization: You can create isolation using time. At any time t, you could flip a coin and decide whether to give all users Treatment or all users Control.
Network-cluster randomization: Similar to geo-based randomization, on social networks, we construct "clusters" of nodes that are close to each other based on their likelihood to interfere.
Network ego-centric randomization: clusters are constructed by minimizing the edge cut between the clusters and each cluster does not employ a specific structure.
Whenever applicable, always combine isolation methods to get a larger sample size.
23 - Measuring Long-Term Treatment Effects
Sometimes the effect that you care to measure can take months or even years to accumulate a long-term effect. Trying to measure a long-term effect is challenging.

There are scenarios where the long-term effect is different from the short-term effect. For example, raising prices is likely to increase short-term revenue but reduce long- term revenue as users abandon the product or service.
One key challenge in determining the OEC is that it must be measurable in the short term but believed to causally impact long-term objectives.
Reasons the Treatment Effect May Differ between Short-Term and Long-Term
User-learned effects. As users learn and adapt to a change, their behavior change.
Network effect. User behavior tends to be influenced by people in their network though it may take a while for a feature to reach its full effect as it propagates through their network.
Delayed experience and measurement. There can be a time gap before a user experiences the entirety of the Treatment effect.
Ecosystem change. Many things in your ecosystem change over time and can impact how users react to the Treatment.
We measure the long-term effect on some experiments so we can extrapolate to other experiments.

The simplest and most popular approach for measuring long-term effects is to keep an experiment running for a long time. You can measure the Treatment effect at the beginning of the experiment (in the first week) and at the end of the experiment (in the last week).
While this is a viable solution, there are several challenges and limitations in this type of long-term experiment design:
For attribution: The measurement from the last week of the long-running experiment (pAr) may not represent the truc long-term Treatment effect
Survivorship bias. Not all users at the beginning of the experiment will survive to the end of the experiment.
Interaction with other new features. There can be many other features launched while the long-term experiment is running, and they may interact with the specific feature being tested.
Alternative Methods for Long-Running Experiment:
Cohort Analysis: You can construct a stable cohort of users before starting the experiment and only analyze the short-term and long-term effects on this cohort of users.

Post-Period Analysis: In this method, you turn off the experiment after it has been running for a while (time T) and then measure the difference between the users in Treatment and those in Control during time T and T+ 1.
Time-Staggered Treatments: [help to determine how long is “long enough” to run the experiment]
Holdback and Reverse Experiment:
Holdback is keeping 10% of users in Control for several weeks (or months) after launching the Treatment to 90% users.
In a reverse experiment, we ramp 10% of users back into the Control several weeks (or months) after launching the Treatment to 100% of users.

paragraphs: LaBerge S. - Exploring the World of Lucid Dreaming
Exercises/action points/stuff to do:
Cataloging your dreamsigns
Keep a dream journal
(When you have collected at least a dozen dreams) Catalog your dreamsigns
Classify each dreamsign using the dreamsign inventory (inner awareness, action, form, context)
Pick target dreamsign categories
Practice looking for dreamsigns while you are awake
“Am I dreaming?”
One way to become lucid is to ask yourself whether or not you are dreaming while you are dreaming. In order to do this, you should make a habit of asking the question while awake.
Look around for any oddities or inconsistencies that might indicate you are dreaming. Do you have any trouble remembering what just happened?
Possible checks:
Jump trying to prolong your time off the ground. If you stay airborne for even a split second longer than normal, you can be sure you're dreaming.
Find some writing and read it once, look away, then reread it, check to see if it stays the same.
Check your watch twice
If you find yourself suspecting you are dreaming, you probably are!
Choose in advance certain occasion when you intend to remember to test your state (e.g. arriving back home from work, every hour on the our, when you check your daily tasks,...)
Decide in advance what you would like to do in your next lucid dream, and imagine doing that.
Periodically checking and acknowledging reality it's an enjoyable habit to cultivate, even without lucid dreams.
Prospective memory training (Pag. 76).

Basically you have to remember to ask yourself If you're awake each day when 4 things happen. And these things change every day. Read them only in the morning and rely on yourself (no external events) to check your status.
Look in the book for more details
Notes:
There are two distinct kinds of sleep: a quiet phase and an active phase. Changes in brain waves, eye movements, and muscle tone are used to define the two states.
If you're awaken in the quite phase, you'll rarely remember dreams.

During the active sleep phase, also called rapid eye movement or REM sleep, your eyes move rapidly about as much as they would if you were awake. You dream vividly and have an erection if you are male and increased vaginal blood flow If you're female. Your body remains almost completely still, to prevent you from acting out your dreams.
Quiet sleep is divided into three substages:
Stage 1: transitional state between drowsy wakefulness and light sleep
Stage 2: bona fide sleep
Stage 3: delta sleep

Approximately seventy to ninety minutes after sleep onset, you enter REM sleep for the first time of the night. After five or ten minutes of REM, and possibly following a brief awakening in which you would likely remember a dream, you sink back to stage 2 and possibly delta.
About REM:
The length of the REM periods increase as the night proceeds
The intervals between REM periods decrease with time (from ninety minutes to perhaps twenty to thirty)
The direction of dreamers' physical eye movement during REM was sometimes exactly the same as the direction that they reported looking in their dreams.
To prove lucid dream exists, he moved the eyes in the dream in a prearranged fashion, and the machine at the lab recorded it while he was in REM phase.
Don't try too hard. If you find you are losing sleep while struggling to have lucid dreams without results, let go of your efforts for a while.
Before it will be worth your time to work on lucid dream induction methods, you should be able to recall at least one dream every night.
You have to get plenty of sleep.

Dreams are not recalled unless the sleeper awakens directly from them. Try setting an alarm clock to awaken you at a time when you are likely to be dreaming. Multiple of ninety minutes from your bedtime.
Don't move from the position in which you awaken. Don't think of the day's concerns.
If you don't remember, keep trying for several minutes, without moving or thinking of anything else.
Try reviving the dream in reverse.
Dream journal should be the first thing you do in the morning. Record feelings, emotional reactions and unusual stuff. Record anything you remember.

Recurrent details are dreamsigns: go through your journal to spot them and recognize them in the next dream. They are unique for you. They could be: inner awareness, action, form (or shape of things) and context .
Wake up 2 hours before you should, do some stuff for 2 hours, then sleep 2 hours again. (Note: seems a bit too much) There's also an exercise to help you in this.
Have the presleep intention to recognize you are dreaming.
Intention and association are crucial to remember to check if you are sleeping.
MILD (Mnemonic Induction of Lucid Dreams procedure)
Set up dream recall
Recall your dream
Focus your intent
See yourself becoming lucid
Repeat

The most common strategy to induce WILD (Wake-Initiated Lucid Dream) is to fall asleep while focusing on the hypnagogic imagery that accompanies sleep onset. (relax completely, observe the visual images (just watch without attachment or desire for action), enter the dream (you shouldn't want to enter the dream, but be carried into it passively)).
At first you'll see a sequence of disconnected, fleeting patterns and images, that will gradually develop onto scenes.
It then gives other examples of way to achieve WILD (e.g. Tibetan).

Another strategy is to lie in bed relaxed, but vigilant, and perform a repetitive mental task. As long as you continue to perform the mental task, your mind will remain awake (e.g. relax, count to yourself (“1 I'm dreaming, 2 I'm dreaming, …), realize you are dreaming). This would be better with an assistant that wakes you up when he realizes you fell asleep.

Even if you find that despite your best efforts to stay asleep you still wake up, all is not lost. Play dead. If you remain perfectly motionless upon waking from a lucid (or nonlucid) dream and deeply relax your body, there is a good chance that REM sleep will reassert itself and you will have an opportunity to enter a lucid dream consciously.
Talk to yourself in a lucid dream, remind yourself that this is a dream.
If the secret to preventing premature awakening is to maintain active participation in the dream, the secret to awakening at will is to withdraw your attention and participation from the dream.
[N.B.: next one are my very summarized notes on content of next chapters]
You can practice skills and work on problems from your wake life in your dreams, and the skills acquired will follow you in wake life. (E.g. solve work problems or practice public speaking)
The fact that your brain works differently while you dream, help with creativity.

“I never run away from things or persons in my dreams anymore. And the strange thing is that in waking life I don't run away either, anymore. I face things head on and don't drag situations out forever.”
In nightmares we are alone.

If you become fully lucid in a nightmare, you will realize that the nightmare can't really hurt you, and you don't need to 'escape' it by awakening. You will remember that you are already safe in bed. It is better to face and overcome the terror while remaining in the dream.
One-third to one-half of all adults experience occasional nightmares.

I do not see every dream as necessarily the expression of a wish. The anxiety experienced in nightmares can be seen as an indication of the failure of the dreamer to respond effectively to the dream situation.
Fear is your worst enemy in dreams; if you allow it to persist it will grow stronger and your self-confidence will diminish.

Anytime I realized I was dreaming, I was required to ask myself the following two questions: (1) Am I now or have I been running away from anything in the dream? (2) Is there now or has there been any conflict in the dream? If the answer was yes to either, then I was honor-bound to do everything I could to face whatever 1 was avoiding and to resolve any conflict.
If in dreams you encounter threatening figures, try to have conciliatory behavior instead of fighting them.
Hostile dream figures may rep- resent aspects of our own personalities that we wish to disown.
You can turn a frightening, negative experience into one that is fun and useful.
Conciliatory behavior toward threatening figures would generally cause them to look and act in a more friendly manner.
List of possible nightmares and how to face them:
Being Pursued.
Response: Stop running.
Being Attacked.
Response: Don't give in meekly tO the attack or flee.
Falling.
Response: Relax and allow yourself to land.
Paralysis.
Response: When you feel trapped, stuck, or paralyzed, relax. Don't allow anxiety to overcome your rationality.

Being Unprepared for an Examination or Speech. Response: You can leave the exam or lecture room. Or creatively answering the test questions or giving spontaneous talk on whatever topic suits you. Be sure to enjoy yourself.
Being Naked in Public.
Response: Who cares in a dream? Have fun with the idea.
Rehearsal (redreaming) can help people overcome recurrent nightmares.
We propose that in your lucid dreams you can benefit from seeking out difficulties, facing and overcoming them.
You can use lucid dream to meet someone who died, to say the last words to them and to start accepting their death. (Or same things for breakups)
Lucid dreaming can help people settle unfinished emotional business with family members and intimate friends.

Mindfulness is a state of attentive awareness in which environmental information is consciously controlled and manipulated while people are engaged in the process of making new distinctions and constructing new categories. Mindlessness, in contrast, is a state of reduced awareness, in which people process information from their en- vironments in an automatic manner.

Our mental functioning in ordinary dreams frequently exhibits remarkable mindlessness; this is how we can fail to notice and correctly interpret the most absurd anom-alies. Mental functioning during lucid dreams, in contrast, is characterized by mindfulness.
Properly practiced, lucid dreaming can enhance your ability to mindfully look for a better way of doing things.

Lucid dreaming might be useful for physical as well as mental healing. Although this is one of the most speculative ideas for the applica- tion of lucid dreaming, anecdotal and theoretical evidence supports the possibility.

The experimental reality, or vividness of mental imagery, determines how strongly it affects physiology. Dreams, which everyone experiences every night, are also the most vivid form of mental imagery most people are likely to experience under normal circumstances.
Therefore, they are also likely to be a source of highly effective healing imagery.
Why should we not be able to initiate self-healing processes by consciously envisioning our dream bodies as perfectly healthy during our lucid dreams?
“If we heal the dream body, to what extent will we also heal the physical body?”
My findings are that healing is possible in lucid dreams.
Of course, these stories are anecdotal. We have no way of knowing whether lucid dreaming had anything to do with the reported improvements.
In dreams you can ask existential questions and get your in deep interpretation answers to them.
Dreams are a reservoir of knowledge and experi- ence, yet they are often overlooked as a vehicle for exploring reality.
Realizing that our experience of reality is subjective. rather than direct and true, may have practical implications.
When you realize that everything is like a dream, you attain pure awareness. And the way to attain this awareness is to realize that all experience is like a dream.
The mind cannot contain anything but thoughts.
Who we really are is not necessarily the same as who we believe ourselves to be. We are not who we think we are in our dreams (or indeed while awake).
What you see in your dreams as yourself it is only an image, a mental model of your self, or to use the Freudian term, your “ego”.
The less we identify with who we think we are, the more likely we are to discover who we really are.

How quickly you can learn this skill depends on a number of factors, such as what other matters are demanding your attention, or how well you remember your dreams. Nevertheless, perseverance will pay off.
Be sure to devote sufficient time to developing the basic skills necessary for practicing the induction techniques.
Gives a list of exercises to train your will and to improve concentration and visualization
