paragraphs: Pattern recognition and machine learning notes
I’ll try to write down only interesting things and things that can be written without mathematical notation (I underlined a lot of formulas and mathematical definitions, I’ll skip those):

If we had been asked which box had been chosen before being told the identity of the selected item of fruit, then the most complete information we have available is provided by the probability P(B). We call this the prior probability because it is the probability available before we observe the identity of the fruit. Once we are told that the fruit is orange, we can then use Bayes’ theorem to compute the probability p(B|F), which we shall call the poster probability because it is the probability obtained after we have observed F.

A widely used frequentist estimator is maximum likelihood, in which w is set to the value that maximises the likelihood function p(D|w). This corresponds to choosing the value of w for which the probability of the observed data set is maximised.

Curse of dimensionality: the problem with an exponentially large number of cells is that we would need an exponentially large quantity of training data in order to ensure that the cells are not empty.

Our geometrical intuitions, formed through a life spent in a space of three dimensions, can fail badly when we consider spaces of higher dimensionality. In spaces of high dimensionality, most of the volume of a sphere is concentrated in a tiny shell near the surface! Also curse of dimensionality: not all intuitions developed in spaces of low dimensionality will generalise to spaces of many dimensions.

Reject option: use an automatic system to classify images for which there is little doubt as to the correct class, while leaving a human expert to classify the most ambiguous cases, introducing a threshold.
Reason to compute the posterior probabilities:
Minimizing risk
Reject option
Compensating for class priors
Combining models
The entropy is the lower bound on the number of bits needed to transmit the state of a random variable.

The Gaussian distribution is the one that maximises entropy for a given mean and variance (or covariance). The distribution that maximises the differential entropy is the Gaussian. We get a Gaussian distribution when we have the sum of different random variables. The sum of two Gaussian variables is again Gaussian
Kullback-Leibler divergence is the average additional amount of information. It also measure the dissimilarity of two distributions.
There is an intimate relationship between data compression and density estimation.
Parametric distributions, governed by a small number of adaptive parameters.
Nonparametric distributions, still contain parameters, but control the model complexity rather then the form of distribution.
Parametric Distributions:
Bernoulli (example: one coin toss)
Binomial (example: multiple coin toss)
Beta
Multinomial (generalisation of Bernoulli for more than two outcomes)
Dirichlet
Gamma
Gaussian (or Normal)
Conditional Gaussian
Mixtures of Gaussians
Student’s t
Gaussian-Gamma
Gaussian-Wishart
Exponential
Uniform
Von Mises
Wishart (the conjugate prior for the precision matrix of a multivariate Gaussian)
Nonparametric Distributions:
Histogram
K-Nearest Neighbour
Kernel density estimators

In many cases we may have little idea of what form the distribution should take. We may then seek a form of prior distribution, called a noninformative prior, which is intended to have as little influence on the posterior distribution as possible (‘letting the data speak for themselves’).
Gamma distribution with a0 = b0 = 0 is a noninformative prior.

Histogram technique can be useful for obtaining a quick visualisation of data in one or two dimensions but is unsuited to most density estimation applications, because of discontinuities and scaling with dimensionality.

Either we can fix K (number of points) and determine the value of V (volume) from the data, which gives rise to the K-Nearest Neighbour technique, or we can fix V and determine K from data, giving rise to the kernel approach. Both methods require the entire training data set to be stored, leading to expensive computation if the data set is large.
The goal of regression is to predict the value of one or more continuous target variables t given the value of a D-dimensional vector x of input variables.
Batch techniques can be computationally costly for large data sets. It may be worthwhile to use a sequential algorithms, also known as on-line algorithms.

Regularization allows complex models to be trained on data sets of limited size without severe overfitting, essentially by limiting the effective model complexity. The problem of determining the optimal model complexity is then shifted from one of fining the appropriate number of basis functions to one of determining a suitable value of the regularization coefficient.

Bias-variance trade-off: The expected value of the error is made by two terms: The first term, called the squared bias, represents the extent to which the average prediction over all data sets differs from the desired regression function. The second term, called the variance, measures the extent to which the solutions for individual data sets vary around their average, and hence this measures the extent to which the output function is sensitive to the particular choice of data set.
In a practical application, therefore, it will be wise to keep aside an independent test set of data on which to evaluate the overall performance of the final system.
A discriminant is a function that takes an input vector and assigns it to one of the K classes. Linear discriminants are those for which the decision surfaces are hyperplanes.
The use of K-1 classifiers each of which solves a two-class problem of separating points in a particular class from points not in that class is known as one-versus-the-rest classifier.

The use of K(K-1)/2 binary discriminant functions, one for every possible pair of classes is know as one-versus-one classifier. Each point is the classified according to a majority vote amongst the discriminant functions.
One way to view a linear classification model is in terms of dimensionality reduction (projecting to one dimension using the weights, from x to y).
The Fisher criterion is defined to be the ratio of the between-class variance to the within-class variance.

The perceptron learning rule is not guaranteed to reduce the total error function at each stage. The perceptron convergence theorem states that if there exists an exact solution, then the perceptron learning algorithm is guaranteed to find an exact solution in a finite number of steps.
For dataset that are not linearly separable, the perceptron learning algorithm will never converge.
The inverse of the logistic sigmoid is known as legit function.
The normalised exponential is also known as the softmax function.

Logistic regression is a model for classification rather than regression. Maximum likelihood can exhibit severe over-fitting for datasets that are linearly separable, that could be solved by adding regularisation term.
For Logistic Regression, there is no longer a closed-form solution, but the error function is convex.
The feed-forward neural network, also known as multilayer perceptron: the model comprises multiple layers of logistic regression models with continuous nonlinearities.
The neural network model is simply a nonlinear function from a set of input variables to a set of output variables controlled by a vector of adjustable parameters.

If the activation functions of all the hidden units in a network are taken to be linear, then for any such network we can always find an equivalent network without hidden units. This follows from the fact that the composition of successive linear transformations is itself a linear transformation.

Neural networks are therefore said to be universal approximations. A two-layers network with linear outputs can uniformly approximate any continuous function on a compact input domain to arbitrary accuracy provided the network has sufficiently large number of hidden units.
The first layer of the network can be viewed as performing a nonlinear feature extraction.
For:
Regression we use linear outputs and sum-of-squares error
Binary classification we use logistic sigmoid outputs and a cross-entropy error function
Multiclass classification we use softmax outputs with the corresponding multiclass cross-entropy error function.
Multiclass classification with two classes we can use a single logistic sigmoid output or two outputs with softmax.

Backpropagation: forward propagate the input through the network to find the activation of all the hidden units. Then compute the derivative of the loss with respect to the wight in a backwards fashion.
The Jacobian matrix is the derivatives of the network outputs with respect to the inputs, evaluated with all other inputs held fixed.
The Hessian matrix is the second derivatives of the error.
Choose a relatively large value of network size and then control complexity by the addition of a regularisation term to the error function.

Early stopping: usually the error is a non increasing function of the iteration index. However, the error measured with respect to independent data, generally called validation set, often shows a decrease at first, followed by an increase as the network start to over-fit. Training can be therefore stopped at the point of smallest error with respect to the validation set.
In some cases, predictions should be unchanged, or invariant, under one or more transformations of the input variables. Approaches to face this:
Training set is augmented using replicas of the training patterns, transformed according to the desired invariance (it’s seen that can also improve generalization). (Data Augmentation)
A regularization term is added to the error function changes in the model output when the input is transformed.
Invariance is built into the pre-processing by extracting features that are invariant under the required transformations.
Build the invariance properties into the structure of a neural network. (Convolutional Neural Networks)
Tikhonov regularization is related to the addition of random noise to the inputs, which has been shown to improve generalization in appropriate circumstances.

The way Convolutional Neural Networks build the invariance properties into the structure of a neural network is by extracting local features that depend only on small subregions of the image. Information from such features can then be merged in later stages of processing in order to detect higher-order features and ultimately to yield information about the image as a whole. Local features that are useful in one region of the image are likely to be useful in other regions of the image as well.
Concepts in CNNs
Local receptive fields
Weight sharing
Subsampling

There may be several feature maps in a given convolutional layer for each plane of units in the previous subsampling layer, so that the gradual reduction in spatial resolution is then compensated by an increasing number of features. The final layer of the neural network would typically be a fully connected, fully adaptive layer, with a softmax output nonlinearity in the case of multiclass classification.

There is a class of pattern recognition techniques, in which the training data points, or a subset of them, are kept and used also during the prediction phase. Like nearest neighbours. Memory-based methods that involve storing the entire training set in order to make predictions for future data points. They are generally fast to “train”, but slow at making predictions.
A Gaussian process model makes predictions that lie on the entire real axis, so we have to then transform it using a logistic sigmoid.

Maximum Margin Classifiers -> Margin is defined to be the smallest distance between the decision boundary and any of the samples. In support vector machines the decision boundary is chosen to be the one for which the margin is maximised.
By definition there will be at least two active constraints -> Support vectors.
Quadratic programming problem: we are trying to minimise a quadratic function subject to a set of linear inequality constraints.
In practice, the class-conditional distributions may overlap, in which case exact separation of the training data can lead to poor generalization.

To solve this we allow data points to be on the ‘wrong side’ of the margin boundary, but with a penalty that increases linearly with the distance from that boundary. We introduce then slack variables. The parameter C is therefore analogous to (the inverse of) a regularization coefficient.
Although predictions for new inputs are made using only the support vectors, the training phase makes use of the whole data set.

There are also single-class support vector machines, which solve an unsupervised learning problem related to probability density estimation. Instead of modelling the density of data, however, these methods aim to find a smooth boundary enclosing a region of high density.
The outputs of a SVM represent decisions rather than posterior probabilities. The relevance vector machine (RVM) solve this. They have relevance vectors (instead of support vectors).

RVM is found to give models that are typically an order of magnitude more compact than the corresponding SVM, with little or no reduction in generalization error compared with the corresponding SVM. Training time, though, can be longer. This is offset by the avoidance of cross-validation runs to set the model complexity parameters (you don’t need regularization for RVM). Furthermore, the computation time on test points, which is usually the more important consideration in practice, is typically much less.
Probabilistic graphical models are diagrammatic representation of probability distributions.

A graph comprises nodes (also called vertices) connected by links (also known as edges or arcs). Each node represents a random variable (or group of random variables), and the link express probabilistic relationship between these variables.
Directed graphs are useful for expressing causal relationships between random variables, whereas undirected graphs are better suited to expressing soft constraints between random variables.

First we introduce one node for each of the random variables a, b, and c and associate each node with the corresponding conditional distribution. Then for each conditional distribution we add direct links to the graph from the nodes corresponding to the variables on which the distribution is conditioned.
There must be no direct cycles. Such graphs are also called Directed Acyclic Graphs, or DAGs.

Generative models: we start with the lowest-numbered node and draw a sample from its distribution. We work trough each of the nodes in order or conditional distributions. We will have achieved our objective of obtaining a sample from the joint distribution.

The primary role of the low-numbered variables (latent) is to allow a complicated distribution over the observed variables to be represented in terms of a model constructed from simpler conditional distributions.
A Markov random field has a set of nodes each of which corresponds to a variable group of variables, as well as a set of links each of which connects a pair of nodes. The links are undirected.

A clique is a subset of nodes in a graph such that there exists a link between all pairs of nodes in the subset. A maximal clique is a clique such that it is not possible to include any other nodes from the graph in the set without it ceasing to be a clique.
A tree is defined such that there is a single node, called root, which has no parents, and all other nodes have one parent.
Intuitively, we might think of a cluster as comprising a group of data points whose inter-point distances are small compared with the distances to points outside of the cluster.

K-means Clustering: first we choose some initial values for the means then in the first phase we minimise the loss with respect to points, keeping the means fixed (we assign points to the nearest center), then in the second phase we minimise the loss with respect to the means, keeping the points fixed (we overwrite each mean with the mean point of corresponding cluster).
Because each step minimizes the loss, convergence is assured. However, it could converge to a local minimum rather than global minimum.
A good initialisation procedure would be to choose the initial cluster centres to be equal to a random subset of the data points.

The K-means algorithm is based on the use of squared Euclidean distance. Not only this limit the type of data variables that can be considered (e.g. categorical), but it can also make the determination of the cluster means non robust to outliers.
Every data point is assigned to uniquely to one, and only one, of the clusters.
The goal of segmentation is to partition an image into regions each of which has a reasonably homogeneous visual appearance or which corresponds to objects or part of objects.

We can also use the result of a clustering algorithm to perform data compression. It is important to distinguish between lossless data compression (reconstruct the data exactly from the compression) and lossy data compression (we accept some reconstruction errors).

EM for Gaussian mixtures: we first choose some initial values for the mean, covariances and mixing coefficients, then we alternate between the expectation (use current values for the parameters to evaluate the posterior probability) and the maximisation (we re-estimate the means, covariances and mixing coefficients) step.
EM algorithms takes more iterations to reach convergence compared with the K-means algorithm, and each cycle requires significantly more computation.
EM algorithms breaks down the potentially difficult problem of maximising the likelihood function in two stages the E step and the M step, each of which will often prove simpler to implement.

Whereas K-means algorithm performs a hard assignment of data points to clusters, in which each data point is associated uniquely with one cluster, the EM algorithm makes a soft assignment based on the posterior probabilities.
The general idea behind sampling methods is to obtain a set of samples drawn independently form a distribution.

To sample randomly from a distribution, you just have to have its integral and a way to sample from uniform distribution (you just project what you get from uniform to the integral) (uniform on the y -> project on the integral -> project down to x).
A first-order Markov chain is defined to be a series of random variables such that the conditional independence property holds for all variables but the last one.
There is also second order Markov chain and Mth order Markov chain.

Gibbs sampling: each step involves replacing the value of one of the variables by a value drawn from the distribution of that variable conditioned on the values of the remaining variables. This procedure is repeated either by cycling through the variables in some particular order or by choosing the variable to be updated at each step at random from some distribution.

In Blocking Gibbs sampling algorithm you choose blocks of variables, not necessarily disjoint, and then sampling jointly from the variables in each block in turn, conditioned on the remaining variables.
Many data sets have the property that the data points all lie close to a manifold of much lower dimensionality than that of the original data space.

Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is widely used for applications such as dimensionality reduction, lossy data compression, feature extraction, and data visualisation. The algorithm seeks a space of lower dimensionality, known as principal subspace, such that the orthogonal projection of the data points onto this subspace maximises the variance of the projected points. An alternative definition of PCA is based on minimising the sum-of-squares of the projection errors.
The variance will be a maximum when we set the transformation matrix equal to the eigenvector having the largest eigenvalue. The first eigenvector is known as the first principal component.
PCA still holds if you don’t reduce dimensionality. In that case there is no dimensionality reduction but simply a rotation of the coordinate axes to align with principal components.
Standardizing means linear rescaling of each individual variable such that each of those has zero mean and unit variance. (With PCA we give the data zero mean ad unit covariance).

One approach is to plot the eigenvalue spectrum for the dataset, and look to see if the eigenvalues naturally form two groups comprising a set of small values separated by a significant gap from a set of relatively large values, indicating a natural choice for M. In practice, such a gap is often not seen.
Kernel PCA: a dataset in the original data space is projected by a nonlinear transformation into a feature space. PCA is then performed in the feature space.

Autoassociative neural networks ([My note] or Autoencoders) : if the hidden units have linear activation functions, then it’s the same as a PCA. Having nonlinear activation functions effectively performs a nonlinear principal component analysis.

MultiDimensional Scaling (MDS) finds low-dimensional projection of the data such as to preserve, as closely as possible, the pairwise distances between data points, and involves finding the eigenvectors of the distance matrix.

In Isometrical Feature Map, or Isomap, the goal is to project the data to a lower-dimensional space using MDS, but where the dissimilarities are defined in terms of the geodesic distances measured along the manifold.
Independence is a sufficient condition for two variables to be uncorrelated. Zero correlation is not a sufficient condition for independence.
Hidden Markov models can be viewed as specific instance of a the state space model in which the latent variables are discrete.
We might train L different models and then make predictions using the average of the predictions made by each model. Such combinations of model are sometimes called committees (mixture of experts).

One important variant of the committee method, known as boosting, involves training multiple models in sequence in which the error function used to train a particular model depends on the performance of the previous models.

The average error of a model can be reduced by a factor of M simply averaging M versions of the model. Unfortunately, it depends on the key assumption that the errors due to the individual models are uncorrelated. In practice, the errors are typically highly correlated, and the reduction in overall error is generally small. It can be shown that there is reduction anyways.
AdaBoost, short for ‘adaptive boosting’ can give good results even if the base classifiers have a performance that is only slightly better than random (weak learners).

The base classifiers are trained in sequence, and weighting coefficient associated with each data point depends on the performance of the previous classifier. Points that are misclassified by one of the base classifiers are given greater weight when used to train the next classifier in the sequence. Once all the classifiers have been trained, their predictions are then combined through a weighted majority voting scheme.
Each base learners consists of a threshold on one of the input variables. This simple classifier corresponds to a form of decision tree known as ‘decision stumps’, a decision tree with a single node.

Tree-based Models work by partitioning the input space into cuboid regions, whose edges are aligned with the axes, and then assigning a simple model (for example, a constant) to each region. They can be viewed as a model combination method in which only one model is responsible for making predictions at any given point in input space. In regression we might simply predict a constant over each region, or in classification we might assign each region to a specific class.
They are readily interpretable by humans.
The optimal value of the predictive variable within any given region is just given by the average of the values for those data points that fall in that region.

Greedy optimisation is generally done by starting with a single root node, and then growing the tree by adding nodes one at a time. For a given choice of split variable and threshold, the optimal choice of predictive variable is given by the local average od the data. This is repeated for all possible choices of variable to be split, and the one that gives the smallest residual sum-of-squares error is retained.

We stop adding nodes when the residual error falls below some threshold. It is also common to use a stopping criterion based on the number of data points associated with the leaf nodes, and then prune back the resulting tree. The pruning is based on a criterion that balances residual error against a measure of model complexity.

Cons: the particular tree structure is very sensitive to the details of the data set, the splits are aligned with the axes of the feature space (which may be very suboptimal) and the splits in a decision tree are hard, so that each region of input space is associated with one, and only one, leaf node model (in regression we’re typically aiming to model smooth functions, and yet the tree model produces piecewise-constant predictions with discontinuities at the split boundaries).
The rank of a matrix is the maximum number of linearly independent rows (or equivalently the maximum number of linearly independent columns).
In general, the eigenvalues of a matrix are complex numbers, but for symmetric matrices the eigenvalues are real.
Lagrange Multipliers
Peace is every step notes
Some of the stuff I underlined:
Although attempting to bring about world peace through the internal transformation of individuals is difficult, it is the only way. Love, compassion, and altruism are the fundamental basis for peace.
‘Peace is every step.
It turns the endless path to joy.’
Peace is not external or to be sought after or attained. Living mindfully, slowing down and enjoying each step and each breath, is enough.

In the midst of our society’s emphasis on speed, efficiency, and material success, Thich Nhat Hanh’s ability to walk calmly with peace and awareness and to teach us to do the same has led to his enthusiastic reception in the West.
Forming a smile in your face can relax hundreds of muscles in our body.
In the rush of modern life, we tend to lose touch with the peace that is available in each moment.
Peace is present right here and now, in ourselves and in everything we do and see. The question is whether or not we are in touch with it.
We are very good at preparing to live, but not very good at living.
Planning for the future is a part of life. But even planning can only take place in the present moment.
How can you remember to smile when you wake up? You might hang a reminder.

Conscious breathing: as you breathe in, you say yourself, “Breathing in, I know that I am breathing in”. And as you breathe out, say, “Breathing out, I know that I am breathing out”. You can also use only two words: “In” and “Out”.
This technique can help you keep your mind on your breath.
We can practice conscious breathing wherever we are, at any time throughout the day.
What is preventing us from being happy right now?
“In” and “Out” is not thinking, are only words to help us concentrate on our breathing.
Our senses are our windows to the world.
Watching a bad TV program, we become the TV program.
Whether we are in the city, the countryside, or the wilderness, we need to sustain ourselves by choosing our surroundings carefully and nourishing our awareness in each moment.

We can breathe mindfully in any position, but the sitting position is the most stable. You can sit cross-legged, sit on a chair, or lie on the floor. Feel free to adjust your position, but do it slowly and attentively.
You do not have to carry a bell. You can use any sound to remind you to pause, breathe in and out, and enjoy the present moment.
I did not think of the future, I did not regret the past. I was entirely in the present moment.
We may see the people around us, but if we lack mindfulness they are just phantoms, and we ourselves are also ghosts. Practicing mindfulness enables us to become a real person.
The purpose of eating is to eat.

When the food is on the table and everyone is seated, practice breathing three times. We look at each person and smile at him or her. After this, we look down at the food in a way that allows the food to become real.
Walking meditation can be very enjoyable. Walking not in order to arrive, but just to walk. Just enjoy the present moment.

Our walking is usually more like running. When we do walking meditation outside, we walk a little slower than our normal pace, and we coordinate our breathing with our steps (e.g. three steps with each in-breath and three with each out-breath).

Next time you hear the phone ring ([My note] or a notification), breathe in a and our consciously, smile to yourself, and recite this verse “Listen, listen. This wonderful sound brings me back to my true self”.
We don’t like being so busy, but every time we have a spare moment, we are afraid of being alone with ourselves. We want to escape.
Wherever we go, our “self” will be with us.

The next time you see a red light, please smile at it and go back to your breathing. The next time you are caught in a traffic jam, don’t fight. Sit back and smile to yourself. Enjoy the present moment. Happiness can always be found in the present moment.
We must practice in a way that removes the barrier between practice and non-practice. We should bring the practice from the meditation hall into our daily lives.

In the West, we are very goal oriented, we forget to enjoy ourselves along the route. “Aimlessness”, you do not put something in front of you and run after it, because everything is already here, in yourself.
“Stopping” may look like a kind of resistance to modern lief, but it is not. It is a way of life.

The foundation of happiness is mindfulness. The basic condition for being happy is our consciousness of being happy. When we do not have a toothache, we are still not happy. A non-toothache is very pleasant. There are so many things that are enjoyable, but when we don’t practice mindfulness, we don’t appreciate them.
Hope is important, because it can make the present moment less difficult to bear. But if you can refrain from hoping, you can bring yourself entirely into the present moment.
I do not mean that you should not have hope, but that hope is not enough.
“There is no way to peace, peace is the way”. Each step we make should be peace. We can smile and relax, everything we want is right here in the present moment.
If we are not fully ourselves, truly in the present moment, we miss everything.
The secret of the success is that you are really yourself, and when you are really yourself, you can encounter life in the present moment.

I recommend that we set up a small room in our homes and call it a “breathing room”, where we can be alone and practice just breathing. It should be respected, and not violated by anger, shouting or things like that. Decorated very simply, and not too bright. The bell will help not only the person in the breathing room, but the others in the house as well.

The practice of peace and reconciliation is one of the most vital and artistic of human actions. Simple practices like conscious breathing and smiling are very important. They can change our civilization.

When we have an unpleasant feeling, return to your conscious breathing and just observe it, identifying it silently to ourselves. Call the feeling by its name. We can use our breathing to be in contact with our feelings and accept them. Our feeling is us, and for the moment we are that feeling.
We only have to observe it with love and attention. If we take care of our anger in this way, without trying to run away from it, it will transform itself.
Steps to deal with feelings:
Recognise each feeling as it arises (mindfulness).
Become now with the feeling (e.g. “Hello, Fear. How are you today?")
Calm the feeling. You calm your feeling just being with it. Don’t avoid the feeling, come and be one with it.
Release the feeling, let it go.
Look deeply into your feeling, to see what is wrong, to see the causes (usually inaccurate perceptions).
Just look after anger. Mindfulness is not a judge.
It is better if you do not listen to or look at the person whose we consider to be the cause of our anger.
Our mindfulness will take care of everything.
When we understand the nature, the roots, of our anger, we will be freed from it.
Anger is rooted in our lack of understanding of ourselves, in desire, pride, agitation, and suspicion. The primary roots of our anger are in ourselves.

I am not saying that someone who viciously attacks us should not be disciplined. But what is most important is that we first take care of the seeds of negativity in ourselves. Then if someone needs to be helped or disciplined, we will do so out of compassion, not anger and retribution.

We are afraid to bring into our conscious mind the feelings of pain that are buried in us, because they will make us suffer. There are people who practice sitting meditation many hours a day and never really face their feelings. If we know how to observe our feelings, we can find the roots of long-standing internal formations and transform them.
“Suchness” = “The essence or particular characteristics of a thing or a person, its true nature”.

We usually think that parents have to nourish their children, but sometimes the children can bring enlightenment to the parents and help transform them. When we look at our parents with compassion, often we see that our parents are only victims who never had the chance to practice mindfulness.

The giver is our parents; we are the continuation of our parents and our ancestors. The gift is our body itself. The one who receives the gift is us. All three are present in our body. All our ancestors and all future generations are present in us.

Our ancestors and our parents have given us seeds of joy, peace, and happiness, as well as seeds of sorrow, anger, and so on. Every time we practice mindful living, we plant healthy seeds and strengthen the healthy seeds already in us. They will take care of negative seeds.

If you have a friend who is very close to you, the “two” of you can “breathe together”. But if you not have seen your friend in a long time, go to her and practice full awareness in each precious moment while you are there.
We often ask “What is wrong?” Doing so, we invite painful seeds of sorrow to come up and manifest. We should learn to ask “What is not wrong?” And be in touch with that.
Blaming has no positive effect at all, nor does trying to persuade using reasons and arguments. If you understand, and you show that you understand, you can love, and the situation will change.
Understanding and love are not two things, but just one.

To develop understanding, you have to practice looking at all living beings with the eyes of compassion. When you understand, you cannot help but love. And when you love, you naturally act in a way that can relieve the suffering of people.
“Darling, do I understand you enough?"
Love is mind that brings peace, joy and happiness to another person. Compassion is a mind that removes the suffering that is present in the other.

The essence of love and compassion is understanding, the ability to recognise the physical, material, and psychological suffering of others, to put ourselves “inside the skin” of the other. Compassion means, literally, “to suffer with”.

We can also meditate on the suffering of those who causes us to suffer. Anyone who has made us suffering is undoubtedly suffering too. We do not need the other person to be present in order to bring about reconciliation.
If love is real, it will be evident in our daily life, in the way we relate with people and the world. The source of love is deep in us, and we can help others realise a lot of happiness.
We have to find ways for old and young people to live together again. It will make all of us very happy.
Once there is seeing, there must be acting. Otherwise, what is the use of seeing?
I try to plant seeds of joy and peace with every step. Peace is every step.
The cloud is essential for the paper to exists. If the cloud is not there, the sheet of paper cannot be there either. So we can say that the could and the paper inter-are.
“To be” is to inter-be. We cannot just be by ourselves alone. We have to inter-be with every other thing.
As thin as this sheet of paper is, it contains everything in the universe in it.
Without a rose, we cannot have garbage; and without garbage, we cannot have a rose.
There is no phenomenon in the universe that does not intimately concern us, from a pebble resting at the bottom of the ocean, to the movement of a galaxy millions of light-years away.
We have to look deeply at things in order to see.
Because we are so distant from our Mother Earth, we become sick. That is why we need to go out from time to time and be in nature.
People in the peace movement can write very good protest letters, but they are not so skilled at writing love letters.
Can the pace movement talk in loving speech, showing the way for peace? If we cannot smile, we cannot help other people smile. If we are not peaceful, then we cannot contribute the peace movement.

You may think that if you were to enter the government and obtain power, you would be able to do anything you wanted, but that is not true. If you became President, you would be confronted by this hard fact - you would probably do almost exactly the same thing as our current President, perhaps a little better, perhaps a little worse.
To transform our situation is also to transform our minds. Situation is mind, and mind is situation.
We have to encourage them to stop polluting our environment and our consciousness.
We have to look deeply into the situation, and we will see the roots of war. We cannot just blame not side or the other. We have to transcend the tendency to take sides.
Practicing nonviolence is first of all to become nonviolence.
“We are all humankind, and our life is one”.
What can we do when we have hurt people?
Take the time to say “I’m sorry”. I will try my best to change myself.
Try to bring out the best part in ourselves, to transform ourselves.
Speak with life and not just with words.
Reconciliation opposes all form of ambition, without taking sides.

If I had been born in the village of the pirate and raised in the same conditions as he was, there is a great likelihood that I would become a pirate. If you take a gun and shoot the pirate, you shoot all of us, because all of us are to some extent responsible for this state of affairs.
“Please call me by my true names,
so I can hear all my cries and laughs at once,
so I can see that my joy and pain are one."
Fourteen percepts of the Order of Interbeing:
Do not be idolatrous about or cold to any doctrine, theory, or ideology.
Do not think that the knowledge you presently possess is changeless, absolute truth.
Do not force others to adopt your views. Through compassionate dialogue, help others renounce fanaticism and narrowness.
Do not avoid contact with suffering or close your eyes before suffering.
Do not accumulate wealth while millions are hungry. Live simply and share time, energy, and material resources with those who are in need.
Do not maintain anger or hatred.
Do not lose yourself in dispersion and in your surroundings. Practice mindful breathing in order to come back to what is happening in the present moment.
Do not utter words that can create discord and cause the community to break.

Do not say untruthful things for the sake of personal interest or to impress people. Always speak truthfully and constructively. Had the courage to speak out about situations of injustice, even when doing so may threaten your own safety.
Do not use religious community for personal gain or profit, or transform your community into a political party.
Do not live with a vocation that is harmful to humans and nature. Do not invest in companies that deprive others of their chance to live.
Do not kill. Do not let others kill. Find whatever means possible to protect life and prevent war.
Possess nothing that should belong to others.
Do not mistreat your body. Learn to handle it with respect. Do not look at your body as only an instrument.

A beautiful river was chasing after clouds. She realised that what she had been looking for was already in herself. She found out that clouds are nothing but water. Clouds are born from water and will return to water. And she found out the she herself is also water. Clouds are impermanent, but the sky is stable. Sky had been with her hearth since the very beginning.
When a cloud came by, she would greet him with loving kindness. When that cloud wanted to go away, she would wave to him or her happily and with loving kindness. She replied that all clouds are her.
There is nothing to chase after. We can go back to ourselves, enjoy our breathing, our smiling, ourselves, and our beautiful environment.
We need a “policy” to dealing with our suffering.
It is important that young people create a path of mindfulness so that our children in the next century can avoid repeating the same mistakes.

Take the hand of your child and invite her to go out and sit with you on the grass. The two of you may want to contemplate the green grass, the little flowers that grow among the grasses, and the sky. Breathing and smiling together - that is peace education. If we know how to appreciate these beautiful things, we will not have to search for anything else. Peace is available in every moment, in every breath, in every step.
I have enjoyed our journey together. I hope you have enjoyed it too. We shall see each other again.

paragraphs: Percival H. - Architecture Patterns with Python
Software systems, too, tend toward chaos. Over time we find that it gathers cruft and edge cases and ends up a confusing morass of manager classes and util modules.
Fortunately, the techniques to avoid creating a big ball of mud aren't complex:
Encapsulation and Abstractions
The term encapsulation covers two closely related ideas:
simplifying behavior and hiding data. In this discussion, we’re
using the first sense.
We encapsulate behavior by identifying a task
that needs to be done in our code and giving that task to a well-defined object or function. We call that object or function an
abstraction.
Layering When one function, module, or object uses another, we say that the one depends on the other.
In a layered architecture, we divide our code into discrete categories or roles, and we introduce rules about which categories of code can call each other.
The Dependency Inversion Principle
High-level modules are the code that your organization really cares about. Low-level modules are the code that your organization doesn’t care about.

So the first part of the DIP says that our business code shouldn’t depend on technical details; instead, both should use abstractions. Why? Broadly, because we want to be able to change them independently of each other.
The second part is even more mysterious. “Abstractions should not
depend on details” we’ll have a concrete example in Chapter 4.
A Place for All Our Business Logic: The Domain Model
One of the most common reasons that
our designs go wrong is that business logic becomes spread
throughout the layers of our application, making it hard to identify,
understand, and change.
Part I. Building an Architecture to Support Domain Modeling
Notes
Behavior should come first and drive our storage requirements. After all, our customers don’t care about the data model. They care about what the system does; otherwise they’d just use a spreadsheet.
To create stable APIs around our domain we present four key design patterns:
The Repository pattern, an abstraction over the idea of persistent storage
The Service Layer pattern to clearly define where our use cases begin and end
The Unit of Work pattern to provide atomic operations
The Aggregate pattern to enforce the integrity of our data

The domain is a fancy way of saying the problem you’re trying to solve. A model is a map of a process or phenomenon that captures a useful property. The domain model is the mental map that business owners have of their businesses.

When we hear our business stakeholders using unfamiliar words, or using terms in a specific way, we should listen to understand the deeper meaning and encode their hard-won experience into our software.

We have an initial conversation with our business experts and agree on a glossary and some rules for the first minimal version of the domain model. Wherever possible, we ask for concrete examples to illustrate each rule. We make sure to express those rules in the business jargon (the ubiquitous language in DDD terminology). We choose memorable identifiers for our objects so that the examples are easier to talk about.

Whenever we have a business concept that has data but no identity, we often choose to represent it using the Value Object pattern. A value object is any domain object that is uniquely identified by the data it holds; we usually make them immutable.
One of the nice things that dataclasses (or namedtuples) give us is value equality, which is the fancy way of saying, “Two lines with the same orderid, sku, and qty are equal.”

Entities, unlike values, have identity equality. We can change their values, and they are still recognizably the same thing. Batches, in our example, are entities. We can allocate lines to a batch, or change the date that we expect it to arrive, and it will still be the same entity.

Python’s __eq__ magic method defines the behavior of the class for the == operator. For both entity and value objects, it’s also worth thinking through how __hash__ will work. It’s the magic method Python uses to control the behavior of objects when you add them to sets or use them as dict keys.
You shouldn’t modify __hash__ without also modifying __eq__.
Magic methods can express domain semantics (e.g. __gt__).
Exceptions can express domain concepts too.
Recap:

Domain modeling: This is the part of your code that is closest to the business, the most likely to change, and the place where you deliver the most value to the business. Make it easy to understand and modify.

Distinguish entities from value objects: A value object is defined by its attributes. It’s usually best implemented as an immutable type. If you change an attribute on a Value Object, it represents a different object. In contrast, an entity has attributes that may vary over time and it will still be the same entity. It’s important to define what does uniquely identify an entity (usually some sort of name or reference field).

Not everything has to be an object: Python is a multiparadigm language, so let the “verbs” in your code be functions. For every FooManager, BarBuilder, or BazFactory, there’s often a more expressive and readable manage_foo(), build_bar(), or get_baz() waiting to happen.
This is the time to apply your best OO design principles: Revisit the SOLID principles and all the other good heuristics like “has a versus is-a,” “prefer composition over inheritance,” and so on.
But we want our domain model to have no dependencies whatsoever. We don’t want infrastructure concerns bleeding over into our domain model and slowing our unit tests or our ability to make changes.

We’ll think of our model as being on the “inside,” and dependencies flowing inward to it; this is what people sometimes call onion architecture. (Presentation Layer -> Domain Model <- Database Layer).

These days, it’s unlikely that your team members are hand-rolling their own SQL queries. Instead, you’re almost certainly using some kind of framework to generate SQL for you based on your model objects. These frameworks are called object-relational mappers (ORMs) because they exist to bridge the conceptual gap between the world of objects and domain modeling and the world of databases and relational algebra. The most important thing an ORM gives us is persistence ignorance: the idea that our fancy domain model doesn’t need to know anything about how data is loaded or persisted. This helps keep our domain clean of direct dependencies on particular database technologies.
The alternative is to define your schema separately, and to define an explicit mapper for how to convert between the schema and our domain model.
The Repository pattern is an abstraction over persistent storage. It hides the boring details of data access by pretending that all of our data is in memory.
The simplest repository has just two methods: add() to put a new item in the repository, and get() to return a previously added item.

In real life, we’ve sometimes found ourselves deleting ABCs from our production code, because Python makes it too easy to ignore them, and they end up unmaintained and, at worst, misleading. In practice we often just rely on Python’s duck typing to enable abstractions. To a Pythonista, a repository is any object that has add(thing) and get(id) methods.
Building a fake Repository for tests Is now trivial!
Building fakes for your abstractions is an excellent way to get design feedback: if it’s hard to fake, the abstraction is probably too complicated.
Repository pattern and persistence ignorance: the trade-offs. Pros
We have a simple interface between persistent storage and our domain model.
It’s easy to make a fake version of the repository for unit testing, or to swap out different storage solutions, because we’ve fully decoupled the model from infrastructure concerns.

Writing the domain model before thinking about persistence helps us focus on the business problem at hand. If we ever want to radically change our approach, we can do that in our model, without needing to worry about foreign keys or migrations until later.
Our database schema is really simple because we have complete control over how we map our objects to tables.
Cons:
An ORM already buys you some decoupling. Changing foreign keys might be hard, but it should be pretty easy to swap between MySQL and Postgres if you ever need to.
Maintaining ORM mappings by hand requires extra work and extra code.
Any extra layer of indirection always increases maintenance costs and adds a “WTF factor” for Python programmers who’ve never seen the Repository pattern before.

If your app is just a simple CRUD (create-read-update-delete) wrapper around a database, then you don’t need a domain model or a repository. But the more complex the domain, the more an investment in freeing yourself from infrastructure concerns will pay off in terms of the ease of making changes.
Repository Pattern Recap
Apply dependency inversion to your ORM
Our domain model should be free of infrastructure concerns, so your ORM should import your model, and not the other way around.
The Repository pattern is a simple abstraction around permanent storage

The repository gives you the illusion of a collection of in-memory objects. It makes it easy to create a FakeRepository for testing and to swap fundamental details of your infrastructure without disrupting your core application.
A key theme in this book, hidden among the fancy patterns, is that we can use simple abstractions to hide messy details.
When we’re unable to change component A for fear of breaking component B, we say that the components have become coupled.

Locally, coupling is a good thing: it’s a sign that our code is working together, each component supporting the others, all of them fitting in place like the gears of a watch. In jargon, we say this works when there is high cohesion between the coupled elements. Globally, coupling is a nuisance: it increases the risk and the cost of changing our code, sometimes to the point where we feel unable to make any changes at all.
We can reduce the degree of coupling within a system by abstracting away the details.
[To create the right abstraction] We’ll apply a trick here that we’ll employ on a grand scale later in the book. We’re going to separate what we want to do from how to do it.
Our goal is to isolate the clever part of our system, and to be able to test it thoroughly without needing to set up a real filesystem.
But there’s another option, which is to modify the sync() function so it can be unit tested and end-to-end tested; it’s an approach Bob calls edge-to-edge testing.

We avoid using mocks in this book and in our production code too. We’re not going to enter into a Holy War, but our instinct is that mocking frameworks, particularly monkeypatching, are a code smell. Instead, we like to clearly identify the responsibilities in our codebase, and to separate those responsibilities into small, focused objects that are easy to replace with a test double.
We have three closely related reasons for our preference:
Patching out the dependency you’re using makes it possible to unit test the code, but it does nothing to improve the design.
Tests that use mocks tend to be more coupled to the implementation details of the codebase.
Overuse of mocks leads to complicated test suites that fail to explain the code.
Difference between mocks and fakes:
Mocks are used to verify how something gets used.
Fakes are working implementations of the thing they’re replacing, but they’re designed for use only in tests.

If we look at what our Flask app is doing, there’s quite a lot of what we might call orchestration. It often makes sense to split out a service layer, sometimes called an orchestration layer or a use-case layer.
Typical service-layer functions have similar steps:
We fetch some objects from the repository.
We make some checks or assertions about the request against the current state of the world.
We call a domain service.
If all is well, we save/update any state we’ve changed.
