Evaluate the merits of a past decision based not on what you know now but only on what you could have reasonably known at the time the decision was made (said by me: be aware of hindsight fallacy).
You need a "succession pipeline" in which the next generation of leaders is exposed to the thinking and decision making of the current leaders so they can both learn and be tested.
Don't ask consultants to do things that they don't normally do. They will certainly revert to doing things in their usual way; their own employers will demand that.
Guardrailing it's intended to help good people perform better, not to help failing people reach the bar.
When you catch someone violating your rules and controls, make sure that everybody sees the consequences.
I typically work at about 50:1 leverage, meaning that for every hour I spend with each person who works for me, they spend about 50 hours working to move the project along.
Virtually nothing goes according to plan because one doesn't plan for the thing that go wrong.
I can visualize the result of pushing through so intensely that I experience the thrill of success even when I'm still struggling to achieve it.
Most of success comes from doing distasteful stuff, like identifying and dealing with problems and pushing hard over long times, not from coming up with the brilliant new idea.
If you're not excited about the goal you're working for, stop working for it.

Assuming people will do what they intellectually want to do is like assuming that people will lose weight simply because why understand why it's beneficial for them to do it. It won't happen until proper habits are developed. In organizations, that happens with the help of tools and protocols. How you decide them is up to you, the main point is that they're important.

My wishes for you are that: you can make your work your passion one and the same, you an struggle well with others on your common mission to produce the rewards, you can savor struggle and reward and you will evolve quickly and contribute to evolution in significant ways.
Tools and protocols.
Coach: platform populated with a library of common situations, which are linked to the relevant principles to help people handle them.
Dot collector: app used in meeting that allows people to express their thoughts and see others' thoughts in real time, and then helps them collectively reach an idea-meritocratic decision.
Baseball card: way of presenting a person's strengths and weaknesses in a pointillist way, created from analysis of dots in meeting and reviews, tests, choices made, etc...
People profile is a text-based summary of what each person is like.
Combinator is a tool that takes data from Baseball cards and allows one to look at people based on their key attributes and compare them to one another.

Issue log: tool to record mistakes and learn from them. Anything that goes wrong must be "issue logged" with the severity of the issue and who is responsible for it specified, so that it's easy to sort through most problems.

Pain button: app designed to let people record the emotions they are feeling as they feel them and then come back at a later time to reflect on them using guided reflection questions. The tool prompts the people who experienced the pain to specify what they will do to deal with that situation, so that the pain is mitigated in the future.
Dispute resolver: tools that provides paths for resolving disagreement in an idea-meritocratic way. It asks a series of questions used to guide the people through the resolution process.

Daily update tool: software application that pulls updates about what each person who reports to me did that day, the issue pertaining to them, and their reflections. It allows people to easily provide data like their morale, heaviness of workload and issues they want to escalate, on a daily basis.
Contract tool: simple app that lets people make and monitor their commitment to each other, taken at the end of meetings.

Process flow diagram: diagram used to help visualize the organization as a machine. We created a process maps for every department in the company that show us clearly all the roles and the responsibilities for each role and how the work flows among them.
Policy and procedures manual: compendium of policies and procedures that people can consult as one would an operating manual.

Metrics: good metrics come about by first thinking of what information you need to answer your pressing questions and then figuring out how to get it. Steps: know what goal your business is achieving, understand the process for getting to goal (your machine, with people and design), identify the key parts in the process that are the best places to measure so you know your machine is working to achieve that goal, and explore how to create levers, tied to those key metrics, that allow you to adjust your process and change your outcomes ("You can't manage what you can't measure").
Sapiens notes
Really long selection of most important parts of the book.

The Cognitive Revolution kick-started history about 70000 years ago. The Agricultural Revolution sped it up about 12000 years ago. The Scientific Revolution, which got under way only 500 years ago, may well end history and start something completely different. This book tells the story of how these three revolutions have affected humans and their fellow organisms.
The Cognitive Revolution

It's a common fallacy to envision these (Homo) species as arranged in a straight line of descent, with Ergaster begetting Erectus, Erectus begetting Neanderthals, and Neanderthals evolving into us. This linear model gives the mistaken impression that at any particular moment only one type of human inhabited the earth, and that all earlier species were merely older model of ourselves. The truth is that from about 2 million years ago until around 10000 years ago, the world was home, at one and same time, to several human species.

Women paid extra to walk upright. An upright gait required narrower hips, constricting the birth canal - and this just when babies' heads were getting bigger and bigger. Women who gave birth earlier, when the infant's brain and head were still relatively small and supple, fared better and lived to have more children. Natural selection consequently favoured earlier births. And, indeed, compared to other animals, humans are born prematurely, when many of their vital systems are still undeveloped A colt can trot shortly after birth; a kitten leaves its mother to forage on its own when it's just a few weeks old. Human babies are helpless, dependent for many years on their elders for sustenance, protection and education.

Since long intestines and large brains are both massive energy consumers, it's hard to have both. By shortening the intestines (cooking food) and decreasing their energy consumption, cooking inadvertently opened the way to the jumbo brains of Neanderthals and Sapiens.
There are two theories. The Interbreeding Theory: Sapiens bred with Neanderthals until the two populations merged. The Replacement Theory: incompatibility, revulsion, and perhaps even genocide.
(Why we rule the world)

Our language is amazingly supple. We can create an infinite number of sentences, each with a distinct meaning. An interesting theory agrees that our unique language evolved as a means of sharing information about the world, but in particular about humans, not animals or other. Our language evolved as a way of gossiping.

Yet the truly unique feature of our language is the ability to transmit information about things that do not exists at all. Fiction has enabled us not merely to image things, but to do so collectively. Sapiens can cooperate in extremely flexible ways with countless numbers of strangers. That's why Sapiens rule the world.

The critical threshold is 150. Below this threshold there is no need for formal rank. Larger number of strangers can cooperate successfully by believing in common myths. Yet no myth exists outside the stories that people invent and tell one another. There are no gods in the universe, no nations, no money, no human rights, no laws and no justice outside the common imagination of human beings.
Ever since the Cognitive Revolution, Sapiens have been able to change their behaviour quickly, transmitting new behaviours to future generations without any need of genetic environmental change.

What happened in the Cognitive Revolution: new ability to transmit larger quantities of information about the world (to plan complex actions), larger quantities of information about Sapiens social relationships (to create larger groups) and information about things that do not really exists (to create cooperation between large number of strangers and to innovate social behaviour).
From the Cognitive Revolution onwards, historical narratives replace biological theories as our primary means of explaining the development of Homo sapiens.

For nearly the entire history of our species, Sapiens lived as foragers, hunter-gatherer. Our eating habits, our conflicts and our sexuality are all result of the way our hunter-gatherer minds interact with our current post-industrial environment, with its mega-cities, aeroplanes, telephones and computers.

An example: if a Stone Age woman came across a tree groaning with figs, the most sensible thing to do was to eat as many of them as she could on the spot, before the local baboon band picked the tree bare.

We are largely at loss in trying to comprehend the beliefs and rituals of ancient hunter-gatherers, the greater part of their mental religious and emotional lives was conducted without the help of artefacts.
The foragers' secret of success, which protected them from starvation and malnutrition, was their varied diet. Farmers tend to eat a very limited and unbalanced diet.

It is vital to ask questions for which no answers are available, otherwise we might be tempted to dismiss 60000 to 70000 years of human history with the excuse that 'the people who lived back then did nothing of importance'. They did a lot of important things, they shaped the world around us. the wandering bands of storytelling foragers Sapiens were the most important and most destructive force the animal kingdom had ever produced.

The historical record makes Homo sapiens look like an ecological killer. The evidence is circumstantial, but it's hard to imagine that Sapiens, just by coincidence, arrived to Australia at the precise point that more than 90 percent of Australia's megafauna disappeared.

How could they cause an ecological disaster? Large animals breed slowly. Human species evolved in Afro-Asia for 2 million years, the big beasts of those lands learned to avoid humans. Australians giants had no time to learn to run away. Humans don't come across as particularly dangerous. Humans deliberately burned vast areas of impassible thickets and dense forests to create open grass-lands, which attracted more easily hunted game, and were better suited for their needs.

The archaeologic record of island after island tells the same story. The tragedy opens with a scene showing a rich and varied population of large animals, without any trace of humans. In scene two, Sapiens appear, evidenced by a human bone, a spear point or perhaps a potsherd. Scene three quickly follows, in which men and women occupy centre stage and most large animals, along with smaller ones, are gone.

Don't believe tree-huggers who claim that our ancestors lived in harmony with nature. Long before the Industrial Revolution, Homo sapiens held the record among all organisms for driving the most plant and animal species to their extinctions.
The Agricultural Revolution
If our minds are those of hunter-gatherers, our cuisine is that of ancient farmers.

Rather than heralding a new era of easy living, the Agricultural revolution left farmers with lives generally more difficult and less satisfying that those of foragers. The average farmer worked harder than the average forager, and got a worse diet in return. The Agricultural Revolution was history's biggest fraud. The culprits were a handful of plant species, including wheat, rice and potatoes. These plants domesticated Homo sapiens, rather than vice versa.
When foraging band was hard-pressed by a stronger rival, it could usually move on. When a strong enemy threatened an agricultural village, retreat meant giving up fields, houses and granaries.
Cultivating wheat provided much more food per unit of territory, and thereby enabled Homo sapiens to multiply exponentially.

The number of children increased, meaning that the extra wheat had to be shared between more children, with weakened immune system and in permanent settlements, hotbeds for infectious diseases. They were more exposed to drought, to thieves and enemies.

It took generations for the small changes to accumulate and transform society and, by then, nobody remembered that they had lived differently. The pursuit of an easier life resulted in much hardship, and not for the last time. It happens to us today (graduates that take demanding jobs).
It may well be that foragers switched from gathering wild wheat to intense wheat cultivation, not to increase their normal food supply, but rather to support the building and running of temple.

Domesticated chickens and cattle may well be an evolutionary success story, but they are also among the most miserable creatures that ever lived. The domestication of animals was found on a series of brutal practices that only became crueler with the passing of the centuries.
Calves are separated from Cows shortly after birth. The females are reared to become the next generation of dairy cows, whereas the males are handed over the care of the meat industry.
In the case of animals such as cattle, sheep and Sapiens, each with a complex world of sensations and emotions, we have to consider how evolutionary success translates into individual experience.

In the subsistence economy of hunting and gathering, there was an obvious limit to long-term planning. Paradoxically, it saved foragers a lot of anxieties. There was no sense in worrying about things that they could not influence.
History is something that very few people have been doing while everyone was ploughing fields and carrying water buckets.
The handful of millennial separating the Agricultural Revolution from the appearance of cities, kingdoms and empires was not enough time to allow an instinct for mass cooperation to evolve.

Three main factors prevent people from realizing that the order organising their lives exists only in their imagination: the imagined order is embedded in the material world, the imagined order shapes our desires, the imagined order is inter-subjective.

An objective phenomenon exists independently of human consciousness and human beliefs (e.g. radioactivity is not a myth). A subjective phenomenon is something that exists depending on the consciousness and beliefs of a single individual, it disappears or changes if that particular individual changes his or her beliefs (e.g. imaginary friends for children). An inter-subject phenomenon is something that exists within the communication network linking the subjective consciousness of many individuals. If a single individual changes his or her beliefs, or even dies, is of little importance.
Because the Sapiens social order is imagined, humans cannot preserve the critical information for running it simply by making copies of their DNA and passing these to their progeny.

When the amount of people and property in a particular society crossed a critical threshold, it became necessary to store and process large amounts of mathematical data. Since the human brain could not do it, the system collapsed. The data-processing system invented by the Sumerians to overcome the problem is called 'writing'.
At the beginning there were two types of signs: one type of signs represented numbers and the other type of signs represented people, animals, merchandise, territories, date and so forth.
Numbers from 0 to 9 are known as Arabic numbers even though they were first invented by the Hindus.

It is an iron rule of history that every imagined hierarchy disavows its fictional origins and claims to be natural and inevitable. Many people who have viewed the hierarchy of free persons and slaves as natural and correct have argued that slavery is not a human invention.
Hierarchy serve an important function. They enable complete strangers to know how to treat one another without wasting the time and energy needed to become personally acquainted.
Differences in natural abilities also play a role in the formation of social distinctions. But such diversities of aptitudes and character are usually mediated through imagined hierarchies.

(a) Chance historical event -> (b) White control of blacks -> (c) Discriminatory laws -> (d) Poverty and lack of educations among blacks -> (e) Cultural prejudices -> (c) and (d). Most sociopolitical hierarchies lack a logical or biological basis - they are nothing but the perpetuation of chance events supported by myths.

A good rule of thumb is 'Biology enables, culture forbids'. Cultural tends to argue that it forbids only that which is unnatural. But from a biological perspective, nothing is unnatural. God created the human body, intending each limb and organ to serve a particular purpose. If we use our limbs and organs for the purpose envisioned by God, then is a natural activity. To use them differently than God intends is unnatural. But evolution has ho purpose. Organs have not evolved with a purpose, and the way they are used is in constant flux. There is not a single organ in the human body that only does the job its prototype did when it first appeared hundreds of million years ago (e.g. wings didn't suddenly appear in all their aerodynamic glory, they developed from organs that served another purpose).

As men competed against each other for the opportunity yo impregnate fertile women, an individual's chances of reproduction depended above all on his ability to outperform and defeat other men. As time went by, the masculine genes that made it to the next generation were those belonging to the most ambitious, aggressive and competitive men. A woman, on the other hand, had no problem finding a man willing to impregnate her.
The Unification of Humankind

Both equality and individual freedom are fundamental values. Yet the two values contradict each other. Equality can be ensured only by curtailing the freedoms of those who are better off. Guaranteeing that every individual will be free to do as he wishes inevitably short-changes equality.

History is moving relentlessly towards unity. The best way to appreciate the general direction of history is to count the number of separate human worlds that coexisted at any given moment on planet Earth.

Homo sapiens evolved to think of people as divided into 'us' and 'them'. 'Us' was the group immediately around you, whoever you were, and 'them' was everyone else. In fact, no social animal is ever guided by the interest of the entire species to which it belongs. The first millennium BC witnessed the appearance of three potentially universal orders, whose devotees could imagine the entire world and the entire human race as a single unit governed by a single set of laws. Everyone was 'us', at least potentially. There was no longer 'them'. The universal orders were: the monetary order, the imperial order ans the order of universal religions. For merchants, the entire world was a single market, for conquerors, the entire world was a single empire, for the prophets, the entire world held a single truth.

Money is anything that people are willing to use in order to represent systematically the value of other things for the purpose of exchanging goods and services. Is a new inter-subject reality that exists solely in people's shared imagination.
The sum of total money in the world is about $60 trillion, yet the sum total of coins and banknotes is less than $6 trillion. More than 90 percent of all money exists only on computer servers.
Money is the most universal and most efficient system of mutual trust ever devised.
Even if Indians still had no real use for gold, the fact that Mediterranean people wanted it would be enough to make Indians value it.

Whereas religion asks us to believe in something, money asks us to believe that other people believe in something. (dark side of money) This trust is invested not in humans, communities or sacred values, but in money. We do not trust strangers, we trust the coin they hold. If they run out of coins, we run out of trust. The world is in danger of becoming one big and heartless marketplace.

An empire is a political order with two important characteristics. First, rule over a significant number of distinct peoples, each possessing a different cultural identity and a separate territory. Second, flexible borders and potentially unlimited appetite. Empire is defined solely by these two characteristics, not by its origin, its form of government, its territorial extent or the size of population.
Empires were one of the main reasons for the drastic reduction in human diversity.
The contemporary critique of empires commonly takes two form: empires do not work and empires should not be done because are evil engines of destruction and exploitation.

The first statement is plain nonsense, and the second is deeply problematic. Empire has been the world's most common form of political organisation for the last 2500 years. Conquered peoples don't have a very good record of freeing themselves from their imperial overlords. Most have remained subjugated for hundreds of years. Typically, they have been slowly digested by the conquering empire, until their distinct cultures fizzled out.

Ideas, people, goods and technology spread more easily within the borders of an empire than in a politically fragmented region. Often was the empires themselves which deliberately spread ideas, institutions, customs and norms. They did so to make life easier and to gain legitimacy.

Even if we were to completely disavow the legacy of a brutal empire in the hope of reconstructing and safeguarding the 'authentic' cultures that preceded it, in all probability what we will be defending is nothing but the legacy of an older and no less brutal empire.
The imperial vision of dominion over the entire world could be imminent.

Since all social orders and hierarchies are imagined, they are all fragile. The crucial role of religion has been to give superhuman legitimacy to these fragile structures. Religion assert that our laws are not the result of human caprice, but are ordained by an absolute and supreme authority.
There is no difficulty for the devotees of one god to accept the existence and efficacy of other gods. Polytheism is inherently open-minded, and rarely persecutes 'heretic' and 'infidels'.

The Roman Empire did not require the Christians to give up their beliefs, but expect them to pay respect to empire's protector gods. When Christians vehemently refused to do so, the Romans reacted by persecuting what they understood to be politically subversive faction.
More Christians were killed by fellow Christians in those twenty-four hours (St Bartholomew's Day Massacre) than by the polytheistic Roman Empire throughout its entire existence.
If God knew in advance that a particular person would use her free will to choose evil, and that as a result she would be punished for this by eternal tortures in hell, why did God create her?
For dualists, it's easy to explain evil. But if Good and Evil battle for control of the world, who enforces the laws governing this war?

Monotheism explains order, but is mystified by evil. Dualism explains evil, but is puzzled by order. There is only logical way of solving the riddle: to argue that there is a single omnipotent God who created the entire universe - and He's evil. But nobody in history has had the stomach for such belief.
Either you believe in a single omnipotent God or you believe in two opposing powers, neither of which is omnipotent. Still, humans have a wonderful capacity to believe in contradictions.
In Old Testament there is no Devil and never claims that the souls of people continue to live after the death of the body.

Siddhartha came to the realization that suffering is not caused by ill fortune, social injustice, or divine whims. Suffering is caused by pattern of one's own mind. If, when the mind experiences something pleasant or unpleasant, it simply understand things as they are, then there is no suffering. A person who doesn't crave cannot suffer, and a person trained to experience reality as it is cannot crave.
To accept sadness as sadness, joy as joy, pain as pain, he developed a set of meditation techniques that train the mind to experience reality and not crave.
When the flames are completely extinguished, craving is replaced by a state of perfect contentment and serenity, known as nirvana.
There is an iron rule of history that what looks inevitable in hindsight was far from obvious at the time.

Chaotic systems come in two shapes: level one chaos is chaos that does not react to predictions about it (e.g. weather), level two chaos is chaos that reacts to predictions about it, and therefore can never be predicted accurately (e.g. markets).
The Scientific Revolution
From 1500, human population has increased fourteenfold, production 240-fold, and energy consumption 115-fold.

The connection between science and technology is so strong that today people tend to confuse that two. Prior 1500, science and technology were totally separated fields. Rulers financed educational institutions whose mandate was to spread traditional knowledge for the purpose of buttressing the existing order. Here and there people developed new technologies, but these were usually created by uneducated craftsmen using trial and error, not by scholar pursuing systematic scientific research.

Science, industry and military technology intertwined only with the advent of capitalist system and the Industrial Revolution. Once the relationship was established, however, it quickly transformed the world.
Before the late modern era, most religions and ideologies took it for granted that deaths was our inevitable fate. The best minds were busy giving meaning to death, not trying to escape it.
A few serious scholars suggest that by 2050, some humans will become a-mortal, in the absence of fatal trauma their lives could be extended indefinitely.

Europeans managed to conquer America and gain supremacy at sea mainly because the Asiatic powers showed little interest in them. The Chinese and Persians did not lack technological inventions such as steam engines. They lacked the values, myths, judicial apparatus and sociopolitical structures that took centuries to form and mature in the West and which could not be copied and internalised rapidly. Modern science and capitalism is the potential that Europe developed in the early modern period that enabled it to dominate the late modern world.

European imperialism was entirely unlike all other imperialism project in history. Previous seekers utilised and spread their view of the world. European imperialists set out to distant shores in the hope of obtaining new knowledge along with new territories.

Previous map were filled with imaginary monsters and wonders, with no empty spaces. During the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, Europeans begin to draw maps with lots of empty spaces. Anyone looking at the map and possessing even minimal curiosity is tempted to ask, "What's beyond this point?" The map gives no answers. It invites the observer to set sail and find out.

The first modern man was Amerigo Vespucci. He argued that the new lands discovered by Columbus were not islands off the East Asian coast, but rather an entire continent unknown to the Scriptures, classical geographers and contemporary Europeans.
A quarter of the world, and two of its seven continents, are named after a little-known Italian whose sole claim to fame is that he had the courage to say, "We don't know".

The European empires did so many different things on such a large scale, that you can find plenty of examples to support whatever you want to say about them. These empire wielded so much power and changed the world to such an extent that perhaps they cannot be simply labelled as good or evil. They created the world as we know it, including ideologies we use in order to judge them.
To understand modern economic history, you really need to understand just a single word. The word is growth. The modern economy eats up everything it can find.
Banks are allowed to loan $10 for every dollar they actually possess.

Humankind was trapped for thousands of years. The way out of the trap was discovered only in the modern era, with the appearance of a new system based on trust in future, using special kind of money called 'credit'. Credit enables us to build the present at the expense of the future.

Credit of one kind of another have existed in all known human cultures, but in previous eras people didn't trust that the future would be better than the present. They believed that the total amount of wealth was limited.

Because credit was limited, people had trouble financing new businesses. Because there were few businesses, the economy didn't grow. Because it didn't grow, people assumed it never would, and those who had capital were wary of extending credit. The expectation of stagnation fulfilled itself.

Smith's claim that the selfish human urge to increase private profits is the basis for collective wealth is one of the most revolutionary ideas in human history. Greed is good. Egoism is altruism. 'When profits increase, the landlord or weaver will employ more assistants', 'The profits of production must be reinvested in increasing production', Smith keep repeating.

Capitalism distinguishes 'capital' from mere 'wealth'. Capital consist of money, goods and resources that are invested in production. Wealth, on the other hand, is buried on the ground or wasted on unproductive activities.

Everybody is terrified that the current economic crisis may stop the growth of economy. So they are creating trillions of dollars, euros and yen out of thin air, pumping cheap credit into the system, and hoping that the scientists, technicians and engineers will manage to come up with something really big, before the bubble bursts. If the labs do not fulfill these expectations before the bubble bursts, we are heading towards very rough times.

Markets offer no protection against fraud, theft and violence. In a completely free market avaricious capitalists can establish monopolies or collude against their workforce. Greedy bosses might curtail the workers' freedom of movement through debt peonage or slavery. This is the fly in the ointment of free-market capitalism. It cannot ensure that profits are gained in a fair way, or distributed in a fair manner.

The individuals who bought the shares, the brokers who sold them, and the managers of the slave-trade companies rarely thought about the Africans (*my point of view* as no one thinks of animals when eat meat nowadays).
We might not like capitalism, but we cannot live without it.

Economic growth also requires energy and raw materials, and these are finite. When and if they run out, the entire system will collapse. While humankind's use of energy and raw materials has mushroomed in these last few centuries, the amount available for our exploitation have actually increased.

There is no limit to the amount of energy at our disposal. Or, more precisely, the only limit is set by our ignorance. All human activities and industries put together consume about 500 exajoules annually, equivalent to the amount of energy earth receives from the sun in just ninety minutes (and think about nuclear energy and gravitational energy). We are living alongside an enormous ocean of energy, all we need to do is invent better pumps.

Around the time that Homo sapiens was elevated to divine status by humanist religions, farm animals stopped being viewed as living creatures that could feel pain and distress, and instead came to be treated as machines.

Pigs are among the most intelligent and inquisitive of mammals, second perhaps only to great apes. Yet industrialised pig farm routinely confine nursing sows inside such small crates that they are literally unable to turn around. Many dairy cows live almost all their allotted years inside a small enclosure; standing, sitting and sleeping in their own urine and excrement.
Treating living creatures possessing complex emotional worlds as if they were machines is likely to cause them not only physical discomfort, but also much social stress and psychological frustration.
Hundred of millions of male chicks die each year, sometimes simply thrown into the rubbish.

Just as the Atlantic slave trade did not stem from hatred towards Africans, so the modern animal industry is not motivated by animosity. Again, it is fuelled by indifference. Most people who produce and consume eggs, milk and meat rarely stop to think about the fate of the chickens, cows or pigs whose flesh and emissions they are eating.

The modern capitalist economy must constantly increase production if it is to survive, and somebody must also the products, or industrialists and investors alike will go burst. A new kind of ethic appeared: consumerism. It encourages people to treat themselves, spoil themselves, and even kill themselves slowly by overconsumption. Frugality is a disease to be cured.
It has succeeded. We are all good consumers. We buy countless products that we don't really need, and that until yesterday we didn't know existed.
The rich take great care managing their assets and investments, while the less well-heeled go into debts buying cars and televisions they don't really need.
The capitalistic and consumerist ethics are two sides of the same coin. The supreme commandment of the rich is 'Invest!', the supreme commandment of the rest of us is 'Buy!'.

The Industrial Revolution turned the timetable and the assembly line into a template for almost all human activities. It brought also urbanisation, the disappearance of peasantry, the rise of industrial proletariat, the empowerment of the common person, democratisation, youth culture and the disintegration of patriarchy.

The collapse of the family and the local community and their replacement by the state and the market. Previously the family was also welfare system, health system, education system, construction industry, the trade union, the pension fund, the insurance company, the radio, television, newspaper, bank and police. The state and market had an offer that could not be refused 'Become individuals'. But it comes at a cost. Many of us now feel alienated and threatened by the power the impersonal state and market wield over our lives.
Most people don't appreciate just how peaceful an era we live in. The real peace is not the mere absence of war. Real peace is the implausibility of war.

Today humankind has broken the law of the jungle. There is at least real peace, and not just absence of war. For most polities, there is no plausible scenario leading a full-scale conflict within one year.

Why? First and foremost, the price of war has gone up dramatically. The Nobel Peace Prize to end all peace prizes should have been given to Robert Oppenheimer and his fellow architects for the atomic bomb. Secondly, while the price of war soared, its profits declined (now wealth consists mainly of human capital and organizational know-how), and peace became more lucrative. Lastly, a tectonic shift has taken place in global political culture. Many elites in history viewed war as positive good, other viewed it as evil but inevitable. Ours is the first time in history that the world is dominated by a peace-loving elite.

But are we happier? If not, what was the point of developing agriculture, cities, writing, coinage, empires, science and industry? Historian seldom ask such questions. Yet these are the most important questions one can ask of history. If economic growth and self-reliance do not make people happier, what's the benefit of capitalism?

The transition first to agriculture and then to industry has condemned us to living unnatural lives that cannot give full expression to our inherent inclinations and instincts, and therefore cannot satisfy our deepest yearnings.
When evaluating global happiness, it is wrong to count the happiness only of the upper classes, of Europeans or of men. Perhaps it is also wrong to consider only the happiness of humans.

If people are richer and healthier, then they must be also happier. But is that really so obvious? Psychologists and biologists researched about happiness and one interesting conclusion is that money does indeed bring happiness. But only up to a point, and beyond that point it has little significance.

Another interesting finding is that illness decreases happiness in the short term, but is a source of long-term distress only if a person's condition is constantly deteriorating or if the disease involves ongoing and debilitating pain.
Family and community seem to have more impact on our happiness than money and health.

The most important finding is that happiness depends on the correlation between objective conditions and subjective expectations. Prophets, poets and philosophers realised thousands of years ago that being satisfied with what you already have is far more important that getting more of what you want. Still, it's nice when modern research - bolstered by lots of number and charts - reach the same conclusions the ancients did.
Medieval peasants were used to feel and smell long-unlaundered shirt. It's not that they wanted a change of clothes but couldn't get it - they had what they wanted.
If you were an eighteen-year-old youth in a small village 5000 years ago, you'd probably think you were good-looking. But if you are teenager today you are a lot more likely to feel inadequate.

Our subjective well-being is not determined by external parameters, is determined by a complex system of nerves, neurons, synapses and various biochemical substances such as serotonin, dopamine and oxytocin. From these comes lasting happiness, not money, social status, plastic surgery, beautiful houses or powerful positions.
But pleasure doesn't mean happiness. Happiness is not the surplus of pleasant over unpleasant moments. Rather, happiness consists in seeing one's live in its entirety as meaningful and worthwhile.

Humans are the outcome of blind evolutionary processes that operate without goal or purpose. Hence any meaning that people ascribe to their lives is just a delusion. So perhaps happiness is synchronising one's personal delusions of meaning with the prevailing collective delusions. As long as my personal narrative is in the line with the narratives of the people around me, I can convince myself that my life is meaningful, and find happiness in that conviction.
These views share the assumption that happiness is some sort of subjecting feeling, and to judge other people's happiness all we need to do is ask them how they feel.

Buddhism has assigned the question of happiness more importance than perhaps any other human creed. Most people identify happiness with pleasant feelings and suffering with unpleasant feelings. They consequently ascribe immense importance to what they feel, craving to experience more and more pleasures, while avoiding pain.

The real root of suffering is the never-ending and pointless pursuit of ephemeral feelings, which causes us to be in a constant state of tension, restless and dissatisfaction. People are liberated from suffering when understand the impermanent nature of all their feelings, and stop craving them.

In meditation, you closely observe your mind and body, witness the ceaseless arising and passing of all your feelings, and realise how pointless it is to pursue them. When the pursuit stops, the mind becomes very relaxed, clear and satisfied. All kinds of feelings go on arising and passing - joy, anger, boredom, lust - but once you stop craving particular feelings, you can just accept them for what they are. You live in the present moment instead of fantasising about what might have been.

True happiness is independent of our inner feelings. The more significance we give our feelings, the more we crave them, the more we suffer. Buddha's recommendation was to stop not only the pursuit of external achievements, but also the pursuing of inner feelings.

Maybe it isn't so important whether peoples' expectations are fulfilled and whether they enjoy pleasant feelings. The main question is whether people know the truth about themselves. What evidence we have that people today understand this truth any better than ancient foragers or medieval peasants?

Homo sapiens in beginning to break the laws of natural selection, replacing them with laws of intelligent design. Sapiens could use selective breeding, but now scientist are engineering living beings.

Biological engineering is deliberate human intervention on the biological level aimed at modifying an organism's shape, capabilities, needs or desires, in order to realise some preconceived cultural idea.

If genetic engineer can create genius mice, why not genius human? If can create monogamous voles, why not humans hard-wired to remain faithful to their partners? There seems to be no insurmountable technical barrier preventing us from producing superhumans. We might fiddle with Homo sapiens to such an extent that we would no longer be Homo sapiens.

What we should take seriously is the idea that the next stage of history will include not only technological ad organisational transformations, but also fundamental transformations in human consciousness and identity. What do we want to become? This question dwarfs the debates that currently preoccupy us. After all, today's debate between today's religions, ideologies, nations and classes will in all likelihood disappear along with Homo sapiens. An yet, the great debates of history are important because at least the first generation of these gods would be shaped by the cultural ideas of their human designers.

Ask scientists why they study the genome, or try to connect a brain to a computer, or try to create a mind inside a computer. Standard answer: we are doing it to cure diseases and save human lives. We cannot stop science, the only thing we can try to do is to influence the direction scientist are taking.

Did we increase the amount of suffering in the world? Time and again, massive increases in human power did not necessarily improve the well-being of individual Sapiens, and usually caused immense misery to other animals.

We are more powerful than ever before, but have very little idea what to do with that power. Worse still, humans seem to be more irresponsible than ever. Self-made gods with only the laws of physics to keep us company, we are accountable to no one. We are consequently wreaking havoc on our fellow animals and on the surrounding ecosystem, seeking little more than our own comfort and amusement, yet never finding satisfaction. Is there anything more dangerous than dissatisfied and irresponsible gods who don't know what they want?
NICE STORIES
Armstrong and Native American: pag. 318.
How to conquer a native american empire: pag. 328.
Why investing in Netherlands rather than Spain: pag. 356.
