Hyper brief (though the one at the end of the book is written really well, and it comprehend also all execises):
Chapter 1 - Charisma Demystified

The most common charisma myth is that you have to be naturally boisterous or outgoing to be charismatic. It's also a myth that you have to be attractive to be charismatic. That's not true, you don't even have to change your personality to get there.
Three quick tips: lower the intonation of your voice at the end of the sentences, reduce how quickly and how often you nod, pause for two full second before you speak.
Chapter 2 - The Charismatic Behaviors: Presence, Power and Warmth
Charismatic behavior can be broken down into three core elements: presence power and warmth.
Power means being perceived as able to affect the world around us. Warmth is goodwill towards others.
Because we can't consciously control all of our body language, we can't just broadcast charismatic body language at will. Our body language express our mental state whether we like it or not.
Charismatic behavior must originate in your mind. If your internal state is charismatic, then the right body language will flow forth effortlessly.

Knowing your internal world starts with one key insight upon which all charisma is built: your mind can't tell fact from fiction. Because of that, imaginary situations cause your brain to send your body the same commands as it would for a real situation.
Chapter 3 - The Obstacles to Presence, Power and Warmth

Any physical discomfort that affects your visible, external state even slightly may affect how charismatic you are perceived to be. When interacting with someone, assume that he or she will fell that whatever you do relates to him of to her.
The first, and optimal, step is to plan ahead to prevent the discomfort from occurring.
Awareness is the second step in dealing with physical discomfort.
The third step is to take action. If you realize that something has created tension in your face, do something about it.
Mental discomfort affects both how we feel and how we're perceived. It can result from anxiety, dissatisfaction, self-criticism or self-doubt.

The single most effective technique to alleviate the discomfort of uncertainty is the responsibility transfer (p.34). The reason this technique works is that when presented with a scenario, our brain first reaction is to consider it as possible.

The act of comparing and evaluating hinders our ability to be fully present. When you're making comparisons notice it and use responsibility transfer technique to alleviate any internal discomfort it may have caused.
Chapter 4 - Overcoming the Obstacles
Skillfully handling any difficult experience is a three-step process: destigmatize discomfort, neutralize negativity and rewrite reality.

Destigmatize an experience means reducing its power by simply understanding that it's normal, common and nothing to be anxious about or ashamed of. To destigmatize, remind yourself that this internal discomfort, whatever it might be, is a normal part of the human experience and by-product of our brain's survival mechanisms. It helps to think of others who have experienced what you're going through.

Shame is the real killer. Of all emotions that human beings can feel, it is one of the most toxic to health and happiness. If our feelings are common, it comes naturally that we shouldn't be ashamed of them.

The best way to neutralize negativity is to realize that you're thoughts aren't necessarily accurate at all. Our mind's view of reality can be completely distorted, and often that happens because the element that our danger-focused brain deems important are usually the most negative ones.

When your brain spins negative scenarios, remind yourself that you might not getting an accurate perception of reality. Try to neutralize them, not to suppress them. Trying to suppress a self-critical thought only makes it more central to your thinking.

Rewrite the reality when you're felling bad, feeling the wrong way for the moment or just want to overcome on obstacle: What's the situation? Which mental state would be more useful in this situation? Which version of reality would help me get there? Think of that version of reality as if it were true: imagine herbs, tastes, visual images, emotions and other sensations. The more realistic the better. You'll get that state of mind.
The way to stop discomfort is to delve into it using these three techniques.
Stretch your comfort zone (p.64).
Chapter 5 - Creating Charismatic Mental States
There is good evidence that imaging oneself performing an activity activate part of the brain that are use in actually performing the activity.
Before giving a presentation create mental movies, imagining how splendidly the speech is going, seeing and hearing the audience's enthusiastic response.
Before an important meeting, imagine the smiles on other person's faces because they like you, as detailed as possible.
Anytime you feel anxious imagine a twenty second hug. It sends oxytocin through your veins.
To get more warmth you should practice gratitude, goodwill and compassion.
To invoke a sense of gratitude view your life through a third-person lens, writing a narrative about yourself cast in a positive light.

To have more goodwill find three things you like about the person you want to fell goodwill toward. A second way is, in an interaction, imagine him and all those around you, as having invisible angel wings. You could also try, while looking at him, to think "I like you".

Self-confidence is our belief in our ability to do or to learn how to do something. Self-esteem is how much we approve and value ourselves. Self-compassion is how much warmth we can have for ourselves. Self-compassion has three-step process: first, realizing that we're experiencing difficulties; second, responding with kindness and understanding toward ourselves; third, realizing that whatever we're going through is commonly experienced by all human beings.
Try Metta (p.88) to better express gratitude.
You can reverse-engineering many emotions by adopting the corresponding body language.
Chapter 6 - Different Charisma Styles
Focus charisma: cultivate your ability to be present.
Visionary charisma: project complete conviction and confidence in a cause.
Kindness charisma: access warmth through gratitude, goodwill, compassion and self-compassion.
Authority charisma: display signs of status and confidence.
Chapter 7 - Charismatic First Impression
You never get a second chance to make a great first impression. Once we've made a judgement about someone, we spend the rest of our acquaintanceship seeking to prove ourselves correct.

Suggestion for a good first impression: like them, people like that; get dressed in an appropriate way; make a good handshake; break the ice with a compliment and continuing with an open-ended question (like "Where are you from?"); keep the spotlight on them and stay focused on positive subjects.
Exit the conversation offering something of value: an information, a connection, visibility or recognition.
What impact on people isn't the words or content used. Rather, they remember how it felt to be speaking with you.
Chapter 8 - Speaking-and Listening-with Charisma
Do not "let people talk until it's my turn". Good listeners know never, ever interrupt. Great listeners know to let others interrupt them. Mater listeners pause before they answer.
It's critical to make others feel good about themselves, you need to create strong positive associations and avoid creating negative ones.
Don't try to impress people. Let them impress you, and they'll love you for it.
Whenever you can, choose to speak in pictures with metaphors.
Avoid talking about what you avoid the others think.
How to communicate power with voice: the lower, baritone, the voice, the more impact it will have; be sure to get the volume right; convey confidence with a slow, measured tempo with frequent pauses.
To convey warmth smile while talking, even on the phone.
Chapter 9 - Charismatic Body Language
When our verbal and nonverbal signals are in congruence the nonverbal amplifies the verbal. When they are in conflict, we tend to trust the nonverbal one.
The emotional contagion is the process by which the emotions expressed by one individual are caught by another.

Imitating someone's body language through mirroring is an easy way to establish trust and rapport. If their demeanor is angry or defensive, though, mirroring would only escalate the tension. In that case, try breaking them out of that posture.

When someone displays high confidence through their body language, we tend to assume they have something to be confident about: people simply accept what you project. The next time you're in a crowded environment, practice getting people to move side for you.
Try to avoid excessive nodding, excessive verbal reassurance and restlessness or fidgeting.
Chapter 10 - Difficult Situations

Benjamin Franklin's favorite way to win over his political opponents was not to do them favors but rather to ask them favors. Having done him a small favor, the opponent had to either consider himself inconsistent, having done a favor for someone he dislike, or rationalize his action by deciding that he actually rather liked Franklin. Another favor you can ask is opinion, and make sure they remind of any help they've given you in the past.
If you have to deliver a bad news, make it easy for them by having objects close by with which they can play, and thus more quickly feel at ease, while conversing with you.

For delivering criticism you have to: think about your timing and the location, get into the mindset of compassion and empathy, be specific about the point you want to make and depersonalize, pointing out that you're critiquing the behavior, not the person. If it's possible, don't mention their action at all.
When you sense defensiveness, move them back to a more positive state of mind verbally (encouraging positive mental associations) and nonverbally (influence their body language using yours).
Close the conversation talking about next steps, making appreciation and bringing out an idea of a positive future.
If you make a mistake, let them say what they want to say. Be fully present, and try to avoid preparing your response. Show them that you understand and that you make sure it won't happen again.

Be fully present even in a phone call. If necessary, close your eyes. If you want to add warmth smile, they'll recognize even if they don't see you. Do no answer the phone in a warm or friendly manner. Answer crisply and professionally and, only after you hear who is calling, let warmth or even enthusiasm pour forth in your voice.
If you have to write an email, write out the email as you normally would, but before send it, simply cut and paste so that whatever pertains to the other person appears first and most prominently.
Chapter 11 - Presenting with Charisma

To start, know whom exactly you're aiming to persuade. Use stories and choose characters that are similar to the people in the audience, they have a strong impact. The more dramatic, the better. Use metaphors and analogies to capture audience's imagination. Make numbers and statistics personal, meaningful and relatable to the audience.
Use the word "you" as much as possible.
To own the stage and project power: first, be sure to have a wide stance, to be well balanced; second, practice without a podium; third, find the right volume.
To project warmth imagine to have a conversation with only one person that's dear to you. Give one to two seconds of eye contact per person.

Pause, breath, slow down. After delivering a key point or an impactful story, pause for a few seconds to let the audience take it in. Color-code your speech indicate where you have to do one second pause and where you have to do two seconds pause. Underline part that need warmth, where you should smile.
If you make an error, remember that business moguls and entrepreneurs make mistakes purposefully to make themselves more relatable to the audience.
Chapter 12 - Charisma in a Crisis

A crisis situation can make you gain charisma. First, retain at least a certain measure of equanimity. Second, express high expectations, simply assigning to people the labels you want them to live is enough, act like you assume they already are meeting high standards. Third, articulate a vision that must vividly illustrate the difference between the way things are now and the way they could be, point out deficiencies in the status quo, contrast this picture to a glorious future, and show how they intend to get there and ultimately act bold and decisive once you've expressed your vision.
Chapter 13 - The Charismatic Life: Rising to the Challenge
Go around asking everyone their opinion, listen intently and in subsequent conversations refer back to the opinion they've offered.
Accept humanity and show it, so accept vulnerabilities and show them.

paragraphs: The design of everyday things notes
Most important ideas:

Two of the most important characteristics of good design are discoverability and understanding. Discoverability: is possible to even figure out what actions are possible and where and how to perform them? Understanding: What does it all mean? How is the product supposed to be used? What do all the different controls and settings mean?
Type of design:
Industrial design: creating and developing concepts and specifications that optimize products and systems for the mutual benefit of both user and manufacturer.
Interaction design: the focus is on how people interact with technology.
Experience design: the practice of designing with a focus placed on the quality and enjoyment of the total experience.

When people fail to follow bizarre, secret rules, and the machine does the wrong thing, its operators are blamed for not understanding the machine. It is time to cast the blame upon the machines and their design. It is the machine and its design that are at fault. Why this deficiency? Because much of the design is done by engineers who are experts in technology but limited in their understanding of people. Engineers are trained to think logically. As a result, they come to believe that all people must think this way, and they design their machines accordingly.
Human-centered design is a design philosophy. It means starting with a good understanding of people and the needs that the design is intended to meet.
Great designers produce pleasurable experiences.
The term affordance refers to the relationship between a physical object and a person. To be effective, affordances and anti-affordances have to be discoverable, perceivable.
A signifier is a mean of signaling the presence of an affordance. It refers to any mark or sound, any perceivable indicator that communicates appropriate behavior to a person.

Many people find affordances difficult to understand because they are relationships, not properties. Affordanes determine what actions are possible. Signifiers communicate where the action should take place. We need both.
Affordances represent the possibilities in the world for how an agent can interact with something. Signifiers are signals.

Mapping is a technical term, meaning the relationship between the elements of two sets of things. Natural mapping, by which I mean taking advantage of spatial analogies, leads to immediate understanding. Groupings and proximity are important principles from Gestalt psychology that can be used to map controls to function: related controls should be grouped together. Controls should be close to the item being controlled.

Feedback is some way of letting you know that the system is working on your request. It must be immediate: even a delay of tenth of a second can be disconcerting. If the delay is too long, people often give up, going off to do other activities. Poor feedback can be worse than no feedback at all, too much feedback can be even more annoying than too little. Feedback has to be planned, and has to be prioritized.
A conceptual model is an explanation, usually highly simplified, of how something works. It doesn't have to be complete or even accurate as long as it is useful.

The combined information about an object is called the system image. It's what can be perceived from the physical structure that has been built (including documentation, instructions, signifiers, an any information available from websites an help lines).

When people use something, they face two gulfs: the Gulf of Execution, where they try to figure out how it operates, and the Gulf of Evaluation, where they try to figure out what happened. We bridge the Gulf of Execution through the use of signifiers, constraints, mappings, and a conceptual model. We bridge the Gulf of Evaluation through the use of feedback and a conceptual model.

Three stages of execution: plan (the action), specify (an action sequence), and perform (the action sequence). Three stages of evaluation: perceive(the state of the world), interpret(the perception), and compare (the outcome with the goal). The goal (form the goal).

We can do many actions, repeatedly cycling through the stages while being blissfully unaware that we are doing so. It is only when we come across something new or reach some impasse, some problem that disrupts the normal flow of activity, that conscious attention is required.
A positive emotional state is ideal for creative thought. A negative emotional state provide focus.
Three levels of processing:
Visceral: all people have the same.
Behavioral: home of learned skills.
Reflective: home of conscious cognition.

Design must take place at all levels. All three levels of processing work together to determine a person's cognitive and emotional state. High-level reflective cognition can trigger lower- level emotions. Lower-level emotions can trigger higher level reflective cognitions

People experience repeated failure at a task. As a result, they decide that the task cannot be done, at least not by them: they are helpless. The learned helplessness. They're trapped in a self-fulfilling prophecy.
Advices for designers:
Do not blame people when they fail to use your product properly.
Take people's difficulties as a signifiers.
Eliminate all error messages, provide help and guidance.
Make possible to correct problems directly from help and guidance messages.
Assume what people have done is partially correct.
Think positively, for yourself and for the people you interact with.

But in my experience, human error usually is a result of poor design: it should be called system error. Human err continually; it is an intrinsic part of our nature. System design should take this into account.
Anyone using a product should always be able to determine the answer to these questions:
What do I want to accomplish?
What are the alternative action sequences?
What action can I do now?
How do I do it?
What happened?
What does it mean?
Is this okay? Have I accomplished my goal?
A constraint provide physical, logical, semantic, and cultural constraints that guides actions and eases interpretation.
Because much of the knowledge is available in the environment, it is surprising how little we need to learn.
Declarative knowledge, knowledge of, includes the knowledge of fact and rules.
Procedural knowledge, knowledge how, is the knowledge that enables a person to be skilled musician, to return a serve in tennis, or to move the tongue properly.
Psychological research suggests that people maintain only partial descriptions of the things to be remembered.

Constraints simplify memory. Constraint are powerful clues, limiting the set of possible actions. The thoughtful use of constraints in design lets people readily determine the proper course of action, even in novel situation.
Type of constraints:
Physical constraints limit possible operations.
Cultural constraints: each culture has a set of allowable actions for social situations.
Semantic constraints are those that rely upon the meaning of the situation to control the set of possible actions. They rely upon our knowledge of the situation and of the world.
Logical constraints: there is a logical relationship between the spatial or functional layout of components and the things that they affect or are affected by.

Short term memory holds something akin to a pointer to an already encoded item in long-term memory, which means the memory capacity is the number of pointers it can keep. The length or complexity of the item has little impact.

The limits on our short-term memory systems caused by interfering tasks can be mitigated by several techniques. One is through the use of multiple sensory modalities. To maximize efficiency on working memory it is best to present different information over different modalities: sight, sound, touch (haptics), hearing, spatial location, and gestures.

Knowledge in the world acts as its own reminder. It can help us recover structures that we otherwise would forget. Knowledge in the head is efficient: no search and interpretation of the environment is required. The tradeoff is that to use our knowledge in the head, we have to be able to store and retrieve it, which might require considerable amount of learning. Knowledge in the world requires no learning, but can be more difficult to use.
The partnership of technology and people makes us smarter, stronger, and better able to live in the modern world. We have become reliant on the technology and we can no longer function without it.
Constraints that force desired behavior:
Forcing functions are a form of physical constraint: situation in which the actions are constrained so that the failure at one stage prevents the next step from happening.
An interlock forces operations to take place in proper sequence.
A lock-in keeps an operation active, preventing someone from prematurely stopping it.
A lockout prevents someone from entering a pace that is dangerous, or prevents an event from occurring.
When searching for a reason, even after you have found one, don't stop: ask why that was the case. And then ask why again. Keep asking until you have uncovered the true underlying causes.
If the system lets you make the error, it is badly designed. And if the system induces you to make the error, then is really badly designed.
A slip occurs when a person intends to do one action and ends up doing something else. A mistake occurs when the wrong goal is established or the wrong plan is formed.

The only way to reduce the incidence of errors is to admit their existence, to gather together information about them, and thereby to be able to make the appropriate changes to reduce their occurrence.
The design of warning signals is surprisingly complex. They have to e loud or bright enough to be noticed, but not so loud or bright that they become annoying distractions.

It might seem that one way to minimize slips is to ensure that people always pay close, conscious attention to the acts being done. Bad idea. If we had to pay conscious attention to every little thing we did, we would accomplish far less in our lives. Many slips can be minimized by ensuring that the actions and their controls are as dissimilar as possible, or at least, as physically far apart as possible.

In well-designed systems, there can be many equipment failures, many errors, but they will not lead to an accident unless they all line up precisely. This is why the attempt to find "the" cause of an accident is usually doomed to fail.
There are several ways to reduce accidents:
Add more slices of cheese.
Reduce the number of holes (or make the existing holes smaller).
Alert human operators when several holes have lined up.

Resilience engineering, the goal is to design systems, procedures, management, and the training of people so they are able to respond to problems as they arise. You can even deliberately shutting down critical facilities to ensure that the backup systems and redundancies work.
Difficulties arise when we do not think of people and machines as collaborative systems, but assign whatever tasks can be automated to machines and leave the rest to people.

One of rules in consulting is simple: never solve the problem you're asked to solve. Why? Because, invariably, the problem you're asked to solve is not the real, fundamental, root problem. It is usually a symptom. The secret to success is to understand what the real problem is.
The real world is not like the university. In the university, professors make up artificial problems. In real world, the problems do not come in nice, neat packages. They have to be discovered.
Double-Diamond Model of Design: designers expand the scope of the problem, converge upon a single problem statement. They expand the space of possible solutions, converge upon a proposed solution.

Customer research is a tradeoff: deep insights on real needs from a tiny set of people, versus broad, reliable purchasing data from a wide range and large number of people. We need both. The design specifications must include both factors: marketing and design, buying and using.

Requirements made in the abstract are invariably wrong. Requirements produced by asking people what they need are invariably wrong. Requirements are developed by watching people in their natural environment.

How can a designer work across so many different domains? Because the fundamental principles of designing for people are the same across all domains. People are the same, and so the design principles are the same.

Each new edition of a product has invariably more features than the previous one. Featuritis is an insidious disease, difficult to eradicate, impossible to vaccinate against. It is easy for marketing pressures to insist upon the addition of new features, but there is no call to get rid of old, unneeded ones.

Most companies compare features with their competition to determine where they are weak, so they can strengthen those areas. A better strategy is to concentrate on areas where they are strong and to strengthen them even more. Then focus all marketing and advertisements to point out the strong points. This causes the product to stand out from the mindless herd.

A rule of thumb is twenty years from demonstrations in research laboratories to commercial product, and then a decade or two from first commercial release to widespread adoption. Except that actually, most innovations fail completely and never reach the public.

Why "qwerty" keyboard? Because long type arms would often collide and lock together, requiring the typist to separate them manually. To avoid jamming, Sholes arranged the keys and the typebars so that the letters that were frequently typed in sequence did not come from adjacent typebars. Note that popular legend has it that the keys were placed so as to slow down the typing. This is wrong: the goal was to have the mechanical typebars approach one another at large angles, thus minimizing the chance of collision. There is an unconfirmed story that a salesperson rearranged the keyboard to make it possible to type the world typewriter on the second row. Even though jamming isn't a possibility with electronic keyboards and computers and the style of typing has changed, we are committed to this keyboard, stuck with it forever.

Plato tells us that Socrates complained about the impact of books, arguing that reliance on written material would diminish not only memory but the very need to think, to debate, to learn through discussion. Reliance on technology is a benefit to humanity. With technology, the brain gets neither better not worse. Instead, it is the task that changes. Human plus machine is more powerful than either human or machine alone.

Write to manufacturers. Boycott unusable designs. Support good designs by purchasing them, even if it means going out of your way, even if it means spending a bit more. And enjoy yourself. Walk around the world examining the details of design. Learn how to observe. Take pride in the little things that help.

I dram of renaissance of talent, where people are empowered to create, to use their skills and talents. Design is a powerful equalizing tool: all that is needed is observation, creativity, and hard work, anyone can do it. With open-source software, inexpensive open-source 3-D printers, and even open-source education, we can transform the world.
Illuminations:

Once you realize that they don't want the drill, you realize that perhaps they don't really want the hole, either: they want to install their bookshelves. Why not develop methods that don't require holes? Or perhaps books that don't require bookshelves.
Don't criticize unless you can do better.
One way of overcoming the fear of the new is to make it look like the old.
The day a product development start, it is behind schedule and above budget.
We are surrounded with object of desire, not objects of use.
The great Gatsby notes
Things I underlined:
People disappeared, reappeared, made plans to go somewhere, and then lost each other, searched for each other, found each other a few feet away.

The groups change more swiftly, swell with new arrivals, dissolve and form in the same breath; already there are wanderers, confident girls who weave here and there among the stouter and more stable, become for a sharp, joyous moment the centre of a group, and then, excited with triumph, glide on through the sea-change of faces and voices and colour under the constantly changing light.
I slunk off in the direction of the cocktail table - the only place in the garden where a single man could linger without looking purposeless alone.
‘And I like large parties. They’re so intimate. At small parties there isn’t any privacy.'
Everyone suspects himself of at least one of the cardinal virtues, and this is mine: I am one of the few honest people that I have ever known.
’There are only the pursued, the pursuing, the busy and the tired.'
It had occurred to him that the colossal significance of that light had now vanished forever. Now it was again a green light on a dock. His count of enchanted objects had diminished by one.
She vanished into her rich house, init her rich, full life, leaving Gatsby - nothing. He felt married to her, that was all.

They were careless people, Tom and Daisy - they smashed up things and creatures and then retreated back into their memory or their vast carelessness, or whatever it was that kept them together, and let other people clean up the mess they had made...

He had come a long way to this blue lawn, and his dream must have seemed so close that he could hardly fail to grasp it. He did not know that it was already behind him, somewhere back in that vast obscurity beyond the city, where the dark fields of the republic rolled under the night.

Gatsby believed in the green light, the orgiastic future that year by year recedes before us. It eluded us then, but that’s no matter - tomorrow we will run faster, stretch out our arms faster… And one fine morning -
So we beat on, boats against the current, borne back ceaselessly into the past.

paragraphs: The hundred-page machine learning book notes
Suff I underlined (only interesting ones, without mathematics symbols and variables):
“All models are wrong, but some are useful” - George Box
“If I had more time, I would have written a shorter letter.” - Blaise Pascal

In supervised learning, the dataset is the collection of labelled examples. Each of those has a feature vector, made by features, and label, that can be either an element belonging to a finite set of classes, or a real number, or a more complex structure.
The goal of supervised learning algorithm is to use the dataset to produce a model that takes a feature vector as input and outputs information that allows deducing the label for this feature vector.
In unsupervised learning, the data is a collection of unlabelled examples. The goal is to create a model that solve practical problems like clustering, dimensionality reduction or outlier detection.
In semi-supervised learning, the dataset contains both labelled and unlabelled examples.
In reinforcement learning, the machine “lives” in an environment, is capable of perceiving the state, can execute actions that bring different reward. The goal of the algorithm is to learn a policy.
The solution of the problem is called the statistical model, or, simply, the model. The process of building the model is called training.

An hyperparameter is a property of a learning algorithm that influences the way the algorithm works. Those values aren’t learned by the algorithm itself from data. They have to be set by the data analyst before running the algorithm.
When vectors participate in operations on matrices, a vector is by default represented as a matrix with one column.
The expectation of a variable, or expected value is given by the sum over all possible values of that value times the probability of that value.
Classification is a problem of automatically assign a label to an unlabelled example.
Regression is a problem of predicting a real-valued label (often called target) given an unlabelled example.
Model-based learning algorithms create a model that has parameters learned from the training data. Instance-based learning algorithms use the whole dataset as a model.

Linear models rarely overfit. Overfitting is the property of a model such that the model predicts very well labels of the examples used during training but frequently makes error when applied to examples that weren’t seen by the learning algorithm during training.

Why we decided to take squared loss? Because it’s convenient. Closed form solutions to finding an optimum of a function are simple algebraic expression and are often preferable to using complex numerical optimisation methods, such as gradient descent. They also exaggerate the difference between the true target and the predicted one according to the value of this difference.
In logistic regression, we maximise the likelihood of our training set according to the model (maximum likelihood). There is no closed form solution, we must use gradient descent.

A decision tree is an acyclic graph that can be used to make decisions. In each branching node of the graph, a feature is examined. If the value is below a specific threshold, then one branch is followed, otherwise, the other branch is followed. As the leaf node is reached, the decision is made about the class to which the example belongs.
At each step, we find a split that minimises the entropy or we stop at this node (weighted average of entropy in the two branches).

SVM uses kernel functions to efficiently work in higher-dimensional spaces without doing this transformation explicitly. The feature space of RBF (for “radial basis function”) kernel has an infinite number of dimensions.

K-Nearest Neighbours (kNN) keeps all training samples in memory. Once a new example comes in, the algorithms finds the k training examples closest to x and returns the majority label (classification) or the average label (regression).
The closeness of two examples is given by a distance function, that can be: Euclidean distance, cosine similarity, Chebychev distance, Mahalanobis distance, Hamming distance, etc...
Each algorithm consists of three parts:
Loss function
Optimization criterion based on the loss function
Optimization routine leveraging training data to find a solution to the optimisation criterion
Decision tree and kNN were invented experimentally based on intuition and optimisation criteria were developed later to explain why those algorithms work.

Gradient descent is an iterative optimisation algorithm for finding the minimum of a function. Starts at some random point and takes steps proportional to the negative of the gradient of the function at the current point. It proceed in epochs, each of which consists of using the training set entirely.
Minibatch stochastic gradient descent consists of approximating the gradient using smaller batches of the training data.
Other algorithms are Adagrad, Momentum, RMSProp, and Adam.
Scikit-learn is a standard library.

The problem of transforming raw data into a dataset is called feature engineering. Everything measurable can be used as a feature, demands from the data analyst a lot of creativity and domain knowledge.
Informative features are features with high predictive power.
A model has a low bias when it predicts the training data well.
One-hot encoding is the practice of transform categorical features into several binary ones.
You should not transform a categorical feature into a single number if you don’t intend to imply that there is an order among the values.
Binning (or bucketing) is the process of converting a numerical feature into a categorical one.

Normalization is the process of converting an actual range of values which a numerical feature can take into a standard range of values (typically [-1, 1] or [0, 1]). This can increase the speed of learning.
Standardization is the process of rescaling values so that they have mean 0 and standard deviation 1 (standard normal distribution).
Is preferred over normalization if the future can have outliers.
How to deal with missing values:
Remove examples with missing features
Use a learning algorithm that can deal with missing feature values
Use a data imputation technique:
Replace the missing value of a feature by an average value of this feature in the dataset or
Replace the missing value of a feature by a value outside the normal range of values or
Replace the missing value of a feature by a value In the middle of the range or
Use missing value as target for a regression problem or
Add a binary indicator feature for each feature with missing values
Question to ask to choose a machine learning algorithm:
Explainability
In-memory vs. out-of-memory
Number or features and examples
Categorical vs. numerical features
Nonlinearity of the data
Training speed
Prediction speed
Split the data in three distinct sets:
Training set: the biggest one, used to build the model
Validation set: used to choose the learning algorithm and find best values of hyperparameters.
Test set: used to asset model quality before the delivery to the client or putting in production.
If the model makes many mistakes on the training data, we say that the model has a high bias or that the model underfits (model too simple, features not informative enough).

If the model predicts well training data but predicts poorly the validation/test set, we say that the model has high variance or that the model overfits (model too complex, too many features -> try a simpler model, reduce the dimensionality of exaples, add more training data, regularise the model).
Bias-variance tradeoff.
Regularization force the algorithm to build a less complex model (slight increase of bias, big decrease of variance). Examples:
L1 regularization: produce a sparse model, performs feature selection (lasso)
L2 regularization: differentiable, usually better results than L1(ridge)
Dropout (for neural networks)
Batch-normalization (for neural networks)
Data augmentation
Early stopping
Use a baseline to assess model performance.
Confusion matrix summarizes classification model’s performances.
Precision is the ratio of correct positive predictions to the overall number of positive predictions.
Recall is the ratio of correct positive predictions to the overall number of positive examples in the dataset.
For multiclass, first you select a class for which you want to assess these metrics, then you consider all examples of the selected class as positives and all the remaining classes as negatives.
Precision-recall tradeoff.
Accuracy is given by the number of correctly classified examples divided by the total number of classified examples. It’s a useful metric when errors in predicting all classes are equally important.
True positive rate is the ratio of true positive predictions to the overall number of positive examples in the dataset.
False positive rate is the ratio of false positive predictions to the overall number of negative examples in the dataset.
ROC curve: use each discrete value as prediction threshold and predict the labels of the examples and then plot false positive rate on the x and true positive rate on the y.
AUC (Area Under the ROC Curve) is the area under the ROC curve, and the higher the better the classifier.
Hyperparameter tuning:
Grid search
Random search
Bayesian hyperparameter optimization
Gradient-based rechniques
Evolutionary optimisation techniques

Cross-validation: you split your training set into several (typically, five) subsets of the same size (folds). You use the examples in all but one set as training set and the leftover as validation set. You repeat this for all the sets and use the average result as final value.
Then you use the entire training set to train the model with the best hyper parameters found in cross-validation and assess it using the test set.
Fee-forward neural network (FFNN), or Mulitlayer perceptron (MLP).
Fully connected layers.
Without nonlinearities, the FNN would be linear, no matter how many layers it has (linear function of linear functions is also linear).
Usual activation functions are TanH or ReLU.
Deep learning refers to training neural networks with more than two non-output layers.
Exploding gradient and vanishing gradient problems.
We can deal with exploding gradient by using gradient clipping (or L1 and L2 regularization).
We can deal with vanishing gradient by using ReLU, LSTM or skipping connections.
Backpropagation is typically used to update values of parameters.
The layers that are neither input not output are called hidden layers.

Convolutional neural networks (CNN) is a special kind of FNN that significantly reduces the number of parameters in a deep neural network with many units. Thy found applications in image and text processing.
We can split the image into square patches using a moving window approach. We can then train multiple smaller regression models at once, each small regression model receiving a square patch as input.

We use the convolution of matrices. One layer of a CNN consists of multiple convolution filters (each with its own bias parameter). Those are trainable parameter that are optimised using gradient descent with backpropagation.
Stride is the step size of the moving window (bigger side -> smaller output matrix).
Padding is the with of the square of additional cells with which you surround the image before you convolve it with the filter.
Pooling applies a fixed operator (usually max or average) to an input matrix.
Typically we use filter size of 2 or 3, stride 2 and max pooling.

Recurrent neural networks (RNN) are used to label (predict a class for each feature vector in a sequence), classify (predict a class for the entire sequence), or generate (output another sequence relevant to the input) sequences.
It’s used ofter for text processing.
It’s not feed-forward, it contains loops.
Each unit has a real-valued state and receives two inputs: a vector state from the previous layer and a vector of states from this same layer from the previous time step.
Uses backpropagation through time. It’s hard to handle long-term dependencies, so usually we use gated RNN, like long short-term memory (LSTM) or gated recurrent unit (GRU).
Other extensions are bi-directional RNNs, RNNs with attention and sequence-to-sequences RNN models.
Softmax function is a generalisation of the sigmoid function to multidimensional outputs.
Kernel regression.

If you have multiclass problem but a binary classification algorithm you should use one versus rest: transform a multiclass problem into C binary classification problems and build C binary classifiers, then pick the prediction that is the most certain.
One-class classification can be used if we have examples of one class and we want to train a model that would distinguish examples of this class from everything else.
Can be used for outlier detection, anomaly detection, and novelty detection
Most widely used algorithms are one-class Gaussian, one-class k-means, one-class kNN, and one-class SVM.
Multi-label classification is used when more than one label is appropriate to describe an example.
We can train several binary classifier, but we have to define the threshold.
Neural networks can naturally train multi-label classification models by using the binary cross-entropy cost function (each unit at the output has the sigmoid activation function).
We can also create a new fake class for each combination of the two original classes (only if not too many classes).

Ensemble learning is a learn paradigm that focuses on training a large number of low-accuracy models (weak learners) and then combining the predictions to create a high-accuracy meta-model (two methods are boosting and bagging).

Boosting consists of using the original training data and iteratively creating multiple models by using a weak learner that try to “fix” the errors which previous model made (example: Gradient Boosting).
Bagging consists of creating many “copies” of the training data and then applying the weak learner to each copy to obtain multiple weak models (example: Random Forest)

Random Forest is bagging algorithm where a certain number of “copies” are sampled with replacement from the training set and then train decision trees with those (reducing the variance of the final model). At each split of the decision tree, a random subset of the features are inspected.
The most important hyperparameters to tune are number of trees (same as number of training set “copies”), and the size of the random subset of the feature to consider at each split.

Gradient Boosting start with a constant model, then the error of this model (residuals) are used as labels to train a new decision tree model. This proceeds until the maximum number of trees are trained.

The resulting model takes into account sum of the result from the constant model, and the results of all the trees times a coefficient (for this reason is called gradient, you’re not adding results of the model, but a fraction of those, so you’re moving like gradient descent).
The most important hyperparameters to tune are number of trees, the learning rate, and the depth of the trees.
Boosting tend to overfit.

Gradient Boosting for classification is similar, but you replace the label, instead of with the error, with the partial derivative of the loss, and then you look for the best update step to optimise that single decision tree.
Sequence labelling is the problem of automatically assign a label to each element of a sequence.
Conditional Random Fields (CRF) is an alternative to RNNs (less performing). It’s a generalisation of logistic regression to sequences.
A task of sequence labelling might be named entity extraction.
Sequence-to-sequence learning have and encoder and a decoder.
The encoder accepts sequential input and generate embedding, a numerical representation of the meaning of the input.
The decoder takes an embedding as input and it’s able to generate a sequence of outputs.
Attention combine some info from the encoder and the current state of the decoder.

Active learning consists of start learning with relatively few labeled examples, and a large number of unlabelled ones, and then label only those examples that contribute the most to the model quality.

Semi-supervised learning we have labeled a small fraction of the dataset; most of the remaining examples are unlabelled. Our goal is to leverage a large number of unlabelled examples to improve the model performance without asking for additional labeled examples.
An autoencoder is a feed-forward neural network with an encoder-decoder architecture. It is trained to reconstruct its input. It has a bottleneck layer in the middle.
A denoising autoencoder adds some random perturbation to the features of the input.

A ladder network is the same of an autoencoder, but the loss function penalises the difference between the outputs of the two layers. Not just the input is corrupted with noise, but also the output of each layer.

One-shot learning typically is used to face recognition (are two pictures the same person?). Siamese neural network is an example of that. You input one image at a time, and then you have a triplet loss function.
Zero-shot learning we want to predict labels for which we didn’t have training data. We can use word embeddings to do that.
In case of imbalanced datasets you can:
Oversample or under-sample
Create synthetic examples (SMOTE or ADASYN)
Tree-based algorithms often perform well on imbalanced datasets.
To combine models:
Averaging or majority vote
Stacking, build a meta-model that takes the output of base models as input (ideally with different features or different nature)
In neural network, if you input is image you have to resize all images so that they have the same size. Pixels are usually first standardised and normalised to the range [0, 1].
Texts have to be tokenised by using word embeddings.

Time spent trying to replicate results from a recent scientific paper may not be worth it. This time could better be spent on building the solution around a less modern but stable model and getting more training data.

Start with one or two layers, train the model and see if it fits the training data well. If not, gradually increase the size of each layer and the number of layer until the model perfectly fits the training data. After this, if the model doesn’t perform well on validation data, add regularization to the model. If, after this, the model doesn’t fit the training data anymore, slightly increase the size of the network. Continue iteratively until the model fits both training and validation data well enough according to your metric.
Neural network specific regularization techniques:
Dropout: each time you run a training example through the network, you temporarily exclude at random some units from the computation.
Early stopping: save the preliminary model after every epoch and assess the performance of that model on the validation set. Stop the training when the performances on validation set get worse.
Batch normalisation: standardise the output of each layer before the units of the subsequent layer receive them as input. It’s always a good idea to try to use batch normalisation.
Data augmentation
To deal with multimodal input you can vectorise each input and concatenate two feature vectors together as input.
To deal with multimodal output you can create a subnetwork that would work as an encoder and then you add two other subnetworks on top of that.

Transfer learning is where neural networks have a unique advantage over shallow models. In transfer learning, you pick an existing model train on some dataset, and you adapt this model to predict examples from another dataset.
You remove the last one or several layers from the first model and replace them with new layers. You freeze the parameters of the first model and train the other on your problem.
Big O notation is used to classify algorithms according to how their running time or space requirements grows as the input size grows.
How to improve code efficiency:
Avoid using loops whenever possible
If the order of elements in a collection doesn’t matter, use set instead of list
Using libraries is generally most reliable - you should only write your own code if you are a researcher or is truly required
If you need to iterate over a vast collection of elements, use generators that create a function that returns one element at a time
Use cProfile package in Python to find inefficiencies in your code
Use multiprocessing package to run computations in parallel
Use PyPy, Numba or similar tools to compile your Python code
In unsupervised learning there is no solid reference point to judge its quality.
Mean integrated squared error (MISE)
Clustering is a problem of learning to assign labels to examples by leveraging an unlabeled dataset.

K-means is an iterative clustering algorithms where we have k centroids, we assign each example to the closest centroid, we calculate as new centroid as the average of centroid in that cluster and repeat.

In DBSCAN, you pick an example, then you put all the examples close enough to it in the same cluster, and then you repeat for each element in the formed cluster. HDBSCAN is same with one hyper parameter less.
One way of determining a reasonable number of clusters is based on the concept of prediction strength (pag.112).
Alternatively, you can use the elbow method or the average silhouette method.
Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) is a soft clustering algorithm (pag. 115).
Spectral clustering and hierarchical clustering are other clustering algorithms.
Dimensionality reduction: most common use is for visualisation.
Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is based on principal components, vectors that define a new coordinate system in which the first axis goes in the direction of the highest variance in the data.

t-SNE and UMAP are designed specifically for visualisation purposes. They uses a similarity metric between two examples to create fuzzy sets and then, with gradient descent try to minimise the change in fuzzy sets in lower space (p.119).
Metric learning.
Learning to Rank:
Pointwise: Given the input, regression to find the best results (not always good, cause results considered in isolation)
Pairwise: Given two results, find which one is better for the input (better than pairwise, but similar problems)

Learning to Recommend:

Content-based filtering: learning what user like based on the properties of the content they consume. Problem is filter bubble, suggesting only content that looks similar to what user already consumed.
Collaborative filtering: giving recommendation to one user depending on what other user consume or rate.
Hybrid: combining recommendation obtained by content-based and collaborative models.
Factorization machine (pag. 126).
Denoising Autoencoder: in the input, set randomly to 0 some of the movies that a user liked and try to reproduce the original set of movies. Then to get new movies, pass the actual list.

Gaussian processes (GP) is a supervised learning method that competes with kernel regression.
Generalized Linear Model (GLM).

Probabilistic Graphical Models (PGMs), also known as Bayesian networks, belief networks and probabilistic independence netwo. A graph is a structure consisting of a collection of nodes and edges that each join a part of nodes. Each node in PGM represents some random variable, and edges represent the conditional dependence of one random variable on another random variable.
Markov Chain Monte Carlo is used if you want to sample from a very complex distribution defined by the dependency graph.

Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) are a class of neural networks used in unsupervised learning, and are implemented as a system of two neural networks contesting with each other in a zero-sum game setting.

Genetic Algorithms (GA) are a numerical optimisation technique used to optimise undifferentiable optimisation function. They use concepts from evolutionary biology to search for a global optimum of an optimisation problem by mimicking evolutionary biological processes (using concepts as “selection”, “crossover”, and “mutation”).

The lean startup notes
Introduction

The stories in the magazines are lies: hard work and perseverance don't lead to success. The boring stuff are the ones that matters the most. Startup success can be engineered by following the right process.
A startup is a human institution designed to create new products and services under conditions of extreme uncertainty.
Vision
Chapter 1 - Start
Building a startup is an exercise in institution building; thus, it necessarily involves management.

The Lean Startup asks people to start measuring their productivity differently. Because startups often accidentally build something nobody wants, it doesn't matter much if they do it on time and on budget. The goal of a startup is to figure out the right thing to build - the ting customers want and will pay for - as quickly as possible.

Unfortunately, too many startup business plans look more like they are planning to launch a rocket ship that drive a car. They prescribe the steps to take and the result to expect in excruciating detail, and as in planning to launch a rocket, they are set up in such a way that even tiny errors in assumptions can lead to catastrophic outcomes. Instead of making complex plans that are based on a lot of assumptions, you can make constant adjustments with a steering wheel called the Build-Measure-Learn feedback loop. Through this process of steering, we can learn when and if it's time to make a sharp turn called a pivot or whether we should persevere along out current path.
Products change constantly through the process of optimization, called tuning the engine. Less frequently, the strategy may have to change, performing a pivot. The overarching vision rarely changes.
Chapter 2 - Define
The Lean Startup is a set of practices for helping entrepreneurs increase their odds of building a successful startup.

The Innovator's Dilemma: companies are very good at creating incremental improvements to existing products and serving existing customers, called sustaining innovation, but struggle to create breakthrough new products, that can create new sustainable sources of growth, called disruptive innovation.
Innovation is a bottoms-up, decentralized, and unpredictable thing, but it doesn't mean it cannot be managed.
Chapter 3 - Learn
What if we found ourselves building something that nobody wanted? In that case what did matter if we did it on time and on budget?

We must learn the truth about which elements of our strategy are working to realize our vision and which are just crazy. we must learn what customers really want, not what they say they want or what we think they should want. We must discover whether we are on a path that will lead to growing a sustainable business.

Learning is the essential unit of progress for startups. The effort that is not absolutely necessary for learning what customer want can be eliminated. This is called validated learning because it is always demonstrated by positive improvements in the startup's core metrics.

You should use experiments to systematically figure out the right thing to build. Each bit of knowledge you'll gather will suggest new experiments to run, which will move your metrics closer and closer to your goal.
It is often easier to raise money or acquire other resources when you have zero revenue, zero customers, and zero traction that when you have a small amount.
The question is not "Can this product be built?". The more pertinent questions are "Should this product be built?" and "Can we build a sustainable business around this set of products and services?".
Chapter 4 - Experiment
Begin with a clear hypothesis that makes predictions about what is suppose to happen. Then test those predictions empirically.

If you rely on market research or conduct a survey, you can ask what customers think they want. Building a product, instead, even if a simple one, you can: have more accurate data about customer demand, interact with real customer and learn about their needs and be surprised when customer behave in unexpected way.

The first step is to break down the grand vision into its component parts. The value hypothesis test whether a product or service really delivers value to customers once they are using it. The growth hypothesis tests how new customers will discover a product or service.

In the Lean Startup model, an experiment is more than just a theoretical inquiry, it is also a first product. Other than useful for experimentation, in this way by the time that product is ready to be distributed widely, it will already have established customers.
Success is not delivering a feature, success is learning how to solve a customer's problem.
Steer

A startup is a catalyst that transforms ideas into products. As customers interact with those products, they generate feedback and data. We need to focus our energies on minimizing the total time through this feedback loop.

The two most important assumptions are the value hypothesis and the growth hypothesis. The first step is to enter the Build phase as quickly as possible with a minimum viable product (MVP). Then you should proceed with innovation accounting: a quantitative approach that allow us to see whether our engine-tuning efforts are bearing fruits It also allows us to create learning milestones.
Chapter 5 - Leap
Startups need to conduct experiments that help determine what techniques will work in their unique circumstances.

Basic assumptions are called leaps of faith, because the success of the entire venture rests on them. If they are true, tremendous opportunity awaits. If they are false, the startup risks total failure.

What differentiate the success stories from failures is that the successful entrepreneurs had the foresight, the ability, and the tools to discover which parts of their plans were working brilliantly and which were misguided, and adapt their strategies accordingly.
Design a customer archetype, a brief document that seeks to humanize the proposed target customer. It is an hypothesis like others, not a fact.

Some dangers: just-do-it entrepreneurs are impatient and don't want to spend time analyzing the strategy, the problem is that rarely users know what they want. Other entrepreneurs fall victim of analysis paralysis, endlessly refining their plans.
Chapter 6 - Test
In an MVP, when in doubt, simplify. The lesson of the MVP is that any additional work beyond what is required to start learning is waste, no matter ow important it might have seemed at the time.
A good strategy is to focus on scaling something that was working rather than trying to invent something that might work in the future.

One of the most vexing aspects of the minimum viable product is the challenge it poses to traditional notions of quality. The best professionals and craftspersons alike aspire to build quality products; it is a point of pride. But if we do not know who the customer is, we don't know what quality is. Just remove any feature, process, or effort that does not contribute directly to the learning you seek.

The most common objection to building an MVP is fear of competitors staling a startup's ideas. But part of the special challenge of being a startup is the near impossibility pf having your idea, company, or product noticed by anyone.
A head start is rarely large enough to matter, and time spent in stealth mode - away from customers - is unlikely to provide a head start. The only way to win is to learn faster than anyone else.
Commit to iteration: no matter what comes of testing the MVP, you will not give up hope.
Chapter 7 - Measure

At the beginning a startup is little more than a model on a piece of paper. A startup's job is to: rigorously measure where it is right now and devise experiments to learn how to move the real numbers closer to the ideal reflected in the business plan.

Innovation accounting enables startups to prove objectively that they are learning how to grow a sustainable business. It works in three steps: first, use a minimum viable product to establish real data on where the company is right now. Second, tune the engine from the baseline toward the ideal. Third choose if pivot or persevere.

If the company is making good progress toward the ideal, it makes sense to continua. If not, the product strategy needs a serious change. When a company pivots, it starts the process all over again, reestablishing a new baseline and then tuning the engine from there. The sign of a successful pivot is that these engine-tuning activities are more productive after the pivot than before.
A smoke test measures only one thing: whether customers are interested in trying a product.
When one is choosing among the many assumptions in a business plan, it makes sense to test the riskiest assumptions first.

Once the baseline has been established, the startup can work toward the second learning milestone: tuning the engine. Every product development, marketing, or other initiative that a startup undertakes should be targeted at improving one of the drivers of its growth model. You should set out with a clear baseline metric, a hypothesis about what will improve that metric, and a set of experiments designed to test that hypothesis.

If you're not moving the drivers of your business model, you're not making progress. That's a sure sign that's time to pivot. The sign of a successful pivot are that the new experiments you run are overall more productive than the experiments you were running before.
The rhythm is: establish the baseline, tune the engine, make a decision to pivot or persevere.

IF you're building the wrong thing, optimizing the product or its marketing will not yield significant results. A startup has to measure progress against a high bar: evidence that a sustainable business can be built around its product or services. That's a standard that can be assessed only if a startup has made clear, tangible predictions ahead of time.

Agile practice: a series of sprints, or one-month iteration cycle. For each sprint, prioritize the work to be done that month by writing a series of user stories, a description of the feature from the point of view of the customer. But also ask yourself if the prioritization you've decided actually make sense.

Instead of looking at gross metrics, look at cohort-based metric. Instead of looking for cause-effect relationship after the fact, launch each new feature as a true split-test (A/B testing) experiment.

Stories can be cataloged as being in one of four states of development: in the product backlog, actively being built, done, or in the process of being validated. Validated is defined as "knowing whether the story was a good idea to have been done in the first place". This validation usually would come in the form of a split test. In that way the team working in the system begin to measure its productivity according to validated learning, not in terms of the production of features.
A metric should be: actionable, or demonstrate a clear cause effect; accessible, as simple as possible so that everyone understands it; auditable, or such in a way that data is credible to employees.
Chapter 8 - Pivot (or Persevere)
Are you making sufficient progress to believe that your original strategic hypothesis is correct, or do you need to make a major change?
The goal of creating learning milestones is not to make the decision easy; it is to make sure that there is relevant data in the room when it comes time to decide.

A company that has achieved enough success to stay alive but has not met the expectations of investors and founder is stuck in the land of living dead. The way to avoid that is to pivot, even if the more money, time and energy has been sunk to an idea, the harder it is.
A pivot requires that you keep one foot rooted in what you've learned so far, while making a fundamental change in strategy in order to seek even greater validated learning.

The true measure of runaway is how many pivots a startup has left. But pivot is hard: first, vanity metrics can allow you to form false conclusions and live in your own reality; when you have an unclear hypothesis, it's almost impossible to experience complete failure, you more often end up in the land of living dead; third, you may be afraid, acknowledging failure can lead to dangerously low morale.
The decreasing effectiveness of product experiments and the general feeling that product development should be more productive is the sign of the fact that a pivot is necessary.
A pivot is a special kind of change designed to test a new fundamental hypothesis about the product, business model, and engine of growth. The types of pivot are:
Zoom-in Pivot: what previously was considered a single feature in a product becomes the whole product.
Zoom-out Pivot: what was considered the whole product becomes a single feature of a much larger product.
Customer Segment Pivot: the product hypothesis is partially confirmed, solving the right problem, but for a different customer than originally anticipated.
Platform Pivot: to change from application to platform and vice versa.
Business Architecture Pivot: to switch from high margin, low volume to low margin, high volume.
Value Capture Pivot: change monetization or revenue models.
Engine of Growth Pivot: change engine of growth (viral, sticky and paid growth).
Channel Pivot: change the mechanism by which a company delivers its product to customers.
Technology Pivot: when a company discovers a way to achieve the same solution by using a completely different technology.
A pivot is nothing more than a new strategic hypothesis that will require a new minimum viable product to test.
Chapter 9 - Batch

The small-batch approach produce a finished product every few seconds, whereas the large-batch approach must deliver all the products at once, at the end. Working in small batches will lead to identify quality problems much sooner.

Whenever a feature is ready to be tested with customers, you should immediately release a new version of the product, which would go live on your website for a relatively small number of people. In that way you can immediately assess the impact of your work, evaluate its effects on customers and decide what to do next. (The order of magnitude suggested is 50 changes per day).
And for hardware startups? You can transform them into software, or product as soon a design is ready with 3D printing.
Another problem with large batches is that they tend to grow over time in a large-batch death spiral.

You should figure out what you need to learn and then work backwards to see what product will work as an experiment to get that learning. Thus, is not the customer, but rather your hypothesis about the customer, that pulls work from product development and other functions.

Although lean production techniques are powerful, they are only a manifestation of a high-functioning organization that is committed to achieving maximum performance by employing the right measures of progress over the long term.
Chapter 10 - Grow

Sustainable growth is characterized by one simple rule: new customers come from the actions of past customers. There are four ways to reach it: word of mouth, as side effect of product usage, through funded advertising, through repeat purchase or use.

The churn rate is defined as the fraction of customers in any period who fail to remain engaged with the company's product. If the rate of new customer acquisition exceeds the churn rate, the product will grow.

The viral engine is when growth happens automatically as side effect of customers using a product. The viral engine is powered by a feedback loop that can be quantified. It is called the viral loop, and its speed is determined by the viral coefficient. It measures how many new customers will use a product as consequence of each new customer who signs up. That should be the variable you should focus the most.
The ability to grow in the long term by using paid engine requires a differentiated ability to monetize a certain set of customers.
You should focus only on one engine of growth.
Chapter 11 - Adapt
An adaptive organization is one that automatically adjusts its process and performance to current conditions.

To accelerate, Lean Startups need a process that provides a natural feedback loop. When you're going too fast, you cause more problems. Adaptive processes force you to slow down and invest in preventing the kinds of problems that are currently wasting time. To go to the root of the problem, use the rule of Five Whys: ask the question "Why?" five times to understand what has happened.
In that way, those who seems individual mistakes can be tracked back to deeper problems.

Suggestion for correct Five Whys: make sure that everyone affected by the problem is in the room discussing; start with narrowly targeted class of symptoms; the problems analyzed should be new; at the beginning of each session, explain the process.
Good idea: ask new engineers to make a change to the production environment the first day.
Golden rules: be tolerant of all mistakes the first time, never allow the same mistake to be made twice.
Chapter 12 - Innovate

Startup teams require three structural attributes: scarce but secure resource, independent authority to develop the business, and personal stake in the outcome. the last one is achieved through stock options or other form of equity ownership.

When you'll have a big company and an innovation team, then it will be important to think about how to protect the parent organization, how to hold entrepreneurial managers accountable, and how to reintegrate an innovation back into the parent organization if successful.
In this situation you should create an innovation sandbox:
Any team can create a true split-test experiment that affects only the sandboxed parts of the product or service or only certain customer segment or territories.
One ram must see the whole experiment through from end to end.
No experiment can run longer than a specified amount of time (few weeks for simple feature, longer for more disruptive innovation).
No experiment can affect more than a specified number of customers.
Every experiment has to be evaluated on the basis on a single standard report of five to ten actionable metrics.
Every team that works inside the sandbox and every product that is built must use the same metrics to evaluate success.
Abort if something catastrophic happens.
There are four major kinds of work that companies must manage:
as an internal startup grows, it should tackle the challenge of scale.
as new mainstream customers are acquired and new markets are conquered, the product becomes part of the public face of the company.
once the market for the new product is well established, procedures become more routine.
at this point, you'll arrive in the domain of outsourcing, automation and cost reduction.

The problem for startups is that employees often follows the products they develop as they move from phase to phase. As a result, strong creative managers wind up getting stuck working on the growth and optimization of products rather than creating new ones.

The way out this dilemma is to manage the four kinds of work differently, allowing strong cross-functional teams to develop around each area. When products move from phase to phase, they are handed off between teams.
Chapter 13 - Epilogue: Waste Not

In our times, out productive capacity exceeds our ability to know what to build. What we are wasting comes not from the inefficient organization of work but rather from working on the wrong things-and on an industrial scale.
By focusing on functional efficiency, we lose sight of the real goal of innovation: to learn what is currently unknown.

Meditation is science, the systematic process of training the mind. A regular sitting practice has been shown to enhance concentration, lower blood pressure, and improve sleep. Meditators develop valuable insights into their personality, behaviors, and relationship. They have greater awareness and sensitivity to others. They have increased emotional stability when confronting the inevitable stresses of life. Meditation skills give rise to unique mental states characterized by physical comfort and pleasure, joy and happiness, deep satisfaction and profound inner peace .Yet,these are only incidental benefits. The higher goal is awakening, a complete and lasting freedom from suffering, unaffected by aging, disease, or circumstances.Through awakening we can develop an intuitive understanding of the true nature of reality.

Conscious experience takes two different forms, attention and peripheral awareness. Whenever we focus our attention on something, it dominates our conscious experience. At the same time, however, we can be more generally aware of things in the background. Those are two ways of "knowing" the world. In meditation, we work with both attention and peripheral awareness to cultivate stable attention and mindfulness.

Stable attention is the ability to intentionally direct and sustain the focus of attention, as well as to control the scope of attention. Attention moves spontaneously in three ways: scanning, getting captured, and alternating.
The scope of attention is how wide or narrow you want your focus to be.

Mindfulness is the optimal interaction between attention and peripheral awareness, which requires increasing overall conscious power of the mind. Mindfulness allows us to recognize options, choose responses, and take control of our lives. It gives us the power to become the person we want to be.

Attention analyzes our experience, peripheral awareness provides the context. When one or the other doesn't do its job, we respond to situations less effectively. Peripheral awareness takes care of many things without invoking attention. Attention usually involves a strong concern for "self", peripheral awareness takes things more objectively "as they are". Attention and peripheral awareness can be either extrospective or introspective.
Metacognitive introspecting awareness is the condition in which the mind "stands back" to observe its own state and activities (introspective peripheral awareness on the overall state of mind).

Consciousness has a limited power source. Both attention and awareness draw energy from this shared source. The goal is to increase the total power of consciousness available for both attention and awareness.
Six point preparation: motivation, goals, expectation, diligence, distractions, posture.

A meditation object is something you intentionally choose to be the focus of your attention during meditation. Although you can choose just about anything, the breath is idea for cultivating attention and mindfulness. That means focusing on the sensations produced by breathing, not some visualization or idea of the breath going in and out.
Four step transition: focus on the present (here and now), focus on bodily sensations, focus on bodily sensations related to the breath, focus on sensation of the breath at the nose.
Consider the beginning of the out-breath as the start of the cycle. Start counting. Once you've succeeded in counting to ten, keep observing the breath sensations, but stop counting.
Make the time to meditate. Make your practice a priority. I don't know anyone who has established a meditation practice in his or her "spare" time.
When you discover you can't control your unruly mind, you may begin doubting your abilities. One solution: trust and perseverance.
You should meditate at the same time everyday. The easiest way is to get up a little earlier.
One daily forty-five-minute sit as a minimum is recommended.

Any comfortable position works for meditation, as long as it's not so comfy that you fall asleep. Remain as still as you can during sitting meditation, despite any discomfort. You simply can't overcome all physical discomfort by adjusting your posture.
We need to approach the practice in a relaxed manner, free from judgement and expectations.
Five hindrances:
Worldly Desire ("I need that/I want that"). Meditation gives you direct, insight into the many ways that desire leas to pain and anxiety.
Aversion ("I hate that/I don't want this"). There is little if any room for negativity in a mind filled with bliss.
Laziness and Lethargy ("I'm too tired/It's too late"). The antidote is just do it.
Agitation due to Worry and Remorse ("What if/I'm ashamed"). The best antidote is the practice of inner purification which result in good behavior.
Doubt ("I can't meditate"). Reexamine your motivation.
